And {{c|1105|Clammon}} was the son of {{c|868|Bivos}}; when
His work begun, he set to populate,
And he began his work, and once again,
The seas with forms that were so very great.

{{c|1105|Clammon}} begat four sons, and these were they:
{{c|1106|Cockle}}, who would explore, so strong and true;
{{c|1107|Myidus}}, who would come to find his way;
{{c|1108|Adapa}}, who would follow and pursue

His dreams; and {{c|95|Venus}} was a daughter fair,
Throughout the waters of the ocean blue,
Who danced on through the sea without a care,
Where all her children grew, and as they grew.

{{c|1106|Cockle}} then had a son, and when the work
Of his was done, he came to be the grand
And great ancestor, and he did not shirk,
Of giant clams, the largest in the land,

That they will dwarf all others who have tried
And through the trials of the sea's long test
To make it through the waters deep and wide,
With their enormity, which beats the rest.

{{c|1107|Myidus}} bore three sons: when day begun
{{c|1109|Zebra}} came, and {{c|1110|Softshell}}, so gentle, mild,
And {{c|1111|Teredo}}, the wayward, wilder one,
Who was the problem, and the problem child,

Known as the sea termite, the one who brought
The shipwrights fright, by boring through the wood,
The planks of ships, the fright the sailors fought,
The ships on which the sailors always stood.

The {{c|1109|Zebra}} {{c|1112|Mussels}} spread, and spread out far
By currents through the waters of the sea,
Wherever they were led, as mussels are,
In their community and company.

The {{c|1110|Softshell}} clams would go away and hide,
Where they could safely live, and safely dwell,
Beneath the sand, beneath the sandy tide,
Within their soft and softened, gentle shell.

{{c|1108|Adapa}} begat two sons: one was named
{{c|1113|Geodoros}}, and he was true and fine,
{{c|922|Ancestor}} of the race, and he was famed,
Sire of {{c|1114|Geoducks}}, in their design,

Beneath the sandy shore, where, as they keep
Their hiding spots, each one a hidden one,
They would for evermore dig burrows deep,
While all the surface waters sweep and run,

Connected by their lots, and by their own,
Throughout the ocean land, and all its floor,
To life beneath the sand, where they have grown
From shore to sandy shore, and evermore.

And {{c|1115|Razoron}} in his own turn became
The {{c|922|Ancestor}} of {{c|1116|Razor}} Shells, so sharp,
The source of all their name and of their fame,
That they will cut, as cuts the ocean's harp,

Through sand, where they would go away and hide
Whenever danger came, until they could,
When danger's time had passed, and it had died,
Emerge into the place where once they stood.

{{c|95|Venus}} became the mother, in her days,
Of clams, the {{c|95|Venus}} clams, so very fair,
Like none before them in their many ways,
That beautify the waters everywhere

That they will make their soft and gentle home;
Among her children, all of them so bright,
Beneath the white and drifting ocean foam,
She bore one special one, one special sight:

{{c|1117|Corbiculacea}}, she who one great day
Would pass from salt to waters fresh, refresh
Her line, and make her passage, make her way,
And give her lineage a newer flesh,

As ancestress, so faithful and so true,
Of the freshwater clams, which, far and wide,
Now live in all the rivers, as they do,
With all the current as their only guide.

{{c|691|Brachios}} begat three sons, for history,
Three houses that he would establish, make,
For all of time, and for its mystery,
And build for all the brachiopods' sake.

{{c|1118|Lingulus}}, the tailed one, was he who stood
To be conservative, and to be so,
And never failed, as no one ever could,
In all he'd ever give, and all bestow,

To innovation's call, and all its claim,
The {{c|1119|Archconservative}}, and so supreme,
Within the house so grand, of all who came
Of {{c|691|Brachios}}' command, and his regime.

{{c|1118|Lingulus}}, son of him who had the same
Name as his own, in all his life's mission,
Would trim, in all his days and all his aim,
Nothing at all from his own tradition.

He kept and he maintained the ancient way
Unto its fullest measure and its height,
The way of the old and the olden day,
Like some most sacred treasure, kept in sight,

That never must be changed, or rearranged,
But kept just as it was, and as it stood,
Or ever be disturbed, or be estranged,
According to the laws, both old and good,

Of his forefathers, who had tried, and who
To keep the ancient way, the way of old,
Had striven on and tried their whole life through
Until their dying day, as they were told.

{{c|1120|Discinidus}}, his son, when he begun
His life, was smaller, and was more inclined
To be the clam's, more like that other one,
Than brachiopods' design, so refined,

That had been very fine for all those years,
And had been built to last, to always stay,
For millions of years past, through all their peers,
And last for evermore, and not decay.

{{c|1118|Lingulus}}, serpentine, so long and lean,
Showed forth his noble line, that stretched along
Through time so long, as it was always seen,
Like some eternal and unchanging song,

That never changed its tune, and never strayed,
And on through all the night, the whole night through,
From morning until noon, from light to shade,
Until the morning light and morning's dew.

{{c|1121|Calciatus}} begat two sons, and the first,
{{c|1122|Craniidus}}, would never, evermore,
Possess a tail, but, at the very worst,
Live on without the sign his fathers bore,

Without that sign of his ancestral line;
And {{c|1123|Articulus}} built his children true,
But cheaply, and who built them by design
Without a thought of what tradition knew:

He built them without thought of all that came,
Without a single thought for all its arts,
Of what tradition brought, and of its name,
And lacking parts that touched their parents' hearts.

Without their anuses, the young ones lay,
Like blobs, and could not swim; but when they heard,
As they would float on all throughout the day,
Metamorphosis' call, the waited word,

And in an instant's time, a single breath,
From blob to something more, and something new,
Would change their paradigm, not unto death,
Upon the ocean floor, so deep and blue.

The sons of {{c|1123|Articulus}}, too, were then
So numerous, they were a mighty force,
And formidable, just like mighty men,
Against the {{c|1124|Bivalve}}'s course, the bivalve's course

Of conquest through the waters of the seas,
And take whatever they were apt to take,
Where they would do whatever they would please,
For their own kingdom's sake, and for its sake.

But as two great hosts, two rival powers,
The {{c|870|Bivalves}} and their boasts, and old and gray
The {{c|854|Brachiopods}}, through all of the hours,
Whose stories have been told until this day,

For ages without end, fought on, and none,
To come between them and to end their war,
Could find a friend to mediate, not one,
From every mountain peak to every shore,

A new threat came to light, a threat more dire,
More fearsome than the dark and open grave,
And terrible than night, more fierce than fire,
More deadly than the cold and breaking wave

That crashes on the rocks with all its weight,
And blocks all progress, greater than the mind
Could imagine, and seals all of life's fate;
And few of any of the living kind

Could ever comprehend the scope and size
Of what would come, and, coming in its wake,
Would end all hope for life beneath the skies,
And stop all future birth for ages' sake.

From {{c|868|Bivos}}' innovation came, in turn,
This radiation, forms in every hue,
Both strong and true, as all the seas would learn,
That filled and crowded all the ocean blue.

From {{c|691|Brachios}}' old way, which held its ground,
Through eons without change, came forms that spread,
And lasted day by day, the eons round,
Throughout the range of every ocean bed,

Of all the ocean's vast and wide expanse,
Where old will meet with new in war and strife
In evolution's slow and ancient dance,
Throughout the whole and all the course of life.

The war between the two would come to see,
Through all the trials of that ancient time,
Which vision would come through, and which would be
The one to earn the victor's crown and rhyme.

Would innovation's art, the new and bold,
Prove stronger in the end, when time would come,
Or would tradition's faithful heart of old,
When it would send its judgment on the sum

Of all of them, on each and every one,
In this most ancient war, in this long fight,
Who answered battle's call when war begun,
From mountain peak to shore, by day and night?

The {{c|870|Bivalves}}, with their new {{c|1125|Forms}}, which were made
Through struggle and through pain, and through their strife,
And tried and tested true, and not afraid,
Sought evolutionary gain for life.

The {{c|854|Brachiopods}} held fast, held on tight
To wisdom of the past, which in the years
Gone by had served their ancestors, its light
Through time's great tests and spurs, and all its fears.

And both the strategies had worth and weight
Upon this ancient earth, where, old and new,
Life has to find its way, in its estate,
Through each and every day, and make it through,

In challenge and in change, in sun and storm,
Where only those, of all, live and endure
Throughout all evolution's range and form,
Who keep their hope alive, and keep it sure.

In every oyster's pearl, so smooth and white,
Through all the waters of the open sea,
And every scallop's swirl, so swift and light,
In every clam's own spree and jubilee

Of filter-feeding, quiet, clean, and pure,
In every form that knows its given part,
Its own appointed place, and will be sure
In evolution's race and in its art,

The legacy lives on, and it remains
Of this most ancient war, which went its way
From dusk until the dawn, through all the plains
Of ocean, mountain, shore, by night and day,

Between the old and new, the old and young,
Between the tried and true, and, as it calls,
The innovation's call, the songs unsung,
That beckon one and all beyond their walls

To risk what they have known, and what they kept,
For something promised by the hope that still,
Though yet unshown to them, while others slept,
Helps all of life to cope with good and ill,

With changes yet to come, when wars will cease,
And peace at last will reign over them all,
When all the wars are done, and there is peace,
The ones who heard and answered life's great call.

The great {{c|1126|Spiralian}} war, and all its strife,
Shows how life finds its way and makes its own,
From mountain peak to shore, how all of life,
Through each and every day, through flesh and bone,

Of struggle between those who make their choice
And choose the safety of the past, its kin,
And those who choose, and each with its own voice,
The future's die, now cast and thrown therein,

Into the deep unknown, the unknown deep,
Where new forms, all alone, through long and dark,
Throughout the night, their constant vigil keep,
Until the morning light will light its mark

And show what time has brought to all the ones
Who never fought; but those who fought so hard,
The fighting ones, the daughters and the sons,
Have their own tale to tell, their own regard,

Of courage in the face of all that came
In evolution's race, where all of these,
The winners and the losers in its game,
Are both faith's choosers, choosing as they please,

Who all believed in their own way, and stood,
Through this eternal and this endless strife,
Through each and every day, as best they could,
That shapes and that defines the whole of life.

But as the new threat rose up, vast and high,
Beyond what each could know, or comprehend,
Or then imagine, underneath the sky,
The war of mice and men would meet its end

And pale beside the force, the greater might
That changed life's very course, and brought the old
And ancient age to end, and brought the night,
An age that none could mend, nor yet could hold.

The greatest war would fade, and pass away
Before the challenges, so very vast,
That time had made and brought forth on that day,
That nothing from the past, so long and vast,

In memory, prepared them for the thing
That waited at the door, the end, close by,
Of their complacent world, which it would bring,
Where banners once unfurled against the sky

In triumph would be folded, taken down
Forever; and the world, about to change,
The world as it then stood, both field and town,
Would change beyond all good, beyond its range.


# Chapter 47: The Cephalopod Rise

This is the story that is told of old:
The {{c|1127|Cephalopods}}, who were very great
(Of ones both new and old, the brave, the bold),
{{c|1128|Arcane}} ones, whose own destiny and fate

Would overthrow the might, and overthrow
{{c|959|Leviathan}}'s own sight, with wisdom deep,
And rule with wisdom in the depths below,
Where all the ancient secrets lie asleep.

The sons of {{c|878|Cephalopus}} all would grow
So great that, in their time, the other kind,
The sons of {{c|879|Scaphopus}}, as all men know,
Not quite so prosperous, were left behind,

And they would fade from memory and lore,
And few of those who hear the ocean's call,
Throughout all history for evermore,
Have ever heard of them, or know at all.

{{c|879|Scaphopus}}' degenerate sons, the ones
Who'd never come to know, in any way,
Once their lives had begun, as humble ones,
The heights their cousins show, and showed that day.

{{c|878|Cephalopus}} begat {{c|1129|Plectron}}, and so
There came from him a noble, wondrous line,
As it was then begat, as all men know,
With all intelligence that is divine.

{{c|1129|Plectron}} begat the son whom all would call
{{c|1130|Ellesmer}}, begun in wisdom's old lore,
The deepest and the oldest lore of all,
From mountain peak to every distant shore.

{{c|1131|Ellesmere}} went deeper, going down below,
Than any secret keeper who had gone
Before him in his time, where none would go,
Down far beneath the brine, and on and on,

Where all the mysteries lay deep and hid
(Above them, where the surface waves are curled)
From all the things the light of daylight did
To lighten and illuminate the world.

{{c|1130|Ellesmer}} begat two sons, who were these:
First {{c|1132|Endos}}, tried and true; then, who would fly
And fly to heaven's height, upon the seas,
And {{c|1133|Actinos}}, the bright one, to the sky.

{{c|1132|Endos}} bore many sons, and when begun
Their work, they moved on slowly through the sea,
And when the work of theirs at last was done,
With great and stately and slow dignity.

The greatest one among them, and of all,
Was {{c|1134|Cameroceras}} {{c|1135|Magnus}}, the great,
Of those who ever answered wisdom's call,
Known as {{c|1136|Cameromagne}}, the potentate,

Whose name through all the ages, as of old,
Over {{c|959|Leviathan}} and his great reign
Rings out with victory, both brave and bold,
And all of his dominion's plans, made vain.

{{c|1136|Cameromagne}} would overthrow the might
Of those who'd ruled the seas through many years,
The sons of old {{c|959|Leviathan}}, by right,
With imperial song, through all the spheres.

{{c|1137|Endoceras}}, his son, when he was grown,
He grew nine thousand {{c|1138|Millimeters}} long;
When all his growth was done, his size was shown,
And so he grew to be both long and strong.

And twenty cubits long he measured, free
From end to end, complete in every part,
From front to back, and he was long to see;
No foe could compete with him or his art.

He dwarfed {{c|959|Leviathan}} {{c|1139|Fourfold}}; his reign,
An age in which the sea was made to be
Ruled by cephalopods on ocean's plain,
Began, by their own law and their decree.

{{c|1133|Actinos}}, by his air, which he contained,
So heavenly and fair, had power there
Within his shell, the air that he retained,
A power that sustained him in the air,

That kept up his ability to rise
Up to the stars, and then to go below,
Descending to the earth from starry skies,
As suited to his end, both high and low.

{{c|1133|Actinos}} begat two sons: one of them
Was {{c|1141|Tarphy}}, who was very young and wild;
{{c|1140|Orthosceros}}, so true, a noble stem,
Was evolution's other favored child.

{{c|1141|Tarphy}} lived very fast in his own youth,
And while his time would last, he coiled it round,
His shell, and coiled it round, and in his youth
A hundred times, and found, and so he found

Great joy in swimming very wild and free,
A hunter, and the hunt was his career
Throughout the waters of the open sea;
But then old age drew near, his path grew clear.

He then uncoiled his shell, and came to rest
Upon the earth below, and there he'd stay,
And settled where he'd dwell, as he thought best,
Where wisdom's waters flow and make their way.

And in his old age he bore children, more,
Who did the very same as he had done,
And countless more of them than were before:
Youth's glory and its fame for every one,

In bounty of the heights, the highest heights,
For those who soar, and those who climb and climb,
Where all of heaven's glory, shining, lights
Their way; and age, where depths will store, in time,

Their safety and their peace, where all things cease,
And wisdom finds its home, its resting-place,
Where all the struggles end in their release,
Where all the wise will roam, in wisdom's grace.

{{c|1141|Tarphy}} begat two sons: and {{c|1142|Oncos}} came
When day begun; and next, to live and thrive,
Came {{c|1143|Barrandeos}}, strong, of noble name,
To live his whole life long, and stay alive.

{{c|1142|Oncos}} lived out his life without much joy,
He, coiled but simple, went through all his days
Without much strife, and nothing to annoy,
And lived quite peacefully in all his ways.

{{c|1142|Oncos}} bore many sons, and when begun
Their lives, among them there came one to see,
Named {{c|1144|Rutos}}, he who was the chosen one,
Great wonders through, and see them, as would be.

{{c|1144|Rutos}} then bore a son, and gave the name
Of {{c|1145|Nautilus}}, begun in wisdom's art,
In wisdom of the deep, in wisdom's flame,
That ancestors would keep within the heart.

The sons of {{c|1145|Nautilus}} live on today,
So glorious, unchanged, and still not stirred,
And just the same as long ago, the way
They were when time was but a blur, and blurred,

In days of {{c|1144|Rutos}}, old, so long ago,
{{c|1136|Cameromagne}}, who conquered every wave
And all the seas, the bold, as we all know,
With all of their strategies, wise and grave.

{{c|1140|Orthosceros}} begat two sons: the one
Was {{c|1146|Ascos}}, who would come to know, in truth,
How graciousness could grow, when all was done;
The other, {{c|1147|Bacchus}}, small, from his first youth,

Would make his vision true through numbers vast,
Through numbers vast and wide on every side,
So many that they filled the seas at last,
So vast that they could never be denied.

{{c|1146|Ascos}} lived out his youth, and in those days
He had a shell, so clumsy and so slow,
That spoke no word of truth of grace or praise,
Unable to bestow, and to bestow

Upon his movements any {{c|1148|Grace}}; and he,
Who swam not with elegance and romance,
Was not one of the many who were free
In ocean's great and very wide expanse.

And so he broke it off, his heavy shell,
To serve his greater need, and see it through,
And many came to scoff at him as well
At such a drastic deed, so strange and new.

But in adulthood he, when he was grown,
Above all others bright, and very bright,
Was graceful as could be, as he was shown,
In beauty and in sight, and in delight.

His sons would carry on this, and they kept
The bliss that comes from sacrifice, its price,
Tradition's bliss, for which they never slept:
The giving up the shell for something nice,

The grace that can't be bought by anyone,
But sought, and won, through willingness to break
And shatter, and it only so is won,
What others never would, or could, forsake.

And their life cycle shows how wisdom grows,
As we can see: from clumsy youth they start,
And so begin, and so, as each one knows,
They enter in, and play their graceful part

When their adulthood comes, and they are grown,
In grace beyond compare, and fair and free,
And each at last will thrive, and make its own,
That fills the water fair, and all the sea.

But {{c|1147|Bacchus}} was so small, and to the eye,
{{c|1149|Insignificant}} he seemed, weak and slight,
Of each and one and all who passed him by,
With nothing much to seek, and little might.

But he bore children, and his children, who,
A million sons and daughters, as he willed,
Would make his vision true, and see it through,
They filled the salty waters, and they filled.

And soon the world was full of all of these,
His progeny, in every living space,
In every place, and filled up all the seas,
In all the ocean's vast and wide embrace.

And what seemed insignificant then grew,
Through all the power of increase, which spread,
To be the most significant, it's true,
And never seemed to cease, but forged ahead.

From small beginnings, then, a multitude
Of fame came forth, and, as he longed, it spread:
A great and fast-increasing, filling brood
That filled the world, as {{c|1147|Bacchus}} wished and said,

To populate the sea, from shore to shore,
Until there was no place in all the brine,
With all his progeny, still more and more,
That didn't show his trace and bear his sign.

The cephalopods have shown, from the start,
And from intelligence, from depth of thought,
The seeds of wisdom grow in mind and heart,
And rule with providence, as wisdom taught,

Over the ancient sea, where once alone,
In every place, {{c|959|Leviathan}}'s decree
Had held power supreme upon the throne,
In every ocean's dream, in every sea.

But wisdom overthrew the order old,
And, in its place, arose to take their stand,
{{c|1150|Lords}} of the sea, the new ones, and the bold,
To challenge all their foes on every hand,

With an intelligence so keen and bright,
And with the power to ascend and climb,
And grace beyond all sense, beyond all sight,
From the beginning to the end of time

Of all the ocean's vast and wide domain,
With wisdom as the crown upon their head,
Where they would hold their throne, and always reign,
And grace as their renown where they were led.

From the might of {{c|1136|Cameromagne}}, who bore
The ancient fight, and won it, and who stood
And came before {{c|959|Leviathan}}'s own door
And won the right to rule as rulers should

With wise authority, and to remain
The masters, on to {{c|1145|Nautilus}}, who'll see
And show the ocean's whole and wide domain,
How ancient wisdom flows, and still flows free,

Through generations long, from age to age,
Of those who keep the way, the ancient line,
In never-ending song from page to page,
From night into the day, as stars that shine,

Cephalopods remind us that the mind,
Though it will often start quite small, will heed,
If it is wise, and of the wisest kind,
And answer wisdom's call, and so succeed,

To grow beyond all measure, and to know
The greatest of all treasures of the mind:
The power to transcend, and further go
Past what the others comprehend and find,

Through an intelligence that is divine,
In forms both strange and new, and strange to see,
That makes all wisdom shine with clearer shine,
Yet beautiful and true, as they will be.

In every octopus, with arms that reach,
And every squid, so glorious, that goes
And jets with grace, and passes each by each,
Through waters deep and blue, where current flows,

In every nautilus that keeps the shell,
The spiral, with its chamber and its coil,
So glorious, that will its story tell,
Its ancient twisting spell, and all its toil,

Of how the wise can keep, and store, and hold
What time has buried deep, while what is new
Will change what has to change, both new and old,
To grow, and to expand their range anew,

The legacy lives on, and will not fade,
From dusk until the dawn, of those who knew
To overthrow the old, and, unafraid,
To take the old order, and make it new,

Not through destruction's might, nor by the force
Of arms, but wisdom's sight, which sees and knows
What must remain, and in its gentle course
What only brings us pain and woe, and goes.

The cephalopods' way lives on, and stays
In every graceful move that they will make,
Lives on until this day, through all our days,
And every way they prove, for wisdom's sake,

That an intelligence, when it's combined
With grace, can conquer any foe, can fight
With heart and sense, and win, with heart and mind,
And help all wisdom grow in all its light

From small to great and vast, from seed to tree,
Until at last the wise inherit all,
And, long and last, the heirs of those will be
Who answer wisdom's call, and hear its call.

From {{c|1130|Ellesmer}}'s deep dive beneath the brine,
While finding something new, a newer shore,
To keep the past alive, and keep its line,
In wisdom's vast review and wisdom's store,

The cephalopods teach us to believe
That heights within our reach, if we rely
On willingness, are what we can achieve,
The willingness within us all to try

To grow beyond the small, and the confined,
To be more than we seem, and more than known,
And answer wisdom's call with heart and mind,
In evolution's dream, and on its throne.

Their arcane wisdom shows us how, in truth,
Intelligence grows true, not by the blade,
Nor by the force of might, in age and youth,
But through the inner sight that wisdom made

That sees what others miss; and they who look
Will find in this the power, close at hand,
To pass all limits, as within a book,
Extend the boundaries, and to expand

The boundaries of what can be, and see
What may be possible for those who reach,
The wise, and all the wise, and all the free,
When they believe, and wisdom comes to teach,

When they believe in wisdom's might to bring,
Through patience and through grace, through gentle art,
Their dreams to come about in everything,
In evolution's race, with all their heart.

The sons of {{c|878|Cephalopus}} will remain
So glorious, because they chose, and then
They chose the way of wisdom, free of stain,
And chose it every day, and chose again,

And let intelligence become their shield,
Against all those who'd try to make it end,
And be their own defense, and never yield,
To make their wisdom die, or make it bend.

And in this they succeeded, where the rest
Had never heeded, never once obeyed
The call to grow, nor ever once addressed
The limits that are spawned by the afraid,

By those who cannot see what it can give,
To those who dare to dive, and to go deep,
What wisdom's gift can be to those who live,
Into the deep, and still alive to keep,

In waters where the wise, beneath the sea,
Can see with clearer eyes, and clearly find
The truth that sets them free, and lets them be
The rulers of the sea, of every kind.


# Chapter 48: The Ordovician Extinction

As the {{c|1151|Leviathans}}' long reign began
To turn, the sons of {{c|1153|Stomatos}}, below,
Beneath the {{c|1152|Krakens}}' new and newer plan,
Began their glorious increase, and so

Began their vast {{c|1154|Multiplication}}, spread
Upon the earth at last, from eve to morn;
And to them, on the earth where they were led,
The daughters who were fair were also born.

From all {{c|1155|Laurentia}}'s shore, and to the lore
Of {{c|1156|Baltica}}, its might, and on and on,
Of old {{c|476|Siberia}}, and furthermore,
To {{c|1157|Avalonia}}, where they all had gone,

And even to the cold and frigid lands
The sons of {{c|1153|Stomatos}} would go, and spread
Upon {{c|1158|Gondwana}}'s far-off, icy strands,
In numbers, glorious, where they were led.

To each son there would fall a star; and well,
From evening on until the very morn,
The wishes made upon a star would tell
Of grandsons, yes, a thousand grandsons born.

The sons of {{c|1153|Stomatos}} would build and raise,
Of {{c|1159|Carbon}}, bodies, and great tombs as grand,
So glorious, so great in all their ways,
As mausoleums' rooms, across the land,

All made of coal, so black and deep, which keeps
Their ancestors asleep; and from the air
They took the {{c|1159|Carbon}}, down where each one sleeps,
And left, in every place and everywhere,

{{c|1160|Dioxide}} in the sky, while, from on high,
Her cloak, as all the ancient stories show,
Away from {{c|202|Terra}} would then come to fly,
And she grew very cold, so long ago.

She grew so frigid, and she gave no cheer,
Unwelcoming, and with a colder face,
No longer warm, no longer drawing near
To those who loved her soft and warm embrace.

Her ice caps grew so very far and wide,
And rose to answer winter's bitter call;
Her seas began to shrink away and hide
Behind the great and frozen icy wall.

And soon {{c|1158|Gondwana}} would become the same,
A wasteland that was white and stark and bare,
As nothing but the ice, and ice's claim,
Where none could make their mark, or could live there.

But to the sons of {{c|1153|Stomatos}} it meant
More: a glorious {{c|1161|Land}} where they could spread
Their realm, where they could settle as they went,
Out far and wide and high and overhead.

The {{c|1162|King}}, {{c|1163|Hirnan}} the great, became the one,
The potentate, who joined in all the earth
The sons of {{c|1153|Stomatos}}, each single son,
In conquest, and he lived where there was mirth,

In joy, and he was happy and content
Within {{c|1164|Holonia}}'s fair province, where,
{{c|1157|Avalonia}}'s land, his days were spent;
He made his home, and kept his dwelling there.

And {{c|1163|Hirnan}} built with might, and he would raise
A billion dikes upright, as he had willed,
And levies strong and tall, in all his days,
His cities over all, and he would build

Across the landscape, far and wide and grand.
The habitats that were within the seas
He then destroyed with pride, by his own hand,
And would not spare a single one of these,

And would not spare a single living space
For any race that might compete or vie
With him, nor any other living race,
For resources, so dim, that ran so dry.

And so the countless hosts and countless might
Of trilobites began to fade and fall
And die away, like ghosts into the night,
Their lands seized every day, and seized them all,

Seized by the sons of {{c|1163|Hirnan}}, who would fight;
Their empire grew by {{c|1165|Conquest}} and war,
And they would never rest, but day and night
They pressed their foes to flight, and pressed them more.

And in the last effort that they would make,
A million trilobites, a frantic throng,
First prayed, and then, for their own living's sake,
Invaded, and they smashed their way along

Through every dike that {{c|1163|Hirnan}}'s folk had made,
And every wall and levy they would build
To keep them from the land, and had arrayed,
The land they'd built with their own hands, and willed.

But alas, it was all in vain; the plan,
The trilobites' campaign, would end in death,
In suffocation, right as it began,
Frustration and despair, and loss of breath.

Not one of all the trilobites would reach
The land, however clever was their plan,
Or strong their will or might; the air, to each,
Was death, by day and night, since time began,

To those who were to live within the sea,
And could not breathe the air, the air and sky
That filled the atmosphere, and could not be
Adapted to the air, that left them dry.

And {{c|1163|Hirnan}} bore two sons, and {{c|1006|Moses}} came,
The first, when day begun; and then, the strong,
{{c|1166|Osiris}}, second, of a noble name,
And he would live on through his whole life long.

{{c|1006|Moses}} became the father of the moss,
Of mosses, who would rather live their days,
Their simple, humble lives, without a loss,
Where small beauty can thrive, in quiet ways.

{{c|1166|Osiris}} bore two more: and one was named
{{c|1167|Polysporos}}, explorer; and the grass
Is like {{c|1168|Anthoceros}}, the other, famed
For peace, whose peaceful days would come to pass.

{{c|1168|Anthoceros}} became, in time, the one
Who fathered hornworts, found most everywhere
In every place, and found beneath the sun,
Who grow so very green, with gentle care.

{{c|1167|Polysporos}} became the father of
The ferns, of flowers bright, and of the trees,
Of great fame, and of all, below, above,
That reach up for the height above the seas.

The sons of {{c|691|Brachios}} had struggled, and
Were not so glorious as long before,
In ages long ago, within the land,
In all the ages and their ancient lore.

The sons of {{c|1118|Lingulus}} would die, and die
In numbers greater than had died before,
In all that had been known beneath the sky;
Their glory, overthrown, was here no more.

And never once again, try as they may,
Their power in the sea, their former might,
Would they {{c|1169|Regain}}, their golden day and sway,
And their great dynasty, and its delight.

But as the rule of {{c|1163|Hirnan}} came to be,
The sons of {{c|439|Metazo}} began once more,
Oppression's tool, and tyranny's decree,
To grow again, as they had grown before.

Alas, the sons of {{c|1163|Hirnan}} did not cease,
Nor stop their plan at that, but carried on
And never made their peace, nor sought release,
Through every hour, until the night was gone,

Their conquest of the world, which gave them mirth:
To see all life bow down and bend the knee
Before their thorny crown on all the earth,
To them, from land to land, from sea to sea.

The {{c|1170|Glomerings}} would mine the rocks, and mine,
And for the fertilizer's sake would break
With care, and with a purpose and design,
The stone, and do whatever it would take

To manufacture phosphorus by tons;
They poured it out in floods, and spread it round,
And when the work was done, the busy ones,
Throughout the world, on every field and ground.

Some of it went upon the crops they grew,
But most went to the rivers, to the sea,
And flowing onward, flowing onward through,
It stayed, and there it would forever be

A poison in the water, which no blade
Could slaughter, and no aid could ever go
And take it out, nor could it be unmade,
Wherever all the waters came to flow.

In all the rivers a thick scum would grow;
The sun was blocked, and life beneath the pall
Was shocked, and oceans, dark and blue, would know
Their blue no more, and stunned were one and all

By this catastrophe, which stretched and ran
Across the wide world, the world entire,
From sea to sea, as only ruin can,
As if it were some dark, unholy fire.

The rotting seaweed choked the water, and,
Throughout the night and day, from week to week,
It smoked with death on every sea and strand,
With death and with decay, and with its reek.

And soon it was impossible to breathe;
The {{c|1171|Smell}} of death would fill up all the air,
So terrible, and in that air would seethe
The poison that was spread through everywhere,

Made life a living hell, where none could stay
In comfort or in peace, unless they'd find
(Where none could ever dwell by night or day)
Release, and leave the misery behind,

In death's cold arms, and in their welcome hold,
Which kept them from the harms the world would spread,
That poisoned world, its harms both new and old,
Where death's flag was unfurled above the dead.

The seas turned lifeless, and the seas lay dead,
And over them there spread the tyranny
Of those who would not deem, as it was spread,
Nor dream, nor would suppose, that it could be

That life had any right at all to stay
And live within their sight, or dare to stand
Against their conquest every single day;
For they would have no rival in the land.

The entire ocean, all of it, fell,
In ruin and in great devastation,
Under the might of {{c|1163|Hirnan}}'s deadly spell
Of death, and ruin spread to each nation

Beneath the sea, which once had been so free,
A home to creatures great and small, to all
Of those who lived and filled the open sea,
Who heard and who had answered life's sweet call.

The mighty houses, once the great delight
Of the great {{c|959|Leviathan}}, and the sign
Of {{c|126|Kraken}}'s dynasty, his royal might,
Were wiped from history, and every line.

From off the earth they passed, and in the end
Their glory could not last; for, far and wide,
It could not stand, nor ever could defend
Itself against the poison's spreading tide,

The waters that they loved, and where they went,
Through every day, through every passing hour,
And where they always moved, and where they spent
Their days in majesty and in power.

Among the trilobites, great houses' fate
Was sealed by poison; {{c|771|Agnos}}, in his turn,
Fell, and the poison would not once abate,
And {{c|776|Ptychos}} told no more, for all to learn;

And {{c|1172|Asaphos}}, so mighty and so strong
In days before, was broken by the sea,
And crippled was he all his whole life long,
As all of them were crippled, and would be.

And never once again would they attain
Their golden day, the glory of the time,
The glory of the old, the ancient reign
Of {{c|954|Ordovician}} rhyme, and of its prime.

And so the golden age came to an end;
The {{c|954|Ordovician}} time was past, and passed;
It closed its final page, which none could mend,
Beyond its living prime, and could not last.

The sons of {{c|1173|Silur}} came to conquer, and,
Upon the ashes of the past, they made
Their claim, and came upon them, came to stand,
To build their future, not to fall or fade.

The {{c|1174|Silurian}} age would rise in turn,
To start anew, from all survivors knew,
Beneath the different skies, where life would learn
Of how to carry on, and see it through,

When all their hope seemed gone, and death held sway,
When all of life had nearly come to cease,
And claimed, in its destructive way, the day,
Till life found once again its way to peace.

From the choice of {{c|1153|Stomatos}}' sons, who chose,
Instead of harmony, and took their stand,
Let conquest be their voice, with all its blows,
Against life's symphony throughout the land,

Came lessons that are written very deep
Of what the world becomes, and how it goes,
Down in the rocks below, where fossils sleep,
When greed its power sums, and when it grows

Into a force so strong that right will fail
To win against the wrong, and life will pay,
And pay it all, the price, and wrong prevail,
For others' avarice, in every way.

The trilobites' last stand against the hand
Of {{c|1163|Hirnan}}, in the face of the disgrace
Of him who seized their waters and their land,
Shows courage hopelessness could not erase,

But it shows also what the cost will be
When battles have been lost, and lost, not long
Before, not by the weak, as here we see,
But by those who are fated to belong

To elements in which they cannot live,
Where others will not grant them any space,
Nor any mercy, and will never give
Them room, nor any other living race.

The ice age that began, and grew, and spread
From {{c|1153|Stomatos}}' great plan, which would just take,
And never give, as some have done and said,
Shows how some choose to live for their own sake:

By taking all they can, and all they may,
And never caring what their actions bring,
Without a care or plan for any day,
To me and you, and every living thing

Who cannot give {{c|1175|Resistance}} to the greed,
To all who suffer and who cannot fight,
That plants destruction's seed in every deed,
And spreads its ruin over all in sight.

The phosphorus that ran in streams and flowed
Into the rivers, choking, now shows how,
As life within the sea was choked and slowed,
We too can come to be, and even now,

{{c|1176|Destroyers}} without thought, who do not see
What all our actions brought to those who share,
As we must share, and what the cost will be,
The water and the air, and everywhere.

The golden age that passed has come to show
That nothing good can last when some destroy,
That nothing long can live and long can grow,
When some will ruin, rather than enjoy

The beauty that is shared, the beauty known
To all who ever cared, in all its forms,
To all who've come to love it, and have grown,
Through calm and through the wild and raging storms.

But from the ashes, new hope comes to rise
Beneath the sun, where those who paid it, too,
And learned the cost, beneath the newer skies,
Of all that had been lost, and lived it through,

Can build a better way for all to go,
Where harmony, and never selfish greed,
For life's eternal day, where it can grow,
{{c|1177|Plants}} every living thing and every seed.

The {{c|1174|Silurian}} dawn, which came at last,
Would bring new hope to those who had to face
The old death, which was gone, and it was past,
Destruction's throes in that most bitter place,

And lived to tell the tale, and tell it true,
Of how they would not fail, though suffering long,
But, through the grief and pain, would come right through
To build life up again, and build it strong.

From {{c|1163|Hirnan}}'s tyranny, and from its blight,
The wheel of time turns on, as it will turn,
To {{c|1173|Silur}}'s dynasty, and its new light,
From dusk until the dawn, for us to learn,

With lessons that are written clear and true,
To hear what history will say and tell,
For all who have an ear, both old and new,
About our living days, and what befell:

That greed destroys all life, and leaves behind
Eternal strife and grief in living things,
But those who choose to share will surely find
Life ready everywhere, with all it brings,

Ready to start again, and so to win
At last, because of love; and from above,
From heaven high, the love that is within
Is blessed, the blessing that is given love,

With power to restore, and to repair,
And make the world anew, as love will do,
Whatever had been lost, with love and care,
For me and you today, and see it through.

The golden age may end, and pass away,
But life will always mend, the whole way through,
What greed has torn apart, from day to day,
With love's eternal heart, which beats anew

In every soul that plays a caring role,
In life's eternal song, the song that rings,
And helps to make the broken living whole,
And makes the weak grow strong in living things.

From {{c|954|Ordovician}} glory, and its might,
The earth keeps turning on, and turning round,
To {{c|1174|Silurian}} story, and its light,
From dusk until the dawn, on every ground,

With life that will not die, but lives, and stays,
And always finds a way, through every night,
Beneath the starry sky through all its days,
To live another day and see the light,

Despite what greed may do to me and you,
And all the harm and ruin it may bring
To all who call earth home and roam it through,
To every creature and to everything.

The sons of {{c|1153|Stomatos}} may think that they
Are glorious, and mighty in the land,
But life will always fight, and every day
Will for its own eternal right still stand,

To fill the world with sight of beauty's face,
Where love has found a way, and made it through,
Of grace in every living, breathing place,
To live another day, and to renew,

Despite destruction's call, which, loud and long,
Will sound, and sound again, through every age,
And threaten one and all, both weak and strong,
On every land and sea, on every page.

The golden age returns, and once more turns,
To plant a better seed in greed's own place,
{{c|1178|Whenever}} anyone among us learns
To choose love over greed for every race,

For future generations, yet to be,
Of life upon the earth, who celebrate,
Across all nations, over land and sea,
The worth of love, and love's own high estate,

Above all else that's known by hearts that grew
And came to see that sharing is the way,
That sharing's way is good, and that is true,
And brings its gladness into every day,

While greed brings only pain, and only woe,
To all who choose to live and choose to take,
And falls like acid rain on those below,
Who never learn to give, for giving's sake.

The {{c|954|Ordovician}} end, the age's close,
Reminds us, with our heart and with our mind,
To be the friend of life, as wisdom knows,
In every form, of every living kind,

So golden ages may return, and stay
Another time, when, in the bitter fight,
Love wins, another, and a brighter day,
Against the dark, the cold, the endless night

Of greed that tries to kill all life, and tries,
But fails, for love's own power, every hour,
Will not let greed {{c|1179|Succeed}} beneath the skies,
And, stronger still, it blooms like a flower,

In hearts that choose to care, and choose to give,
That grows beneath the sun, and will not cease,
For life that's everywhere, and all that live,
Until all time is done, and all is peace.


# Chapter 49: The Terrestrial Colonization

While sons of {{c|542|Cambrius}} would flourish well
Within the seas, the sons, upon the plain,
Of {{c|545|Symbio-Mygus}}, in field and dell,
With daughters of {{c|1180|Charina-Plantus}}, twain,

Pushed out their frontiers, pushing far and wide;
But soon enough, before long, they would face,
Across the world and all the world's divide,
{{c|1181|Competition}} in their own dwelling place.

For {{c|752|Euthy}}, she who was a daughter brave
Of {{c|748|Mandibulus}}, who lived for her brood,
Who always gave her all, her young to save,
Was being chased among the waves, pursued

Throughout the waters by her mortal foe,
{{c|1182|Anomalocaris}}, who gave his chase
And would no mercy to her ever show
Across the wide and the watery space.

Her precious eggs would need her care and aid,
Protection; so she did what she must do:
Her trust in {{c|936|Hausa}}, everywhere she strayed,
She placed, and so it was that she went through.

She jumped up through the shimmering blue sky,
Up to the heavens, shining bright above,
Up rocks that reached so very far and high,
Protecting all the ones that she would love.

And so it was she burst out from the sea,
The first of all to make that mighty leap,
And came upon the land, so wide and free,
Out from the waters, dark and very deep.

Upon the ground she fell, and lay, and there,
Within that air so thin and very strange,
She suffocated in the open air,
Throughout that foreign and that unknown range.

But she and her own husband, who was true,
Protected all the eggs, and would defend
Their legacy, because the two then knew
The eggs must live, and live until the end.

Among the daughters of brave {{c|752|Euthy}}, all
(Created by the circumstance begun)
Who left the ancient waters at her call,
Was {{c|1183|Myry}}, she the trepanated one.

Like all her sisters, she was born, and yet
The water made her mourn, for lying there,
She suffocated, and it made her fret,
Within the ocean's deep and liquid lair.

Her father, seeing this, and seeing all,
Pierced holes above her legs, ten thousand, so
That he would never miss, both great and small;
She breathed, where breathing never begs, below.

And through these holes she found that she could take
The blessings that from {{c|936|Hausa}} come, so pure,
Directly, and receive, for her own sake,
Into her frame, so steady and so sure.

And her descendants, even to this day,
Still keep the holes that saved her as their own,
And breathe still in the very selfsame way;
Through terrestrial strife they've cut, and shown.

And so the daughters, all of them, who came
From {{c|1183|Myry}}, heard the call upon the land
To breathe the air so sweet, and heard the same:
{{c|1184|Myriapods}} complete, a mighty band.

And {{c|1183|Myry}}, she the pierced, went to explore
The new lands, and she found, as she had dared,
That in the lands she loved, from shore to shore,
She was not alone, but this zone she shared.

Tradition gives this place the name, and grace,
Of "{{c|1183|Myry}}'s coast"; but, as we have been shown,
She was not first, though so it names the place,
By history rehearsed, the truth made known.

We call it "{{c|1185|Coast}} of Three Kingdoms" now, so,
To honor every side, and every one,
We name it truthfully, that all may know,
Of history's great tide, when it was done.

And {{c|1183|Myry}} saw with wonder, and she found
{{c|608|Cities}} that were not torn, but built and grown,
That neither rain had torn, nor thunder's sound:
The cities of the {{c|550|Lichen}}, born, and known,

Born of a covenant, a pact, to make
A {{c|1186|Partnership}} divine, a pact between
{{c|545|Symbio-Mygus}}, and for both their sake,
Joined with {{c|547|Charina-Planta}}'s line, and seen.

The cities sprawled out wide on every hand,
Each living with the other, well and strong,
Half mold, half moss, together on the land;
{{c|1187|Mycelium}} would delve, and dig along

Deep down into the earth for earthly gold,
While all the thallus, as the sunlight fell,
{{c|1188|Basked}} in the sun's bright blessing, brave and bold,
From heaven's light, caressing it so well.

These cities spread themselves so very far,
And when the cities met, they would marry,
Beneath the light of every shining star,
And fungi and the plant would both carry

On with their ancient promise and their vow,
And each one nation wed the other, so,
To live together, then, and live it now,
Like sister and like brother, as they grow.

But {{c|1183|Myry}} was not gentle in her ways;
She ate the cities whole, and swallowed all,
Her elemental ways, in all her days,
And stole what made them whole, both great and small.

But as she ran around from place to place,
She dropped upon the ground on every side
{{c|1189|Cells}}, scattered round, a fertile, living trace,
And scattered through the atmosphere, and wide.

Across the globe they fell, and fell around,
And left in every place her meal's own trace;
Her messy eating's spell upon the ground
Was there for some to steal, and to embrace.

And soon the sons of {{c|454|Mygus}} built anew
Great {{c|608|Cities}}, with {{c|549|Charina}}'s daughters, spread,
Without a guilt, and these the two then grew
Across each earthly arena they led.

But {{c|1183|Myry}} bore two sons: when day begun
Came {{c|976|Cain}}, the first; and then, so meek and kind,
Came {{c|977|Abel}}, then, the second, other one,
Her peaceful, loving child, of gentle mind.

And in the process of the time it came
That each would bring an offering, and laid
An offering so true, and in his name,
For {{c|296|Mithra}}'s judgment, due to him, and made.

And {{c|976|Cain}} brought, as his gift, the fruit and yield
Of ground; and {{c|977|Abel}} brought the firstlings of
His flocks, and not the fruit out of the field,
The best that he possessed, and of his love.

And {{c|296|Mithra}} had respect for {{c|977|Abel}}'s part,
His sacrifice so true, and blessed the one;
But {{c|976|Cain}}'s, which he had brought to him apart,
He would eschew, and of it would have none.

Then {{c|976|Cain}} was very wroth, and then there fell
His countenance; and, seeing all amiss,
The {{c|295|Lord}} said unto {{c|976|Cain}}, who was not well,
"Why is thy heart in pain? Why, then, is this?

If thou doest well in all of thy days,
{{c|1190|Shalt}} thou not then excel? But at the door,
If thou doest wrong in all of thy ways,
{{c|1191|Sin}}'s desire is strong, and lies in store."

But {{c|976|Cain}} then talked with {{c|977|Abel}}, at the board,
His brother, as kin would; and in the field,
When they were both alone, the hatred stored
In {{c|976|Cain}}, which he had grown, would not be healed.

And in the field he rose up, and against
His brother rose, and took the knife to break,
With {{c|1192|Murder}}'s sharpened knife, and so dispensed
With {{c|977|Abel}}'s gentle life, for murder's sake.

And {{c|296|Mithra}} called to {{c|976|Cain}}, and called him so:
"Where is thy brother, {{c|977|Abel}}, who is slain?"
"I know not," {{c|976|Cain}} replied, "I do not know;
Am I to be his guide? Must I explain?"

"What is it thou hast done this day?" he said;
"Thy brother's blood, which thou hast spilled, doth pray,
And cries out from the ground, the blood now shed;
Thy curse is found, and comes to thee to stay.

No more shall all the ground give strength to thee,
For all thy time upon this very earth,
Through all thy length of days; and thou shalt be
A wanderer, as if from thy own birth."

Then {{c|976|Cain}} cried out in fear, and in despair:
"From earth and from thy face I am driven;
My punishment's too dear, too much to bear!
No rest, no resting place, to me given.

A fugitive I'll be, and wander, so,
And whosoever sees me on my way
Will slay me, strike me dead, where'er I go;
I cannot hide my head, nor get away."

But {{c|296|Mithra}} set a mark upon him well:
"On him {{c|1193|Sevenfold}} vengeance there shall be,
Whoever it shall be who thee shall fell,
Upon that person fall, for all to see."

And {{c|976|Cain}} went forth in shame, and went away
Out to the {{c|1195|East}} of {{c|1196|Eden}}'s gate, and there,
Into the land of {{c|1194|Nod}} by name, to stay,
To meet his chosen fate, and his despair.

And there it was that {{c|976|Cain}} would know his wife,
And she would bear a son, of noble name,
{{c|1197|Centipus}}; and there Cain would build a life,
A city, and the city bore his fame.

The city that he built was named for him,
For {{c|1197|Centipus}}; and {{c|976|Cain}} would be the one,
Whose fame would never fade, nor would grow dim,
Predecessor of {{c|1198|Caintipedes}}, each one

(Who were {{c|1199|Misspelled}} by all the {{c|1004|Romans}} old,
And so they're called the "centipedes" today),
Who hunt with poison bite, and, strong and bold,
Throughout the night, and all throughout the day.

But {{c|977|Abel}}'s gentle wife, his loving bride,
Was heavy with new life within her heart,
With child, when {{c|976|Cain}}'s great rage, from deep inside,
Would come and tear her husband's heart apart.

Into a million pieces, very small,
The body then of {{c|977|Abel}}, in distress,
Had come to fall; his wife, though, after all,
Became the mother, ancestress no less,

Of millipedes, so very meek and mild,
Who eat the leaves that fall upon the ground,
And never harm a beast, nor harm a child,
And decompose them all, wherever found.

{{c|1200|Enraged}} at {{c|977|Abel}}'s death, and at the sight,
Then {{c|1183|Myry}} drew her breath, and at great length
She lunged at {{c|976|Cain}}, and lunged with all her might,
And so they fought their final fight with strength.

And both of them then passed to {{c|729|Ghedos}}' realm;
But, lying in their corpses, lay within,
Where death holds fast, and death is at the helm,
{{c|1201|Seeds}} for another day that would begin.

In death, the sons of {{c|454|Mygus}} took revenge;
{{c|1202|Hera}}, a daughter who was good and true,
For all the wrongs, she came there to avenge,
And {{c|1203|Freyr}}, the one so strong all through and through,

In the twentieth generation, found
Their habitation, as it has been told,
In all the stories, deep within the ground,
Within the corpses cold, and dead, and old.

And as they grew within them, as they grew,
They built their cities there, until at last
Their hyphae met, the hyphae that they drew,
When all their growing time had come and passed.

And when they met, they wed, and they were one,
And heard what {{c|296|Mithra}} said, and said it true:
"O couple, now your wedding has been done,
Prosperity is yours, and with you two.

But barren you shall be, for decades long;
{{c|1204|Postpone}} your marriage-bed, and wait instead
For decades, wait and see, and so be strong,
Until the word is given, and is said.

And when the children you shall bear are born,
They'll multiply, and fill from shore to shore
The earth with life, from evening until morn,
As husband and as wife, for evermore."

And they would follow his command, and they,
Through all the fertile land, by cells alone
Were married, cell to cell, and in their way
Not with the nuclei that were their own.

Each cell was shared by two, by two that wed,
In every cell they made, in every one;
Each nucleus lived through, and was not dead;
Their sacrifice well-paid when it was done.

{{c|1205|Dikaryotic}} cells, in all their kind,
Their story always tell, and make it known,
The patience and the love, and call to mind,
Blessed from above, the love that they had shown.

{{c|1206|Decades}} they waited, and they waited long,
On {{c|1183|Myry}}'s daughters, all of them that lay,
{{c|1207|Decomposing}}, and they were working strong,
In patient ministry, by night and day.

And they became the ancestors of all
That turn the death into new life again,
The high fungi, processors, great and small:
The {{c|1208|Mushrooms}}, and the knife that cuts our pain,

The knife of penicillin, which can heal
Us in our darkest night; and so they came,
The great fungi, arising, by their zeal,
From where their love had chosen, as its aim,

To wait for {{c|296|Mithra}}'s word, and so to wait,
Through all their patience, and to let resound
Their love, and let it ring, however late,
Down in the earth, where wisdom could be found.

Among the sons of great {{c|322|Plantus}}, the ones
Who stayed, when day begun, with {{c|454|Mygus}}' own,
Two brothers there were, and of all the sons
Their fame was everywhere, and it was known:

{{c|1153|Stomatos}} and {{c|1209|Hepatos}}, who then went
Their separate ways; connected to the cells
Of living networks, each where choosing bent,
That always work, as every story tells,

At the cellular level they would build,
With sons of {{c|1210|Glomulus}}, so glorious,
Their partnership's great revel, as they willed,
Together, all of them victorious.

{{c|1153|Stomatos}} looked and saw the holes that lay
In {{c|1183|Myry}}'s sides and souls, and so he would
Pierce holes into himself as well, that way
To breathe the air, and so excel for good.

But {{c|1209|Hepatos}} refused the foreign art,
And used his ancient ways, the old, instead,
The magic that was used, and kept apart,
And kept on with his faithful, steady tread.

{{c|1209|Hepatos}} became, in time, the sire
Of those who keep the ancient way, and will,
The {{c|1211|Liverworts}}' green and humble choir,
Until this very day, who keep it still.

But {{c|1153|Stomatos}} became, through all his line,
{{c|922|Ancestor}} of fame, and of every kind
Of plant; and he became, by his design,
The root, that dances on, with life entwined.

Today we honor him, and call his name,
The bright transhumanist, who would not cease,
{{c|940|Eloh}}, not dim, but bright, a burning flame,
And never would desist, nor seek release

From being better still, and better yet;
When his beliefs must change, he'd rearrange,
Through all the strength of mind and will he set,
His understanding, though the change was strange,

To make his vision new, and see it through,
To rise up higher, and to climb, and grow,
Forever growing past the self he knew,
Beyond the self that he had come to know.

And as the sons of {{c|1153|Stomatos}} would rise
Upon the earthly stage of that first age,
Like kratos, power rising to the skies,
Then {{c|1212|Hillu}} struck back in a mighty rage.

So many lineages through their days
Would then be lost, and lost for evermore,
Through all their pilgrimages and their ways,
Upon that ancient and primeval shore.

Upon the {{c|1185|Coast}} of {{p|Three Kingdoms}}, by grace,
First met upon the land, as it was planned,
The great wisdom of life, in that one place,
By {{c|296|Mithra}}'s guiding and his gentle hand.

There {{c|554|Plant}} and fungi wed, and while they wed,
The arthropods were nourished on them, so
That on their partnership the three were fed:
It was the first tri-partnership to grow.

From sea to land they came, both great and small,
Each seeking its own fame, and its own quest;
It was the partnership, though, over all,
Above all other ways, that proved the best.

The lichen cities showed, and show us how
The seeds of love are sowed between each kind,
Between the most unlike, and even now
They share each other's hike, and walk combined

Through life upon the earth, where, as they go,
Their partnership gives birth to what, confined
In isolation, none could ever grow:
A beauty none could see, nor ever find.

From {{c|752|Euthy}}'s desperate and daring leap
To save her children, came, and came to stay,
The pierced way of {{c|1183|Myry}}, ever to keep
The way of breathing still, from day to day.

From {{c|976|Cain}} and {{c|977|Abel}}'s strife, and from that fight,
Came death, and then new life, and in its turn
The {{c|1213|Centipedes}} who hunt, came forth to light,
The millipedes who shunt, and work, and churn

{{c|1214|Decay}} into the earth, so rich and good,
And from the fungi's love, so long and slow,
So patient, for new plants, as good earth should,
So blessed from up above, there came to grow

The mushrooms' mighty power, in their worth
Within the darkest hour; and from the change,
So brave, of {{c|1153|Stomatos}}, on all the earth
Came all the plants, and all their spreading range.

The {{c|1185|Coast}} of {{p|Three Kingdoms}} shows us how
The wisdom of all life will find its best
And truest way, as it did then, and now,
Through partnership's display, made manifest.


# Chapter 50: The Silurian Recovery

Then {{c|1173|Silur}}, son of {{c|756|Chelicer}}, surveyed
The world in ruin's blur, and, standing near,
Amid the devastation and decayed,
Saw opportunity's creation, clear.

Then {{c|1173|Silur}} shouted out with all his might,
And he declared his vision, without care,
To all the sons of {{c|325|Animus}} in sight,
For any who had gone before him there:

"I did not steal the lore of kingship's crown;
I found it, and I picked it up, foreseen
My destiny, though in the gutter, down,
By that sword I had found, its edge so keen.

But it was all the people's voices' sound
That placed it on my head, and on the throne
Set me, the one who fit, and so they crowned
The one to make it his, and his alone."

And so began the era, wild and strange
(Which rose from ashes, rising over all),
Of the {{c|1174|Silurian}} chimera's range,
From {{c|954|Ordovician}}'s crashes and its fall.

{{c|1173|Silur}} would bear two sons: when day begun
Came {{c|1215|Eurypter}}, the first; and, strong and vast,
Came {{c|1216|Chasmas}} then, the second, younger one,
And lived his whole life long until it passed.

And {{c|1216|Chasmas}} would beget two sons: the one,
{{c|1217|Belangkas}}, to explore; and, by the sea,
{{c|1218|Xiphos}}, to dwell beneath the shining sun,
A dweller, as he was destined to be.

{{c|1218|Xiphos}} became the father of a kind
Of crabs who keep their horseshoe-shaped design,
Who kept this single wish within their mind,
Through to the end of time, along their line.

{{c|1217|Belangkas}} climbed onto the land up high,
Where none had ever claimed the land before,
To try what no one else had dared to try:
To claim it all, from shore to farthest shore.

He took it out of {{c|1163|Hirnan}}'s hand, to stand
Where he could make his dwelling and reside,
In his own rule, and make his own command
Of territories, spreading far and wide.

Like {{c|1219|Myriapus}}, in the days of old,
Upon the open terrestrial plain
He found that his own story would be told
In suffocation's agony and pain.

But he then pierced wounds into his own side,
And air that he could breathe would come to give
Relief unto his lungs; and satisfied
He was, and breathing, he could come to live.

{{c|1217|Belangkas}} then begat two children, who
Were {{c|1221|Opiliona}}, a daughter fair,
And {{c|1220|Soliber}}, a son both tried and true;
She carried life abroad, and everywhere.

{{c|1221|Opiliona}} spread the moss, and so
No loss would be too great for her to bear;
Across the world she made the green moss grow,
So deep was all her mother's love and care.

She grazed upon the green, and grazed as well
On daughters of {{c|1222|Millipa}}, spread around,
On all that could be seen, where they would dwell
Throughout the earthly steppe, wherever found.

{{c|1221|Opiliona}} was a mother great,
A {{c|1223|Farmer}} with long legs; and wisdom pleads,
For she was like no other, and her gait,
That we remember her and all her deeds

As one who would confer upon the land
Great blessings, and who tended every field,
Who blessed it with her own maternal hand,
And made the green moss grow, and made it yield.

Her legs were beautiful, and very long;
"{{c|30|Granny}} {{c|1224|Long}} Legs" is what they came to call
Her, and she was the subject of a song,
And she was well beloved by one and all.

And "{{c|30|Granny}} {{c|1225|Harvest}}," they would call her too,
For all her work, through every joy and strife,
For all the work that she would come to do
To spread the green that was the hue of life.

And so, in honor of her life and love,
"{{c|1226|Daddy}} {{c|1224|Long}} Legs" is what we call them still,
Her children, with a name we still speak of,
Though "{{c|1226|Daddy}}" seems to suit a lady ill

When it {{c|1227|Names}} her descendants. All the same,
They're also known by her, by what she'd do:
They're "{{c|1228|Harvestmen}}" as well, their story's name,
Named for her harvest, and her labor, too.

{{c|1220|Soliber}} begat two: the first one, who
Was {{c|1229|Pneumaran}}, a son both tried and strong,
And {{c|1230|Kitzi}}, small, but tried as well, and true,
Who'd live and thrive through all his whole life long.

And {{c|1229|Pneumaran}} begat two sons: the one,
{{c|1231|Solaran}}, beyond all of mortal ken,
Was of the shining sun; and, when begun,
{{c|1232|Acares}}, the other, born among men,

A dwarf among his kin he was; and yet
He'd win a place in history, we find,
A place that we will never once forget,
As father of the mites, the smallest kind,

Who, when their work is done, live on the land,
And they are everywhere, in every place,
All over it, built by their tiny hand,
The smallest ones of all the living race.

{{c|1232|Acares}} bore two sons: when day was new
Came {{c|1233|Sarco}} first, as fate would come to tell,
And then came {{c|1234|Trombo}}, second of the two,
Who'd live in peace, or not, as it befell.

And it would tell his story very well,
Of how there are some souls who choose the light,
While others, as the stories of them tell,
Are those who rather choose to choose the night.

The sons of {{c|1233|Sarco}} clean the world, and they,
As dust mites, seen wherever they may go,
Will take the greatest care to sweep away
The dust that, if it stayed, would cause us woe,

A problem for us all, both great and small,
For all who live within the house, and share
The room, who answer, every one, the call
Of life so sweet, and live in it with care.

Among the sons of {{c|1234|Trombo}}, some will dwell
In peace, and stay, of gentleness and grace
A blend that suits them all, and suits them well,
Within their own appointed way and place.

But others are the plague, the ones who've made
All good souls vague with worry; and their ways,
For {{c|1235|Parasites}} they're called, make us afraid,
And {{c|1236|Stifle}} life throughout our living days.

{{c|646|Horrific}} are they in their greed, and so
They plant destruction's seed in every land,
And make it grow, and make it spread and grow,
And ruin all they touch with greedy hand.

Among the peaceful ones, there are the sons,
Red velvet mites, who bring us pure delights,
Of {{c|1234|Trombo}}, gentle, as the story runs,
From whom we learn of love's own sacred rites:

A story of the heart, and of the part,
Where all true loves align, in every place,
That love plays in the world, with all its art,
In nature's plan, with beauty and with grace.

And {{c|1231|Solaran}} begat two sons: the true
{{c|1237|Solifugon}}, the first; and one so small,
{{c|1238|Ricinulon}}, the second son, who knew
Of duty, which he answered, and its call.

{{c|1237|Solifugon}}, so great in fame, became
The father of the ones who race the face
Of all the earth, the {{c|189|Wind}} {{c|741|Spiders}} by name,
Who travel over it at racing pace.

{{c|1238|Ricinulon}} was father of the name
Of small {{c|1239|Tick}} {{c|741|Spiders}}, little and yet strong,
Who heeded, as they hunted, hunting's claim,
And lived their small and quiet lives along.

{{c|1230|Kitzi}} begat two sons: when day was born,
The elder, {{c|1240|Byblos}}, first, and then would be
Young {{c|1241|Paras}}, coming after in the morn,
Small in his station and in his degree.

{{c|1240|Byblos}}, the Book {{c|1242|Knight}}, both by night and day,
To guard the books, the store of ancient lore,
Continues still, until this very day,
In his own way, of all who came before.

His sons, the Book {{c|1243|Scorpions}}, are as well,
With all their might, companions, night and day,
Of knowledge, and they shield it where they dwell,
The books from those who'd tear their joy away.

{{c|1241|Paras}} begat two more, and one would be
{{c|1244|Mesos}}, born to explore, and to the last
The other, {{c|1245|Holoxos}}, the strong, would see
His whole life long in strength, until it passed.

{{c|1244|Mesos}}, he was a hunter fierce indeed,
Who'd dart across the globe to find his {{c|1246|Prey}},
His mind and body's gluttony to feed:
A small but mighty fee he'd take away

From all the life around him on the ground,
From all the living, small, that he would meet
In every place where he was to be found,
For all of them were his, for him to eat.

But {{c|1245|Holoxos}} walked where the {{c|1247|Blood}} would flow
From fallen kin: the sons, who were so thin,
Of {{c|746|Arachnus}}, who lay so very low,
And sons of {{c|1219|Myriapus}}, who had been

Victorious in other time and place,
Before death took them, cold, and they were dead.
He drank their blood, and in death's cold embrace
Bore two sons, searching paths where blood was shed:

{{c|1248|Thyrus}} would draw his breath, through all his days,
From old tradition, peaceful, and from those
Already dead, submissive in his ways,
{{c|1249|Drinking}} the blood of those in last repose.

But {{c|1250|Ricinus}} was one who turned to dark,
And everywhere he went, and he would go,
He left upon the world his evil mark;
He fed on living blood, to make it flow

Like some unholy flood of evil's greed,
Which flows, and flows, and never comes to cease,
Which in the world will plant destruction's seed,
And robs the world of life, and of its peace.

{{c|1250|Ricinus}} drinks the life of those who know,
{{c|1251|Injecting}} with his bite, all through the night,
Both joy and strife, his {{c|1252|Venom}}, as they go,
Which paralyzes those he's marked to fight.

The {{c|1253|Paralytic}}, sweaty poison's sting
Is never petty; like unholy rain,
To those who can't {{c|1254|Escape}} it, it will bring
The evil of his venom, and its pain.

{{c|1250|Ricinus}} swells like some unholy cup,
With innocents' own blood, and as he grows,
{{c|1255|Inflated}} with the blood he's taken up,
A stolen flood of life within him flows.

He's {{c|1256|Fat}} with others' pain; and like a stain
Upon the world of life, he cuts right through,
Unholy, like the sharpest knife, the bane
Of all the good that lives in me and you.

Through {{c|1250|Ricinus}} the blood of women scorned
May taint us, bringing into mortal veins
A flood of it, of which we have been warned,
The weight of all their many bitter pains.

When {{c|290|Lilith}}'s blood flows in us, we can't win;
{{c|1257|Typhus}} will bring its blight to me and you;
Against the poison's might, which lies within,
The {{c|1258|Spotted}} {{c|1259|Fever}} comes to us all, too,

To all of us who cannot fight alone
Against the evil we let in our world,
Against the very thing that we have sown,
Where it can win, with all its flags unfurled,

Against the good and true in you and me,
Against the good in all of human kind,
That lives in us, wherever we may be,
In heart and soul, in body and in mind.

In what {{c|1250|Ricinus}} gives there live as well,
In mitochondria lives {{c|290|Lilith}}'s own,
The {{c|1260|Midichlorians}}, and there they dwell,
Bacteria, the greatest vengeance known

In stories new and old, of those who mark
The world with evil, and who choose to be
The ones who choose the evil and the dark,
And having chosen, never will be free.

And after them, the daughters, too, would come,
{{c|360|Malarius}}' dark days, and {{c|1261|Lyme}}, and all,
Of {{c|290|Lilith}}, with their evil ways, the sum,
The other sisters, who are held in thrall,

Possessed by pestilence and death, and they
Bring sickness to the body and the soul,
And they will steal our very breath away,
And take from us the health that made us whole.

{{c|1250|Ricinus}}, father of the {{c|1262|Ticks}}, who show
No love, but only greed and hate, becomes,
{{c|1263|Engorged}} with others' fate, the sign, and so
Shows us the fate of evil, how it sums

Into a force of wrong so strong that right,
Though all the good within us comes to try,
Can never win against it in the fight,
Until the day the good will rise up high.

But {{c|1215|Eurypter}} would father and would found,
More than the line of {{c|1216|Chasmas}}, and design,
A dynasty more great and more renowned,
And make a nation, he and all his line,

Which would take up its rightful share of might
And glory, and would fill the world, and guide
The world with sight of what is good and right,
Of what the good can do when they are tried.

And they would shine like morning light, the way
Through every place that's dark, where evil's face
Is shown, but evil cannot win the day
When good comes forth, and shows its rightful grace.

From {{c|1173|Silur}}'s opportunity, his prize,
And to {{c|1221|Opiliona}}'s loving care,
Seen in calamity before his eyes,
For all the life that's growing everywhere,

From the Book {{c|1264|Knights}}, who stand guard and defend,
Each day, and light our way through every day,
The knowledge upon which we all depend,
To those who choose the dark and go astray,

And leave their evil mark on all around,
The {{c|1174|Silurian}} age, as it bestows,
On all the world, wherever they are found,
Shows how each choice we make takes root and grows

Into the world we see, for you and me.
Some choose to heal and mend what others tear,
Who, in the end, with greed and hate, will be
The ones who seal our fate, and our despair.

And others, in their selfishness, can't wait
To take, for their own sake, what others need
To live, and never learn, however late,
To give, but only take, and take for greed.

The lesson, clear as day, shows us the way
To choose, for all eternity, to bless
And heal, and what to be, and not to stray,
Or else to leave behind us all a mess

That others will be left to scrub and clear,
And others will be left to clean and mend,
In places yet unseen, both far and near,
From now until the time of time's own end.

From {{c|1173|Silur}}'s royal crown and its renown
To those who'd drown the world in pain and death,
The blood-suckers, who come to drag it down,
Each choice we make will always draw its breath

From what we hold most dear: from love, the love
That casts out fear, sincere, or else from fear,
Which kills all love, the love we're speaking of,
And blocks the light that shines on us, so near.

The choice is ours, and ours alone, to make,
Upon life's winding road, where we must bear,
In every step along the way we take,
The heavy load of what our choices there

Will bring to all the living things that share
This world with us, in ways both great and grand,
And terrible, for you and me; and there
We are the ones who must decide and stand,

And choose, and must decide each single day
Which path we'll take, the path of good or ill,
And which way we will travel on our way,
Each one of us, by our own choice and will.

The {{c|1174|Silurian}} age began with one
Who had a plan, and would rise from the fall,
From ruin's call, and when the wreck was done,
Would build a hope that rose, and build for all.

It also shows that some will choose the side
Of death, with every breath, and choose the night,
And there, within the darkness, will abide,
And turn away forever from the light.

The choice is ours: to use our mortal might,
Along the living way on which we tread,
For good or ill each day, for wrong or right.
From opportunity's own call, which led

To rising past the golden ages' fall,
The {{c|1174|Silurian}} shows the world we make,
The ages past, to build what lasts for all,
Is found by each, for everyone's own sake.

Choose well, for what you choose, you'll lose or gain,
And what you choose is what you come to be,
For all the days your deathless ways remain,
Through all the days of all eternity.

From where {{c|1173|Silur}} had made his royal start
To all the ticks, the lesson, plain to see,
Is clear, from all their bloodsucking and art:
We are, each one, what we will choose to be.


# Chapter 51: The Sea Scorpions

{{c|1215|Eurypter}}'s sons would then {{c|1265|Usurp}}, as none
Could do, the sons of {{c|1266|Cephalus}}, to reign,
And ruled, victorious, when they had won,
Where those they conquered once had their domain.

{{c|1215|Eurypter}} married fair {{c|1267|Pulmona}}, who
Was {{c|1268|Beloved}} everywhere; but on the name
That they should bear, they disagreed, the two,
And neither one would yield, nor say the same.

Each had their own design, each their own say
For their ancestral line, and for its name:
"{{c|1269|Eurypterids}}," was what he'd always say;
"{{c|1270|Arachnopulmonates}}," was her own claim.

{{c|1215|Eurypter}} and {{c|1267|Pulmona}} bore a pair,
{{c|1271|Eurypteron}} and {{c|1272|Styloner}}, begun
As children like no others anywhere,
In rivalry so deep that there was none

Who ever could keep {{c|1273|Peace}} between the two,
For each would go his way, and walk his road,
Who each walked different paths, as each one knew,
And neither one would share the other's load.

{{c|1271|Eurypteron}} and {{c|1272|Styloner}} would fight
For all the things that could be won or bought,
Like no two other siblings, with their might,
Throughout the day and night, as on they fought.

Their mother died, and they could not decide
Who would inherit all, and who would be
The one, by honor's law and honor's guide,
To take her whole estate, and so be free.

{{c|1271|Eurypteron}} laid claim upon the skies;
On land, which he had built with his own hand,
{{c|1272|Styloner}} set his heart and set his eyes.
So {{c|1271|Eurypteron}} flew, as he had planned,

Across domains he knew were his by birth,
And claimed them as by law; and, by the book
Of heritage, he walked upon the earth,
Did {{c|1272|Styloner}}; but each of them would look

Upon it differently, although the two
Were brothers born, and from one mother came,
And though they shared one mother, as they knew,
They never saw one world, nor saw the same.

{{c|1271|Eurypteron}}, in flight across the sky,
Who ruled where winds blow high above the earth,
Began a dynasty of those on high,
And from the moment of their very birth

To death's appointed day, they'd hold their sway,
And they would rule up there, above the ground,
And they would rule the sky in their own way,
Wherever winds were blowing all around.

{{c|1271|Eurypteron}} begat two sons: the strong
{{c|1274|Diploper}}, and {{c|1275|Eurypterus}}, beyond
All others in fertility, who long
Would go past any measure to respond.

His numbers were his treasure; he was most
Fertile of all; and with each single one
Of generations, he, of all the host,
{{c|1275|Eurypterus}}, as each one was begun,

His house would grow ten thousand-fold, and so,
Beyond what any other line could try,
His numbers multiplied, and they would go
In all of space and time, beneath the sky;

{{c|1276|Myriad}}-fold they grew, a multitude,
And filled the waters of the sea and shore,
Of offspring tried and true, a mighty brood,
And grew, and grew, and multiplied the more.

{{c|1274|Diploper}} then begat two sons: the one,
{{c|1277|Waeringos}}, tried and true, the first to last;
And {{c|1278|Carcinos}}, when day had now begun,
The strong one, lived his whole life till it passed.

And {{c|1277|Waeringos}} begat two sons, and then
{{c|1279|Humiller}} came, who was so strong and brave,
A son beyond the common, mortal ken,
And {{c|1280|Adelops}}, who later on would save

His line, through numbers vast, so that it would
Forever last; and he would heed the call
Of duty, small, as numbers only could,
With many children, who were, one and all,

Resilient, and were true, and they would be,
As small things are, so hard to break or kill,
As tenacious as bugs beneath the sea,
And they would hold on fast, and hold on still.

{{c|1279|Humiller}} married {{c|1281|Pterra}}, one so fair
In beauty and in grace, and in their place,
Together, in their dwelling, they would bear,
When day was first begun, one son of grace:

{{c|1282|Slender}}, and fast, and sly, he'd rule, and dwell
