The cynodont would dig himself a den
Where temperature stayed level and the spell
Of surface heat and cold lost force again

To reach the body; and the burrow kept
The later generations safe when fire
Rained from the sky—when great volcanoes wept
Ash across the world, and the entire

Surface of all the earth became too hot
Or cold for those above the ground to bear,
The ones who lived beneath it all would not
Receive the killing dose of ash and air.

And {{c|1673|Cynos}} knew nothing of this. He dug
Because the burrow kept his young secure,
Because the den, consistent, warm, and snug,
Was kinder than the drying world's unsure

And swinging heat of the {{x|Permian}} night
And day—he dug for practical intent
And present reasons, and the hidden light
Of that decision, tactical, that went

Beyond all tactics, it would penetrate
A world one hundred thousand years ahead
When everything above ground met its fate
And only burrowers remained not dead.

So {{c|1673|Cynos}} in his burrow raised his young
With warm milk—not yet true mammalian,
And still he laid his eggs, but with the tongue
Of ancient motherhood, {{c|1721|Pygmalion}}

Of what care would become—he sat above
His clutch and warmed them with his body's heat,
The first experiment in active love,
In giving warmth as the parental feat.

So honor {{c|1673|Cynos}} for the dog-toothed gift—
For differentiation, for the warm
And buried life that gave the future's lift
To those who'd need it most in coming storm.


# Chapter 78: The Gorgon's Reign

Among all {{c|1672|Theraps}}' children, none struck fear
As deeply into every living heart
As {{c|1722|Gorgo}}—gorgonopsid, whose career
Was built on being death refined to art:

The saber-toothed therapsid, apex lord
Of all the late {{x|Permian}} world, who walked
With a long killing fang that was the sword
And scepter of the age—a blade that talked

No other language than the chase's skill
And bringing down the large. For {{c|1722|Gorgo}} found
In carnage and in every hard-won kill
The purest form of living, and her bound

At {{c|1723|Dicyno}} and all his herds was swift—
She ran with semi-upright gait across
The {{x|Permian}} red plains, and with the gift
Of saber canine teeth she turned the loss

Of opportunity to instant death:
Two great and curving fangs that penetrate
The neck of any prey and rob the breath
From it before it knew its own last gate.

She was large—some of {{c|1722|Gorgo}}'s children grew
To bear-size, heavy-bodied, low-slung still
In part the older sprawl, but swift right through
The short, fierce sprint to accomplish the kill

Before prey could flee. In {{x|Permian}} lands
The tiger's equal, or the lion's, she
With all her ancient fury, {{c|1722|Gorgo}} stands
And scans the herd of {{c|1723|Dicyno}}, to see

With shining calculation, as the kind
Of hunter built for nothing but this part:
To read the herd's interior, to find
Its weakness, mark the one whose slowing heart

Will make the chase worthwhile to her—the old,
The young, the limping one, the lagging one
That moves less smoothly—{{c|1722|Gorgo}}, calm and cold
And focused, chooses well before the run

Has even started who will die today.
Such is the mind that predators possess:
Not toolmaker's cleverness, not the way
Of problem-solving, but, in its finesse,

Close attention to the world around her,
The reading of behavior, the precise
Assessment of the frame—{{c|1722|Gorgo}} found her
Her wisdom in the eyes, which did suffice

For knowing every creature in the herd
By the quality of its movement, by
The subtle hesitation—like a word
Misspoken, that a listening ear and eye

Can catch before the speaker's sentence ends—
{{c|1722|Gorgo}} heard hesitation in the gait
Of prey before the chase itself extends
Into a sprint, and chose the one whose fate

Was sealed before she ever moved. And so
The gorgonopsid was the first great stage
Of mammal-lineage hunts, set to grow
Into the {{x|Permian}}'s last closing age,

An apex that the world had never seen
In quite this form: a warm-ish blood, and speed,
And saber-tooth combined, and with a keen
And searching mind in service of its need.

She was the {{x|Permian}} heroic peak—
The form three hundred million years of life
Before had seemed preparing it to seek:
A predator of one design, a knife

Above all others—matched against, immense,
{{c|1723|Dicyno}}'s horn-billed millions grazing wide
Across the whole {{p|Pangean}} plain—the tense
And beautiful equation of the pride

Of predator and plenty of the prey
In balance, each one shaping, as they played,
The other through selection's ancient way
Of honing edge on edge, the parents made

Of all the speed and size they came to share—
Without her, the dicynodonts would not
Have grown so large; without the tether there
Of hunting's haunt, the prey forgets its lot:

It grows so careless, soft, abundant, slow—
And {{c|1722|Gorgo}} was a gift, unwanted, though
{{c|1723|Dicyno}} needed—the shadowing foe
That kept the herd alert and on the go.

This was the {{x|Permian}}'s finest hour—
The ecosystem balanced, rich, complex,
Predator and prey each at its power,
Each shaping what the other would be next.

And it would end. It always ends. The reign
Of any apex is a flash, a breath
Of geologic time, a brief campaign
Of dominance, before arriving death

Of circumstance that no plan can foresee.
But while it lasted, honor {{c|1722|Gorgo}}'s sway—
The saber and the sprint, the skill to see,
To read all life and take it, day by day,

Across and through the {{x|Permian}} red plain.
The finest predator the age could make,
Who ruled the world and will not rule again—
The gorgonopsid gone for beauty's sake.


# Chapter 79: The Last Paleozoic Sea

Before the great death came, before the fire
And poison of the age's ending wept
Its curtain down, the sea kept its choir
Of all the beauty that the oceans kept

Through all the ages—the {{x|Permian}} sea
Was rich beyond what any age before
Had managed: every reef that there could be
Alive with color, every ocean floor

Abundant—let us pause here at the shore,
Before the dying, let us stop and see
The {{x|Paleozoic}} sea's final store
In its last fullness; let us come to be

The witnesses of what will not survive:
The coral gardens first, the rugose kind,
{{c|1705|Coleios}}' neighbors, who would keep alive
The reef's foundations, stone from sea designed

In oral structures, made in time to be
Of four-fold symmetry in polyp flesh
On limestone, the foundation and decree
Of the ancient {{x|Paleozoic}}'s fresh

And living architecture—this would go.
The rugose coral would not cross the line
Of the extinction, nor tomorrow's show
Of the {{x|Triassic}} sea—their four-fold sign

Would vanish from the reef, replaced in time
By the six-fold scleractinian form—
But for now they rose in every sublime
Arrangement on the reef, beneath the warm

And shallow sea above them, lit with green
And blue and orange in the filtered light.
And there was {{c|1705|Coleios}}, too, in the scene—
The ink-bearers, the masters of the night

And day of open water: {{c|1708|Teuthis}} sped
And pulsed through all the columns of the sea,
While {{c|1710|Octopos}} walked where stone gardens spread
Across the reef, with minds by three times three

To read the world. And in the waters, too,
With curled, cylindrical, and solid frame,
The belemnite {{c|1706|Belemno}} swam right through,
A sleek torpedo, hunting, as he came,

For small and smaller prey through acres wide
Of {{x|Permian}} sea, his hard inner core
The only wall between his soft inside
And hungry world outside it, at its door.

And {{c|1707|Sepos}}, the cuttlebone-bearer, hung
In the mid-water, and he changed his hue
Just like a living stone on which was flung
A canvas, every color, through and through,

At once, a living and a shifting flag
Of skin that could be anything the eye
Required—the boast, the color-changing brag
Of {{c|1705|Coleios}}' great house against the sky

Of ocean overhead. The ammonites,
Who since {{x|Devonian}} had swum this deep,
The coiled ones, whose geometry's delights
Bore daughters spiral-perfect, and the sweep

Of solar mathematics in design—
Still coiling, still abundant, still the most
Common of fossils in that ancient wine
Of time; they too would nearly turn to ghost

At the great extinction, reduced to one
Or two survivors who would spread again
Throughout the {{x|Mesozoic}} like the sun
After the storm—but now theirs was the reign:

Uncounted through the {{x|Permian}}'s great sea,
Their shells the very meter of the age.
And {{c|1711|Malacos}} held all the floor in fee:
Great {{c|1712|Decapos}}, within his heavy stage

Of armor, crossed the bottom, claw raised high;
{{c|1713|Euphausios}} filtered cold waters wide
In clouds of millions, feeding every eye
That looked upon abundance—the inside

Of the great ocean's engine, krill-built base
That fed the food web from the bottom up.
And {{c|1153|Stomatos}} within his shallow place
Still struck his shrimp-fist punch, and filled the cup

Of force within a microsecond's blow
Of club against the snail's hard, coiling shell—
This world was rich past all accounts could show,
So rich no reckoning could ever tell,

Enough to fill a thousand books, and still
Leave volumes yet unwritten of the kind
That the {{x|Permian}} sea had kept—until
The fire came, and all that it would find

Was changed at once. So let us pause, before
The curtain falls without applause, and be
Its grateful witnesses, before the shore
Of all the {{x|Paleozoic}}'s last sea

Is poisoned—let us stand here in the light
That still pours clean and warm through waters clear
As any sky, and, with the reef in sight,
The current flowing, cuttlefish, and near,

The otter-smooth belemnite, let us praise
The sea's accomplishment: unbroken grace,
Three hundred million years of beauty's days,
At last shut, not diminished in its place,

And still a billion lives complete before
The ending—the {{x|Paleozoic}} sea
Was not a failure when it closed its door:
Each life, lived fully, is a victor, free.

Honor the last {{x|Paleozoic}} deep—
The reef that predates every reef we know,
The ocean that the {{x|Permian}} would keep
In trust for us to mourn, long, long ago.


# Chapter 80: The Dicynodont Bread

Now hear of {{c|1723|Dicyno}}, with beak and tusk,
The patient one, who fed the world through all
The {{x|Permian}}'s late age, who walked till dusk
Through every landscape, from the stately hall

Of the tropical basin to the high
And arid plateau; who moved in great herds
Of thousands under the {{p|Pangean}} sky,
On its wide plains, and said with all his words

Of his abundant living: I am near.
I am the bread of this world, and its balm,
The patient herbivore without a fear
Too large for me to bear—{{c|1723|Dicyno}}'s calm

In {{x|Permian}} ecology renowned:
Where others starved or fled away to die,
{{c|1723|Dicyno}} found a way, and what he found
Were roots beneath the soil, the drought-struck, dry

And woody vegetation that repels
The other plant-eaters—and so his beak
Was built for cropping, and his fossil tells
Of brotherhood with tortoise, and the peak

Of grinding: not with teeth; but two great tusks
Projecting, both, out of the upper jaw
For digging roots and tearing at the husks
Of plants left whole by every other maw

Untried—he was a dietary monk
Who ate what others left behind, who found
In every desert margin, every drunk
And withered, dying vegetation, ground

Still worth exploring for the root below.
The dicynodont became most widespread
Large vertebrate on land of any show
The {{x|Permian}} staged—redundant, as said,

But only in the sense that numbers vast
Were needed, so the pyramid could stand
Of {{c|1722|Gorgo}}'s hunger—each of them the last
Meal of another's; and the grid, the strand

Of energy from plant to herbivore
To carnivore was kept by the supply
Of {{c|1723|Dicyno}}'s abundance, the world's store
Of fuel, with the provider's nose held nigh

The ground; forever he would be the one
Who turned the sun's gift in the plant to flesh
That others needed—in this way the sun
Itself walked through the ecosystem's mesh

As {{c|1723|Dicyno}} bore it from plant to prey.
There were hundreds of species in his line—
From rabbit-small to hippo-wide, each way
Of being {{c|1723|Dicyno}} stood as a shrine

To versatility of one sole plan:
The beak, the tusk, the barrel body low
And close to the ground—and from each began
A different niche, a different overflow

Of adaptation: one who dug, below,
His den beside the termite mound; the one
Who waded in the furrowed rivers slow
Of {{x|Permian}}, half-sunk in mud; and one

Who roamed dry land, a hundred miles of red
Rock in a season, chasing thunder's train
Along the monsoon's trail to the brief spread
Of green that followed after any rain—

{{c|1723|Dicyno}} roamed everywhere that the ground
Of {{x|Permian}} grew green, on every plain
And hillside the great continent around.
He was the sheep of {{x|Permian}}'s domain—

The innocent abundance that supports
The wolf—the one whose death was the first plan
Of the ecosystem's energy courts;
And he submitted when his role began

To this one role without complaint or flight
Beyond what flight was useful; fit and true
To his own purpose, present in the light
Of each {{x|Permian}} dawn the whole herd knew.

The broad-backed herd that crossed the plain at dawn
Was his; and every track that followed heard
The predator behind, a shadow drawn:
This is the world that works, by hunger spurred:

The eaten and the eating, in their dance
Of ancient sculpting, each one shaping each
The other; {{c|1722|Gorgo}}'s greeting, at each glance,
Unto {{c|1723|Dicyno}} was the way to teach

Each generation in the ancient art
Of being faster, slightly, than the one
Behind you—and the herd's panicking heart
Was {{c|1723|Dicyno}}'s whole education, sun

By sun, and through each generation's length.
So honor {{c|1723|Dicyno}}, who fed the world,
Who walked in every nation, by his strength,
And turned the desert's last green leaf unfurled

To flesh the predator would need—and who
Was the one bread that came before the cup,
Whose patience and abundance seeded through
The pyramid of life from bottom up.


# Chapter 81: The Eve of the Cup

There was a time—a brief and final time—
When all the world seemed rich enough to last:
The {{x|Permian}} at its height, its sublime
And complicated order, the vast past

Three hundred million years arrived at this:
An evening of the age, the gathered sum
Of all that life had built, a final kiss
Of ordinary beauty—as they come,

{{c|1723|Dicyno}} scattered in the morning light
Across {{p|Pangean}} plains, {{c|1722|Gorgo}} above
Watching upon the ridge; the sea, alight
With {{x|Paleozoic}} wealth, and the love

Of creature for its living, for the air
And water, and the food, the den it made
From nothing; and the {{x|Permian}} was fair
In this last hour before it came to fade.

The gymnosperm woods on the ridges stood
In their new quiet, past the coal swamp's loud
And tropical confusion—gone for good:
A quiet, arid landscape, but a proud

One: there the cone-trees on the red rock plain
Like dark green candles in the desert air,
The reptiles, basking, in the warm domain
Of {{x|Permian}} summertime, without care

For what lay under {{p|Siberia}}'s ground,
What lay beneath the frozen land up north
Of {{p|Pangea}}'s great shoulder: there, unbound,
Bacteria-rich basalts, cooking forth

Out of the planet's own deep heat, to rise
In pressure up against the surface crust,
In what the world would come to recognize
As the catastrophe—a buried gust

Of magma seeking every crack and seam
Within the {{p|Siberian}} basement rock
Toward the surface, in a patient dream
Of an eruption ticking like a clock

That only earth could read; and though it stirred,
The world above knew nothing of its hour.
And {{c|1673|Cynos}}, in his burrow, heard no word
Of doom below the cool ground's dark power

He dug his den into; and all he knew
Were insect sounds that filled the desert night,
The wind across the cone-tree, and the few
Dry scraps of debris in the desert light.

And {{c|1722|Gorgo}}, on her ridge at sundown, spied
The herds of {{c|1723|Dicyno}} moving on to
The water at the dusk; and she, clear-eyed,
Marked out the old and slow one in her view

And felt the readiness she always felt
Before the hunt: the tightening, the stare;
And yet the world she hunted in had dealt
No sign of change, no warning anywhere

That she could read. And yet, deep down, a breath
Of gas leaked in {{p|Siberia}}'s rock, wet
With sulfur, through a fissure—early death
Of ordinary air, in one place set

Small, just above the coming fire—a hiss
So faint that nothing living with a face
Or ears could ever hear, and all would miss:
The breath of what was building, the first trace

Of the small exhalation of a world
Preparing to unburden its long thirst
For the surface—the first edge, gently curled,
Of killing that was coming, and the worst.

Take this image: all the world entire
At table—every living thing in place,
Consuming its last meal before the fire.
The reef beneath the {{x|Permian}} sea's face

Was feeding on the current's plankton bloom;
The herd of {{c|1723|Dicyno}}; and she who'd kill,
Who watches, all within a single room
Of ordinary evening, and the still

Necessity of life—and somewhere north,
In {{p|Siberian}} rock, the common, known,
Becoming something else; there, coming forth,
Breathing its first breath out of sulfur, blown

Into the stillness and unknowing air,
While all the world at table, free of doubt
Or grief, was eating all of what was there,
Not knowing what the evening was about.

This is the final supper of the age—
Not made dramatic, not with dread foretold,
And not announced with thunder on the stage,
But just the ordinary evening, rolled

Into the eve of ending, past belief—
And still the meal goes on, and none can feel
What they cannot see coming, and no grief
Is in them as they take their evening meal.

Honor the {{x|Permian}}'s last evening's light,
The ordinary beauty of the full
World eating, sleeping, hunting, through the night,
Finding the grace of each day—and the pull

Of one more sunrise, each one unaware
Before the morning that would change the world.
The cup was coming; all sat gathered there,
Abundant, in their ancient peace, unfurled.


# Chapter 82: Good Permian Friday

Then {{p|Siberia}} opened, not one blow:
The way a wound will open, slow at first,
A fissure reached the surface from below
Upon a day like others—the first burst

Of basalt, thin and local; then there came
Another and another, till the whole
Became a thousand miles of vent and flame,
The mother of volcanic fields, the toll

Of an eruption past all other scale
That living memory had ever spanned—
Two million cubic miles of basalt's trail
Of fire written on {{p|Siberian}} land,

In layers, laid down year by weary year:
This was no single blast, but a whole age
Of burning, and a hundred-thousand-year
Sustained eruption. Then, stage after stage,

The gases filled the sky; the first, the dread
Carbon dioxide, and the warming, came
Before the cooling—and then, cried instead,
Sulfur dioxide, storming like a flame,

The atmosphere with acid—every cloud
That formed above the {{x|Permian}} dry land
Came down again as acid rain, a shroud
Of chemical death spread over the strand

Of every forest that remained—the trees
Burned where they stood, though not from any blaze,
But from the rain itself, the acid's ease
Of stripping chlorophyll from all the sprays

Of canopy: the gymnosperm woods, made
By {{c|1702|Conifera}} on hill, ridge, and slope,
Went brown at first, then gray, and fell, decayed—
The bridge between the sun and life lost hope:

The photosynthesis could not proceed
In acid air; the base of the career
Of energy was failing—every creed
Of all the eating built on plant, on mere

Nothing at all. The ocean was not spared:
Carbon dioxide took its bow, and passed,
Dissolving into waters widely shared,
Into the global sea, and there, at last,

Carbonic acid formed from gas and brine;
The ocean's chemistry was stormed, and fell
Its pH; carbonate in every line
Of shell dissolved; and coral, long and well

Built through three hundred million years, grew weak
And then to nothing; reefs' oral design
Dissolving; the sea warmed, its depths grew bleak,
Anoxic, without oxygen; the brine

Bred hydrogen sulfide—the toxic gas,
The purple poison of the deep, which rose
In killing blooms to surface; purple glass
Of water at the shore where nothing grows,

The ocean's tombs of former life; its door
Shut fast. And 96 percent of all
The species of the sea would cross no more
The boundary; brachiopods would fall.

The rugose coral, wholly; and the old
And few trilobites would meet the fire
Of that last great extinction, final, cold,
And permanent; the line that would expire

Of trilobites had stretched back to the morn
Of {{x|Cambrian}} explosion, had survived
Each sign of mass death in the oceans borne
Through its long history, but here arrived

At its own end: not with a bang, but slow
Souring with acid, year by patient year,
Of every sea it swam in, far below.
On land, the acid rain, the heat severe;

The food web's base collapsed; {{c|1723|Dicyno}}'s herds
Could find no meat of plant to eat; and so
The race to starvation ran on, past words,
From herbivore to carnivore below—

{{c|1722|Gorgo}} starved when {{c|1723|Dicyno}} starved; the floor
Of the food pyramid was carved away,
And everything above it fell. No more:
Some seventy percent, from that dark day,

Of vertebrates on land would die; the knell
Of gorgonopsids, final, absolute:
The gates closed on her line, and as they fell,
Her ancient house left neither branch nor root.

The saber-toothed, the racing hunter, shrewd
And proud and fierce, was taken—not by tooth
Of any rival, but by lack of food—
And so the {{x|Permian}} went down in truth

To the last word that all life understood:
That the whole world can end not with a war
Between the living, but when fails the good
That creatures need—the bright and open door

Of photosynthesis, the friend of all
That breathes. {{x|Good Permian Friday}}, the name:
The {{x|Paleozoic}} world's death and fall,
Not villainy, not error, not the blame

Of a wrong path chosen; only the curled
And patient force of geologic time
Expressing what it must, beneath the world—
Volcanoes did not choose to kill; sublime

And ancient earth let go of what was found
To have built up within; the cost was paid
By every living thing above that ground—
The world was lost, and in its loss remade,

The way that love itself must, now and then,
Give up the form it had, and let it fall,
Die so that it may be reborn again,
And rise the stronger for it, after all.


# Chapter 83: The Harrowing of Hell

After the fire, silence. Not the peace
Of silence, but the empty room, the closed
Theater, when the crowd has found release,
Has come, and broken chairs alone disclosed

The weight of what had happened. All the land
Of {{x|Permian}}, in the extinction's wake,
Was not recovered: horror's noon would stand,
With everything that mattered still at stake

And nothing yet decided—and the air
Still poisonous with methane and the last
Of sulfur's burning at the throat; each bare
And rocky hillside scoured by the past

Months of the acid rain, the soil all stripped
Of its organic layer; in its place,
The chemistry of topsoil long since ripped
Away—bare rock, bare clay, the gray, bare face

Of mudstone and the desert's gray expanse,
Once the wide {{x|Permian}} plain. Over all
Of this came the gray fungi's still advance,
Their silent reign, champagne of all who fall.

For when the primary producers fail,
When photosynthesis has ceased its toil
Across the continents, by every scale,
The kingdom that will profit, on the soil,

Is that which eats the dead: the fungi rose
In silence, after green—in fossil sheets
Of fungal spores have come, in place of those
Of pollen and plant spores, whose old repeats

Marked every {{x|Permian}} layer above,
A spike of fungal plenty, in the place
At the extinction boundary—a shove
Of death-eaters into the empty space

Of ecosystems—the composting host
Who had renewed the world, unseen, and slow,
In quiet work, each at its living post,
Of the decomposition, long ago.

And now they were the only presence, wide
And living, in the aftermath; the stir
Of all metabolism, side to side
Of the immense and empty lands that were.

The fungal world ate all the dying shed,
Ate up the fallen forests, the unfurled
And rotting bodies, every kind of dead
Organic matter in the wrecked old world—

And slowly, by their eating, they began
To bring the broken back into the ground,
Composting and completing, so the span
Of the next life could have its cycle found:

For soil is only dead things, processed through
The fungal network's discipline, and turned
To mineral, and to the rest, anew,
That plants can use again; the fungi churned

And plowed through hell in the literal sense
Of harrowing: they turned the dry and starved
Dead soil, and broke the rock-face, hard and dense,
With acids, and the hard compaction carved,

Made ready what the green would need to grow
Again: the undertakers, placid, still,
The workers of the interval, the slow
Between the old seed and the new, the till.

Then, through this poisoned world, a few remained—
Not the great or the famous, the well-known,
The celebrated—but the small, ingrained
In burrows, those who ate the dead—the stone

And scale of anything that could digest
The poorest meal in the most thrifty way—
And {{c|1673|Cynos}}, in his burrow's sealed-off nest,
Safe from the surface's worst, woke one day

Into a world reduced to nothing more
Than possibility; he spoke no word
Of lamentation, breathing at the door
Of his burrow the clearing air that stirred

Above, emerging into gray and bare
And empty landscape; and the love of breath
Drove him into the day, and not to care
About its emptiness, its hush of death.

And {{c|1724|Lystro}} too, dicynodont, had passed
Somehow alive—the less selective one,
The eater, the defiant front held fast
Of {{c|1723|Dicyno}}'s line; and when all was done,

There {{c|1724|Lystro}} found, when the extinction ceased,
A strange and solitary plenty: ground
That was his own in full, the west and east
Of the {{x|Triassic}}'s early land around

Was {{c|1724|Lystro}}'s, with no rival to compete;
The first years of the {{x|Triassic}}'s long strife,
Without a predator, his land complete,
Were his inheritance, his walk of life

The empty continent, in its extent,
Was walked by one small herbivore with beak,
Who ate whatever grew, and never went
Beyond the root and tuber he would seek.

{{c|1724|Lystro}} knew only he was hungry, and
That he was still alive, and it was well:
In the hell of the aftermath, to stand
Alive is all achievement; and that spell

Of bare survival is not lesser than
The {{x|Permian}}'s glorious peak; it's more,
Indeed, it is the greater; one who can
Endure the harrowing is heir, therefore,

To the next world, the whole world entire.
So let us honor those who harrowed hell,
The ones who kept alive life's fragile fire
Through silence: fungi, composting as well,

Survivors burrowing below the ground,
And {{c|1724|Lystro}} coasting in the gray world, sped
Forward upon the simple need, unbound,
To go on living; none of them was led

To know they were the seeds of everything
That followed; living, nothing more, though rough
And bare, they knew, and only hunger's sting.
That is enough. It always was enough.


# Chapter 84: A New Beginning

Then—after harrowing, after the long
Silence of all the poisoned world—the green.
Not all at once: no resurrection song
Announced it; and the first was never seen

By any eye that could report it; one
Small spore that landed on a bare stone slope
In the early {{x|Triassic}} morning sun,
The lonely, plain arrival of a hope

In the form of a bryophyte, a moss,
Whose spore had ridden out the acid years
In cryptobiosis—death, but not loss—
And waiting—and the stone's first trickled tears

Of mineral were all on which it fed.
The moss spread slowly, barely seen at all
Against the gray; but where its seeding spread,
The soil began, invisible and small:

The bond of moss and mineral would turn
Rock surface into the beginnings of
A substrate where the next seed's root could earn
A place to grow—and so it was the love

Of life asserted itself in small ways,
Too small to witness, but too vast to stop—
The temper of the {{x|Triassic}}'s first days
Was to rebuild from the last stone, the prop

Of any world: a single moss, alone
On one bare rock, the first year just begun
Of the new age, from dormancy now grown,
Unfurled; the worst was over, and was done;

The green was coming back. And next to come,
{{c|1702|Conifera}}, whose seeds had waited long
Within the soil through acid rain's hard drum,
Her cones' seeds, in their dormancy, held strong

Through all the dying, as they'd always lain
In waiting for the right conditions; now
The right ones, in {{x|Triassic}} morning, plain,
Were only this—enough to show her how:

Less poison and less heat; a little rain
With water less of acid, and so sweet
Enough for her to germinate again;
Her seeds broke through the soil, a quiet feat.

And from survivors—{{c|1724|Lystro}} and his kind,
And {{c|1673|Cynos}} from the burrow, and the few
And battered remnants—evolution's mind
Began again its patient work of new

Diversity: in every empty niche
Survivors radiated; {{c|1673|Cynos}} found
A world without an old, established, rich
Predator to contend with on the ground;

He searched out each ecological space
Available—small hunters, and the shy
And burrowing; and in a later race
Of time, the first true mammals would draw nigh,

The harbingers of warm blood at the full,
Of milk that's given freely to the young,
Of fur against the cold; all this, the pull,
Was coming, written in the code that clung

In the survivors' bold genetic store
Of memory: what {{c|1673|Cynos}} nearly was
Already; needing only time, and more
Of niches: opportunity, the cause

Of a new age, the seeding. And the sea,
The ocean too, was healing, slow and pained,
Its chemistry returned by slow degree
Toward kinder states: less acid, and regained

More oxygen dissolved; the sulfide's span
Grew less as the volcanoes ceased; and when,
In the new oxygen, the ray-fin clan,
The schism from the other fish that then

{{c|1505|Actinus}} had made in far coal-swamp days
Of plenty: of his clans, the most of all
In number, {{c|1699|Teleosteos}}, his rays,
Began to seize the empty ocean's hall.

The teleosts, who had been modest in
The {{x|Permian}} sea, their range of kinds slight
Beside marine invertebrates' great kin
That had held sway—now found the ocean, quite

Empty; they found that the invertebrates
Had drowned in acid; and they filled the space,
Each niche whose occupant had met those fates,
Into each depth and current, every place.

Teleost radiation then began,
The largest vertebrate explosion yet
In ocean history; and so it ran
Through the {{x|Triassic}}, slowly to offset

The emptiness with plenty; in the end
The ray-fin fish would form one half of all
The vertebrates on earth, and would extend
The universal presence, great and small,

In every water on the earth; but near
The aftermath it all began, the way
Resilience's daughters always appear:
Unclear, unpromising, and small, and gray—

A few survivors eating in a sea
Emptied of life, and finding, as all those
Revivers find, that emptiness can be
An opportunity in gray-hued clothes.

The first {{x|Easter}} of the {{x|Triassic}} was
Without a witness who could know it well—
Only the ordinary, classic cause
Of life's persistence, which no one could tell

From simple hunger, or from the bare, stern
Mechanics of survival; and yet still
This too is resurrection: the return
Of green upon the bare and empty hill,

The wet and patient moss on limestone; fern
Uncurling from the ash and soil; and, there,
{{c|1724|Lystro}} walking in the new age's turn
At its first morning; and the toil, the care

Of building up again, not knowing so,
That you rebuild—just being, and alive,
And going forward, going, on they go
Toward whatever life can give, and thrive.

Honor the {{x|Triassic}} morning—the gray
Light of the new world, filling, more and more,
With green of those who lived—with each new day
A little less of death, a little lore

Becoming history—the tale of life
That always finds a way to be again
After each fire and after every knife
Of mass extinction—and the old refrain

Of green returning, of the clearing sea,
And of the first small mammal, looking round
At morning, seeing chances, empty, free:
New world, new age, a cradle, safe and sound.

---

# Pisces (4宮) - Days 85-112


# Chapter 85: The Return to the Sea

The land was bare. The sea was bare. And yet
Within the bare world lay the oldest call—
The water that gave birth to life, the wet
And welcoming abyss, first source of all,

That still remembered every form it made
And held within its chemistry the means
Of feeding, floating, breathing in the shade
Of waves—and now, in the {{x|Triassic}}'s scenes

Of devastation, some of {{c|1669|Sauros}}' kin
Looked seaward from the ruined shore and chose
The oldest path: to go back, to begin
Again in water what the land would close.

For this was not the first time. Long before,
In {{x|Permian}}'s last age, a humble line
Had tried the water—{{c|1244|Mesos}}, from the shore
Of all {{p|Gondwana}}'s southern lakes, the fine

And lizard-shaped, with newt-like tails that swept
The shallows of fresh water for their prey—
First of {{c|1661|Amnios}}' children who had crept
Back toward the water from the land's dry way.

But {{c|1244|Mesos}} was not truly {{c|1669|Sauros}}' son—
His place within the family was clear:
Of {{c|1677|Paraps}}' stock he came, and not of one
That bore two windows, the diapsid gear—

But he had shown the way: that those who sealed
Their eggs against the water could return
To water: so the covenant, revealed
As two-way door, not exile, not a burn

Of bridges back to {{c|1725|Tethys}}' ancient home.
{{c|1244|Mesos}} perished in the {{x|Permian}}'s end—
The lesson lived: the sea was free to roam
For any who had lungs and limbs to bend

Toward the swimming shape. And in the wake
Of the {{x|Great Dying}}, when the ocean lay
Still poisoned, slowly healing—for the sake
Of empty niches stretching every way—

New lines of life remembered {{c|1244|Mesos}}' road:
First came {{c|1726|Ichthyos}}—children of the scale
Who read the water's oldest fluid code
And built their bodies for the current's trail.

They entered from the shoreline lizard-shaped
And small, with legs still bearing toes and claws,
But over generations they had draped
Their limbs in flesh and fins without a pause

Or hesitation; for the sea would pay
Each change that brought them to the swimming plan;
The adaptation hurried on its way
Because the prize was vast: the boundless span

Of empty ocean, free of any foe,
Where any who could swim and hunt would find
A feast of fish wherever they would go
Across the healing waters of the mind

Of {{c|1725|Tethys}}, slowly waking from her grief.
And {{c|1726|Ichthyos}} grew large, then larger; some
The size of whales in the {{x|Triassic}} reef
Of the healing sea; {{c|1727|Shonisauros}}, from

The western {{p|Tethys}}, reached the length of ships,
Enormous eyes like dinner plates that peered
Through dim {{x|Triassic}} waters—at his lips
He had no teeth at all; his jaw was cleared

For a wide suction mouth to draw in prey
Like a great vacuum of the ancient deep.
And in those same {{x|Triassic}} waters, gray
And strange, the clans of {{c|1728|Thalattos}} would creep

Along the shallow coast with bent-down snout
And crushing teeth for shellfish on the floor—
A group of {{c|1669|Sauros}}' house, a branch without
Long issue in the ages—and no more

Than brief {{x|Triassic}} test, a passing style
In strange-faced, shallow-water coastal role—
But in their time, magnificent, worthwhile:
The snub-nosed hunters where the tide would roll.

And from the {{c|1677|Paraps}} line—from {{c|1678|Turtlos}}' own
Deep kindred—came the {{c|1729|Nothros}} to the shore:
Long-necked and paddle-limbed, in {{p|Tethys}}' zone
They hunted fish with needle-teeth, and bore

The first of {{c|1730|Sauropteros}}' ancient mark:
The flipper built from what had been a hand,
The body streamlined for the coastal dark,
The lungs that breathed at surface, then the grand

Descent to hunt below. So {{c|1729|Nothros}} was
The father of a dynasty to come—
His paddle-form would echo down because
His children's children's children would become

Plesiosaurs—but that is yet to tell.
Beside him {{c|1731|Plakos}} took a different way:
Heavy-bodied, built like a living shell,
He dove to the floor of the shallow bay

And crushed the mollusks with his pavement teeth—
So broad and flat for grinding shell to dust—
A bottom-feeder in the reef beneath
{{x|Triassic}} shallows, armored, slow, robust.

And {{c|1731|Plakos}} looked like {{c|1678|Turtlos}} in his way—
Round-bodied, armored, patient on the floor—
And this was not coincidence: the clay
Of {{c|1677|Paraps}}' ancient body-plan once more

Expressed itself in water as on land:
The turtle-shape, the armored, patient form
That carries home upon its back, the planned
And fortress-bodied refuge from the storm.

Seven lines tried out the {{x|Triassic}} sea:
{{c|1244|Mesos}}' old memory, {{c|1726|Ichthyos}}' speed,
{{c|1728|Thalattos}} and his strange coast-crawling spree,
{{c|1729|Nothros}}' long neck and {{c|1731|Plakos}}' patient greed,

And others yet unnamed who dipped their toes
And found the water welcoming or cold—
But all wrote down the lesson that life knows
And has rehearsed since the first story told:

The sea is never truly left behind.
The covenant of {{c|1661|Amnios}}: a door,
And not a wall—and those with lungs could find
The ocean's invitation evermore.

So honor those who turned from ruined land
And chose the healing water's ancient way—
Who traded claw for flipper, foot for hand
Rebuilt to swim; life returns to the bay

It left, and finds it waiting, patient, deep,
As it had waited since the world was young,
And full of room for those who choose to leap:
The sea from which the oldest life had sprung.


# Chapter 86: The Ruling Reptiles

Now hear of {{c|1681|Archon}}, youngest son and last
Of {{c|1679|Eureps}}, in a coal-swamp hollow log
Born small, who seemed the least of all the cast
In {{c|1669|Sauros}}' line, worn creature of the bog,

So small he hid in undergrowth and ran
On hind legs faster than his brothers could.
Not armored like the plated {{c|1677|Paraps}} clan,
No venom, and no size—but {{c|1681|Archon}} stood

On the {{x|Triassic}} stage, where every throne
Was vacant, and {{x|Permian}} lords were ash—
And in that emptiness he made his own
A realm of speed and metabolic flash.

For {{c|1681|Archon}} had a gift his brothers lacked:
A heart divided into chambers four
That pumped the blood more strongly, cleanly packed
With oxygen to every cell and pore—

And some of {{c|1681|Archon}}'s children ran so hot
Their blood approached the warm—not mammal-warm,
Not {{c|1673|Cynos}}' careful thermostat; their lot
Was heat and fire enough to outperform

The sluggish sprawl of {{c|1680|Squamos}}' kindred cold.
Two sons had {{c|1681|Archon}} in {{x|Triassic}} morn:
Great {{c|1732|Cruros}}, firstborn, heavy, proud, and bold,
And {{c|1733|Avemeta}}, lighter, later-born.

{{c|1732|Cruros}}, the elder, was the one who claimed
The rivers and the lowland flood-plains first—
His children were the crocodile-line, famed
For ambush, armor, patience, and the burst

Of violence launched from the water's edge.
Rauisuchians walked on upright limbs
And hunted like great wolves along the sedge
Of {{x|Triassic}} rivers, and on their rims

{{c|1732|Cruros}}' line built up its river domain:
Phytosaurs with the crocodilian shape
Long before crocodiles would claim that reign—
These were the first to wear the water's drape

Of armor-scale and elongated snout,
Of eyes that watched above the water's line
And waited for the prey to venture out—
The river-king design, a pattern fine

For each watercourse on {{p|Pangaea}}'s face.
And {{c|1732|Cruros}}' children were {{x|Triassic}} lords—
They ruled the land and water, and their race
Seemed destined for ten thousand years of hordes

And hunting-realms along the riverside.
No creature in the young {{x|Triassic}} stood
Against rauisuchians' hungry stride
Or challenged the phytosaur's neighborhood.

But {{c|1733|Avemeta}}—lighter, quicker, small—
Took to the uplands and the drier ground
Where {{c|1732|Cruros}}' heavy children could not crawl
As easily; there {{c|1733|Avemeta}} found

His own advantage: hollow bones for speed,
Long legs for running, small frames that could eat
The scraps and edges—every humble deed
Of second sons who make a life complete

From what the firstborn leaves behind.

                                       From him
Would come the dinosaurs—but that is next—
Now {{c|1733|Avemeta}} ran along the rim
Of {{c|1732|Cruros}}' realm, both humble and perplexed

At his own smallness, giants in his sight.
The archosaurs then split {{p|Pangaea}}'s spoils:
And {{c|1732|Cruros}} held the lowlands in despite
Of any rival, master of the soils

And watercourses; {{c|1733|Avemeta}} crept
Through upland scrub and arid highland where
The rainfall was too sparse, the rivers swept
Too thin to hold a crocodilian's lair.

This is the lesson of the ruling line:
That greatness need not first look like power;
That at the outset {{c|1681|Archon}}'s true design
Was not the elder son's triumphant hour

But in the younger, patient and unseen,
The one who ran on hollow bones and stayed
Along his brother's borders, in between,
And waited for the world to be remade.

{{c|1732|Cruros}} ruled the {{x|Triassic}} entire—
But {{c|1733|Avemeta}}'s heirs would inherit
What {{c|1732|Cruros}} lost when the world caught fire:
For the future favors patient merit.

So honor {{c|1681|Archon}}'s house of hollow bone
And heart of chambers four and upright stride—
The ruling reptiles who would seize the throne
Of every continent and every tide.


# Chapter 87: The Long-Necked Fisher

The strangest child of the {{x|Triassic}} shore:
{{c|1734|Tanystros}}, archosauromorph, whose frame
Defied all reason with a neck that bore
More vertebrae than sense could rightly claim.

His body had a man's length, and no more—
A sturdy, lizard-shaped and humble thing—
But from his shoulders grew a neck before
His head that stretched, an impossible string:

Three times the length of body, stiff and straight,
A fishing-rod of bone, a tiny head
Perched at the far end, baited with the weight
Of small sharp teeth for catching fish—instead

Of swimming to his prey, {{c|1734|Tanystros}} stood
On the {{x|Triassic}} shoreline, on the rocks
Above the {{p|Tethys}} shallows, where he could
Spear what he sought below from coastal stocks

Without his body entering the waves.
Think of a heron frozen in its stance—
But stretched to the absurd, a shape that saves
Its lungs from water by the sheer expanse

Of neck between the breathing chest and jaws
That hunted underneath the surface foam—
A compromise that broke all normal laws
Of vertebrate design: to fish from home

Without the toil of swimming.

                               Nor was he
Alone in strangeness; the {{x|Triassic}} age
Was such a time as no age since would see:
It was a living and evolving stage

Of trial, where at once each body plan,
Each variation, found its room to thrive,
Was tried in the great recovery's span
For months or millions of years, kept alive

Before the sorting came. And he had kin:
The {{c|1735|Protorosauros}}, a long-necked clan
Of archosauromorphs, whose claim was thin
On history and brief—and so they ran

The {{x|Triassic}} coasts in their odd parade
Of reaching necks and small-toothed fishing heads,
Of bodies built for shoreline's serenade
Where ocean meets the rock in tidal beds.

Some of {{c|1734|Tanystros}}' kindred went to sea—
Not fully, but enough to paddle out
Beyond the shallows, swimming partially free
Of shore, their long necks sweeping all about

For fish beneath them as they surface-swam—
Half in the water, like the first attempt
Of {{c|1681|Archon}}'s wider family to cram
Themselves into the sea's biome, exempt

From the commitment {{c|1726|Ichthyos}} had made
Of leaving land behind for evermore—
These were the dabblers, wading in the shade
Along the {{x|Triassic}}'s uncertain shore.

Through the first ten million years of that age,
The boundaries between the land and sea
Were blurred by those who stood on every stage
At once—who were not fully what they'd be,

Experimenting with the ocean's edge.
{{c|1734|Tanystros}}' clan would perish long before
{{x|Jurassic}} dawned; their evolution's pledge
Was local, brief, a footnote in the lore

Of {{x|Triassic}} time. And yet they gave birth
To truth the {{x|Mesozoic}} would yet prove:
That border between ocean and dry earth
Is not a wall but gradient, a groove

That life moves back and forth across at will—
From {{c|1244|Mesos}} in {{x|Permian}} lakes to these
Long-necked {{x|Triassic}} fishers on the sill
Of {{p|Tethys}}' coast, to plesiosaur seas

That were to come—each age found those who'd stand
Astride the boundary, and who refused
To choose between the kingdom of dry land
And ocean depths. The line for them was used

As highway, not as barrier.

                               Give praise
To shapes the strange {{x|Triassic}} morning made—
{{c|1734|Tanystros}}, with his neck's absurd displays,
The fishing-rod design that briefly swayed

Above the waves and caught his silver prey
Without a single stroke of swimming fin—
A shape that served its own {{x|Triassic}} day
And asked for nothing but the fish therein.

Not every form endures. Not every plan
Survives the sorting of the ages' test.
But all that lived, however brief its span,
Was life's own answer to the question—blessed

With the same stubborn will to eat and breed
That moves the stars and turns the spiral arm.
{{c|1734|Tanystros}} on his rock fulfilled his need
Then vanished; the {{x|Triassic}} took no harm

From having made him—for the sea keeps room
For each experiment, however strange,
And honors every shape between the bloom
Of life and death across its endless range.


# Chapter 88: The First Terrible Lizards

Of {{c|1733|Avemeta}}'s children, hear the start—
Not the great and terrible they became,
But the humble, the small, the racing heart
Of creatures that did not yet know their name.

For the first dinosaurs were modest things:
No larger than a dog, with hollow bones
And hands that grasped, and legs like coiled springs
Built for running over {{x|Triassic}} stones.

In uplands of the south, {{p|Gondwana}}'s land,
Where {{c|1732|Cruros}}' river-children held no sway,
The earliest of {{c|1733|Avemeta}}'s band
Appeared: {{c|1736|Deinos}}, and his {{x|Triassic}} day

Was spent in running, catching, staying small,
While {{c|1732|Cruros}}' rauisuchians would prowl
The lowlands and the river-valleys, tall
And heavy; little dinosaurs would howl

And chirp in upland scrub and thin-aired heights.
{{c|1736|Deinos}} is "terrible," {{c|1669|Sauros}} "lizard"—
The first to bear that name had modest sights:
Not terrible: much more like a wizard

Of economy: slight frame, hollow bone
That saved the weight, long legs for upright stance,
And hands with grasping fingers that had grown
Three-fingered, dextrous, built for catching chance

Bug, lizard, little mammal in the brush.
They ran on two legs—bipedal and light,
With tails outstretched for balance in the rush
Of hunting dashes through {{x|Triassic}} night.

{{c|1737|Eoraptoros}} was among the first—
"Dawn plunderer," the later name that men
Would give his bones—but in his own time, versed
In nothing grander than to eat, and then

To eat again tomorrow. He was small—
Three feet of hunter in {{p|Gondwana}}'s south,
Undifferentiated teeth for all
His prey: he ate whatever reached his mouth.

{{c|1738|Herrerasauros}} ran beside him there—
A little larger, with a sliding jaw
That let his lower bite extend and snare
His prey with an articulated maw

That other reptiles lacked: innovation
That hinted that the hunting age was near:
The theropods would build a predation
Empire spanning every biosphere.

But they were few, with no {{x|Triassic}} share—
Not yet: rauisuchians owned the plains,
The phytosaurs held every river's lair,
And {{c|1736|Deinos}}' children lived on what remains

The great ones left behind—the edges, scraps,
The upland territory none wanted,
The arid margins of {{x|Triassic}} maps
Where rainfall failed, and large beasts were daunted.

Thus kingdoms are begun: not at the heart
But at the fringe; not on the fertile plain
Where strong ones fatten, but within the part
Where one who rents the margin must obtain

From every turtle, beetle, all he can.
The pressure of the edge made {{c|1736|Deinos}}' line
So lean and so efficient, with a plan
To make more out of less, to run the fine

Machine of flesh on less fuel, water, air,
And still outrun the ones who wished them dead.
Three lines would branch from {{c|1736|Deinos}}' early lair:
{{c|1739|Theros}}, the beast-footed, who would be fed

On flesh and carry on the hunting art;
{{c|1740|Sauropos}}, who would grow to walk on four
Great legs and eat the green world, counterpart
Of {{c|1739|Theros}}' violence—the herbivore

That would become the largest thing to stride
Across the earth; and, third, the bird-hip kind,
{{c|1741|Ornithis}}, pelvis rearranged inside
To hold a greater gut, and so designed

For breaking down the cellulose in food.
Three houses of the dinosaurs were born
In {{x|Triassic}} uplands, a threefold brood
From {{c|1733|Avemeta}}'s children, small and worn

And unremarkable—who did not know
They held the future {{x|Mesozoic}} world
Within their hollow bones and racing flow
Of warm-ish blood—the banners yet unfurled

Of tyranny and thunder and the sky.
Honor the small beginnings—every great
And overwhelming line that storms on by
Was once a creature running, running late

For dinner in the uplands, chasing bugs
Through scrubland no empire deigned to own—
And finding there, in poverty's tight hugs,
The seeds of every future ever sown.


# Chapter 89: The Dolphin Shape

There is a shape the ocean loves.

                                    The sea
Asks every swimmer the same question: How
Will you move through me?—and the answer, free
Of lineage or bias, is the prow

Of dolphins: fusiform, with tapered head,
The crescent tail that drives from side to side
Or up and down, the form all oceans wed
To speed in water: tested, proven, tried

By every group that ever hunted fish
In open ocean at the swimming pace
Of something that must catch its fleeing dish
Or starve—the water shapes them to the race

And every time the answer is the same.
{{c|1726|Ichthyos}} found this answer first among
The reptiles of {{x|Triassic}} time; his claim
To dolphin form was older, deeper, wrung

From fifty million years' {{x|Triassic}} sea
Before the dolphins of a later age
Would find it too—convergence's decree,
The ocean's only universal page:

That physics trumps all ancestry; the form
That works in water works for fish and whale,
Ichthyosaur alike—the ancient norm
Of hydrodynamics that writes one tale

In every lineage that tries the deep.
By mid-{{x|Triassic}}, {{c|1726|Ichthyos}}' young bore
No trace of the limbed ancestor who'd creep
Ashore between his hunts. Legs were no more:

Flippers now, four paddles for the steering,
A tail with flukes, curved like a half-moon blade,
A dorsal fin for poise, and the veering
And cutting of a body purpose-made

For speed—{{c|1726|Ichthyos}} could not walk on land
And did not need to; and he gave live birth
In water, like the mammals' later brand
Of sea-return—no egg upon the earth

Required, no beach to haul up on to lay—
His young were born tail-first in the ocean
And swam beside their mothers from that day,
Fully formed, already in the motion

Of the hunt.

             And great {{c|1727|Shonisauros}} grew
To the length of whales—fifteen meters long—
In the {{x|Triassic}} seas of {{p|Tethys}}, through
The corridors of {{p|Panthalassa}} strong

And wide, where the enormous ocean stretched
From pole to pole on {{p|Pangaea}}'s far side—
And smaller {{c|1726|Ichthyos}} hunted and fetched
Their fish and squid through every current and tide.

Their eyes were larger than all other beasts'—
Enormous orbs that drank the deep-sea dark
And let them hunt below the light at feasts
Whose annals the deep wrote in each hunt's arc.

In twilight zones where cephalopods hide
And fish escaped the sunlit layer's glare,
But {{c|1726|Ichthyos}} pursued, the dark defied,
And guided onward by the ancient prayer

Of eyes; faint bioluminescence seen.
And in their ears, the bones that once were jaw
Of their land-dwelling forebears, now marine,
Conducted sound through water, and would draw

The intimate vibration of the deep
That told of prey and predator and reef
And current, so he did not need to keep
His surface-senses, having found relief

In the new senses water offered free.
This is the lesson of convergent form:
The universe has favorites: the sea
Rewards the same solution to the storm

Of physics, whether mammal, fish, or scaled
Reptilian swimmer—and the dolphin shape
Is not a choice but an equation, nailed
By mathematics of the fluid's drape

Across a moving body—there is one
Best answer to the question of the speed
In water; every lineage that's won
The ocean's race has read the selfsame creed.

Sharks found it first in {{x|Devonian}} tide—
The tuna found it in the bony fish—
{{c|1726|Ichthyos}} found it on the reptile side,
And dolphins later from the mammal's wish—

And each time the same fusiform design,
The tapered snout, crescent-tail propulsion,
The countershading, dark along the spine,
Warm pale belly below, the expulsion

Of drag and the embrace of speed.

                                     Then praise
Ichthyosaurs, who wore the ocean's shape
Long before dolphins claimed it in their days—
Who proved that evolution's finest drape

Is worn by many lines, each in its turn,
And every one that answers water's call
Will find the same shape waiting, theirs to earn—
The dolphin form that is the sea's for all.


# Chapter 90: The Turtle's Cousins

Now hear the deeper tale of sea-return—
For when the {{c|1729|Nothros}} paddled from the shore
And {{c|1731|Plakos}} crushed his shells, they bore a turn
In {{c|1677|Paraps}}' ancient story, something more

Than any mere adapting to the wave:
They were the turtle-kindred going home.
Remember {{c|1677|Paraps}}, eldest son, the grave,
Of solid, heavy skull, who would not roam

Like {{c|1679|Eureps}}, with two windows in his head?
For {{c|1677|Paraps}} built the shell—the {{c|1678|Turtlos}} line
Who through the meadows bear their homes instead—
And {{c|1677|Paraps}}' deeper family, the fine

And old connection with the {{c|1681|Archon}}'s house,
Made him the sister-branch of all that ruled:
{{c|1678|Turtlos}} and {{c|1681|Archon}}, quiet as a mouse
The former, and the latter never fooled

By any rival's bluff—but sister-kin
Beneath it all, turtle and dinosaur
Joined at the root, both carrying within
The same deep heritage from {{c|1669|Sauros}}' floor.

{{c|1730|Sauropteros}}, the flipper-bearers, these
Were {{c|1677|Paraps}}' ocean-children, stem and root
Of turtle-form adapted to the seas:
Not {{c|1678|Turtlos}} himself, but that ancient suit

Of body-plan expressed in marine terms.
And {{c|1729|Nothros}} was the first to show the signs:
The paddle-limb; the barrel chest affirms
A lung-breathing diver's need; and the lines

Of body built for underwater flight—
Not fish's tail-propulsion, but the wing
Beneath the waves, the flippers' pulling might
That drew him through the water: ancient swing

Of arms later plesiosaurs would hone
Into an art. But {{c|1729|Nothros}} was the first,
In {{x|Triassic}} {{p|Tethys}}, where coastal stone
Of {{p|Pangaea}}'s granite shelf dropped, immersed

In deeper water; and the fish that hid
There, sheltered, were his own to hunt and catch
With long neck's reach; his needle teeth would bid
For anything that swam into the snatch.

His children grew; some kept nothosaur form,
Like otters, coming to the shore to rest
And breed—but others ventured through the storm
To deeper water, and these were the best

Adapted for the open sea, and these
Became {{c|1742|Plesios}} in the later age—
Plesiosaurs who never left the seas,
Who wrote {{x|Jurassic}} ocean's grandest page.

And {{c|1731|Plakos}}, cousin on the bottom shelf,
The other path: the turtle's echo, slow,
Round, armored, and content to feed himself
On shellfish in the shallows' warm tableau.

He was in sea what {{c|1678|Turtlos}} was on land:
The patient, armored, steady form and low
That {{c|1677|Paraps}} always built, the bodies planned
For long endurance and not made for show.

The {{c|1730|Sauropteros}}—{{c|1729|Nothros}}, {{c|1731|Plakos}}, too,
And plesiosaurs yet to come—were all
Born of the ancient purpose running through
Each child of {{c|1677|Paraps}}' house: the turtle's call

To build the body strong and carry on,
Whether upon the land in shell-and-plate
Or in the sea with flipper-paddle drawn
Through water—{{c|1677|Paraps}}' children navigate

Both worlds with one patient architecture.
Here is the lineage the oceans keep:
{{c|1678|Turtlos}} on his log, the vast conjecture
Of plesiosaurs hunting in the deep,

Are kindred—branches of one ancient tree
Rooted in {{c|1677|Paraps}}' solid skull, which spread
And flowered on the land and in the sea
In forms that look unlike, but share the thread

Of one deep plan: the patience armored, slow,
Lung-breathing endurance, the certain way
Of living—these equations, high and low,
Of {{c|1677|Paraps}}' house are written to this day

In every turtle basking on his stone
And each plesiosaur below the reef
Of {{x|Mesozoic}} seas—they share the bone
Of common ancestry, the shared belief

That life is best lived slowly, strongly, deep,
With armor on your back, air in your lung,
And patience as the covenant you keep
With the world that was and the world yet young.

Then honor the bond—{{c|1678|Turtlos}} on the land
And {{c|1730|Sauropteros}}, down beneath the wave—
Both children of one father's patient hand,
Both built to last, both certain, and both brave.


# Chapter 91: Pangaea Divides

The world was one, and then the world was not:
{{p|Pangaea}}, the {{p|All-Land}}, the single face
Of continent that held in one great lot
Each shore and every mountain, every place

Where life had built its kingdoms on the stone—
Began to crack along its ancient seams
Where mantle heat, persistent and alone,
Had pushed against the crust in magma-streams

A hundred million years.

                               The rift began
At the {{x|Triassic}}'s heart: unzipping, slow,
The continental skin, the split that ran
From north to south, the mantle's blood aglow

Dripped in the crack and filled it up with new
Seafloor, basalt that cooled in salt water,
Pushed halves apart: a centimeter's due
Each year: geology's patient slaughter

Of unity, to make the world diverse.
{{p|Laurasia}} to the north, {{p|Gondwana}} south—
The ancient names that, in divided verse,
The parted lands would carry in the mouth

Of all the ages still to come. And wide
Between them grew the {{p|Tethys}} Sea; the warm
And shallow waters of its growing tide
Fed new corals, new fish, the reborn swarm

Of marine life in the expanding space.
But first the breaking: the {{x|Carnian}} rains.
In mid-{{x|Triassic}} time they drowned each trace
Of the dry, arid world, and all the plains

That had been desert for ten million years
Grew wet at once: {{x|Carnian Pluvial}}
Episode, a whole million years of tears
From skies that had forgot alluvial

And the monsoon—and now recalled them all.
The cause: volcanic and tectonic shift
Of plates and currents, requiem and pall
For dry {{x|Triassic}} lands, and yet a gift

Of water to a world that had been parched—
But water that arrived too fast, too much,
And ecosystems that had slowly marched
Toward desert-adaptation lost their touch

And struggled in the sudden wet.

                                  This was
The proto-disruption, not extinction,
Ecological reshuffling, because
Old arrangements lost their high distinction

In the changed climate: what had thrived in drought
Now drowned in rain, and what had waited for
The wet now flourished—and the sorting out
Left {{c|1732|Cruros}}' children weakened at the core

While {{c|1733|Avemeta}}'s nimble dinosaurs,
At home in margins, in all things changing,
Found new chances in the {{x|Carnian}} doors
That opened on a world rearranging.

The rains withdrew; the world resumed its drift.
But now the balance tilted: {{c|1736|Deinos}}' kin
Had gained a foothold from the climate's shift,
And {{c|1732|Cruros}}' dominance, though far from thin,

Was never quite so absolute again.
The cracking still went on: {{p|Pangaea}}'s seams
Grew wider by the year; and it was then
The isolated lands' own separate dreams

Began: each landmass carrying its own
Cargo of creatures to isolation,
Where evolution worked on local bone,
Local climate—each a separate nation

Of life, evolving its own solutions.
The {{p|Tethys}} became an ocean highway,
Warm equatorial contributions,
Currents connecting east and west midway

Of the world; {{c|1726|Ichthyos}} and {{c|1729|Nothros}} swam
Its corridors, the reptiles of the sea,
Who followed fish across the growing dam
Of the new seafloor, spreading by degree

In basalt, mile by mile, along the rents
Between the lands. {{p|Pangaea}}'s breaking: seed
Of every future difference: events
That gave each continent its unique creed

Of creatures: marsupials of the south,
Placentals of the north, the island birds,
Lemurs of {{p|Madagascar}}—from the mouth
Of this great cracking came the different words

Of life's vocabulary on each shore.
But now, in the middle {{x|Triassic}} age,
The breaking had just begun—nothing more
Than wider seaway and a wetter stage

For the same cast of characters to play
Their parts upon—{{c|1732|Cruros}} by the river,
{{c|1736|Deinos}} on heights, {{c|1726|Ichthyos}} in the bay,
{{c|1673|Cynos}} in his burrow, stubborn liver

Through each age's change.

                              Honor the breaking—
For the one world had to become many
Ere the richness of the many-making
Could fill the earth with more life than any

Lone continent could hold; the division
Was not a wound, but multiplication,
Not loss, but a widening of vision
Of what life could be in separation.


# Chapter 92: The Cynodont's Vigil

While the great ones ruled the {{x|Triassic}} plains—
While {{c|1732|Cruros}} held the streams and the lowlands
And {{c|1736|Deinos}}' children ran in upland lanes—
The young of {{c|1673|Cynos}} lived in small commands

Of burrowers, nocturnal, careful bands
Who had inherited {{x|Permian}} loss
And carried in their milk-producing glands,
Fur-touched skin, the memory of the cross

That {{c|1668|Synaps}}' dynasty had borne: the fall
From {{x|Permian}} to {{x|Triassic}} shadow,
From the world's great lords down to creatures small
Enough to hide in a grassy meadow.

For {{c|1673|Cynos}} had been great—remember this—
His father {{c|1672|Theraps}}, and before him, too,
Grandsire {{c|1670|Pelyon}}, ruled in tooth and kiss
The {{x|Permian}} world; each hellion that slew

And gentle grazer of synapsid age
Had answered to the house of {{c|1668|Synaps}} then—
But the {{x|Great Dying}} wrote a different page,
And those who lived were not the mighty men

Of {{x|Permian}} heights; but burrowers, small,
The ones who ate the least and needed least,
The underground endurers, who through all
Outlived the fire and the poisoned feast.

And now, in the {{x|Triassic}}'s middle years,
The children of {{c|1673|Cynos}} grew smaller still—
For archosaurs above pressed down with fears
And appetite on all that came to fill

A niche above the size of shrews.

                                      The night
Became the cynodont's domain—the dark
Where cold-blooded archosaurs lost their might
And the warm-blooded mammal-kin could mark

Their ground by scent and sound, and by the feel
Of whiskers in the dark—those whiskers that
{{c|1673|Cynos}} had first grown, the sensory wheel
Of vibrissae that turned the blind and flat

The world of night into a map of touch.
And in the late {{x|Triassic}}, from the least
Of {{c|1673|Cynos}}' shrinking children, came the clutch
Of first true mammals: {{c|1743|Mammos}}, lowly, least

Of all the heirs of {{c|1668|Synaps}}' ancient line,
Who bore the full inheritance at last:
The three ear-bones that heard the world's design
In frequencies the reptiles could not cast

Their hearing toward. Their fathers' jaw-bones, old,
Had moved into the middle ear, become
The hammer, anvil, stirrup—fold on fold
Through a full hundred million years, the sum

Of {{c|1668|Synaps}}' extra jaw's slow migration
Toward a new and finer use: the ear,
Acute and intimate: transformation
Of what had been a jaw. So, year by year,

Did evolution steer the surplus bone
And turn it into something new: a sense
So delicate it heard the forest's tone
In registers exquisite and intense.

And milk—for {{c|1743|Mammos}} gave his young the gift
Of milk: the mother's body was the source,
Within—an evolutionary shift
That freed the newborn from the egg's set course

And bound it to the mother's warmth instead—
A cord of nourishment more free to bend
Than any yolk-sac: where the mother fed,
The infant fed, a bond no harm could end,

And portable across whatever land
Or climate or disaster came.

                                  And fur—
The full and covering warmth, the body's band
Of insulation that allowed the stir

Of metabolism through the cold night,
That kept the body's engine running when
The archosaurs went slow—the mammal's right
To all the nighttime world, the moonlit den

Where small eyes gleamed and small teeth cracked the shell
Of beetle, and small whiskers read the dark,
Small bodies kept themselves alive and well
On what the daylight giants left—the bark

And seed and insect of the shadow-world.
A vigil of a hundred million years
Of smallness, of the patient flag unfurled
In darkness, of the nighttime pioneers

Who kept the old synapsid flame alive
Through the {{x|Mesozoic}}'s long dominion
Of archosaur lords—content to survive
And wait and hold, keeping one opinion:

That the night was theirs, and that the future
Was written in the milk and fur and bone
Of the smallest creatures—that the suture
Between the past and the world yet unknown

Lay in the burrow: mammal, warm and small,
Who heard in frequencies that the giants
Could never know, and would outlast them all.
So honor the vigil's quiet clients

Of night, who kept alive the ancient fire
Of {{c|1668|Synaps}}' dynasty through all the dark—
And waited—night rewards their desire,
The patient inherit each empty park.


# Chapter 93: The Pack Hunters

In late {{x|Triassic}} washes, dry and bare,
Where the red sandstone baked beneath a sun
That knew no ice at either pole—the air
Of classic greenhouse, where {{c|1744|Pangaea}}'s run

Of warmth made desert of the land within,
There {{c|1745|Coelos}} hunted.

                    Slender, light, and fast,
A theropod, a small dog's weight, but thin,
But longer, with a whip-tail and the cast

Of a creature built wholly for the chase—
And {{c|1745|Coelos}} ran in packs across the flats
Of western {{p|Gondwana}}; and in the race
The hunt was not the solitary bats

And claws of one lone predator's design
But something new: coordinated run
Of many hunters in a curving line
That drove the prey toward the others—one

By one, the pack's members each played their part
In strategy beyond one single brain—
The hunt required a group, required the art
Of signals, calls sent out across the plain,

The reading of another's body-lean,
The understanding that if I go left
Then you go right—between us and between
The prey, the route of escape narrows—deft

And terrible in its efficient skill.
And {{c|1745|Coelos}} left his kin entombed in stone:
At what our later maps call {{p|Ghost Ranch}}, still
Lies buried there a mass of fossil bone

To tell the tale: dozens of {{c|1745|Coelos}}' clan
Buried together in a single flood,
A troop preserved in death, the social plan
Of group life written in the ancient mud.

They were not large—three meters, lightly built,
With grasping three-fingered hands, hollow bones—
But what they lacked in mass they had in guilt-
Free cooperation: hunting in the zones

Of chance that only groups can hope to reach.
This was {{c|1736|Deinos}}' first great innovation—
Not size, not strength, not venom's toxic breach,
But social bond, pack coordination

That would echo through the theropod line
A hundred million years: the raptor crew
Of the {{x|Cretaceous}} hunting in a fine
And deadly chorus—actors, all, on cue—

In a play that {{c|1745|Coelos}} had first rehearsed
On the {{x|Triassic}}'s arid scrubland stage.
The prey they hunted? Anything that durst
To walk the open ground: in that late age,

{{x|Triassic}} heritage of mid-sized game:
Small ornithischians browsing the brush,
The last rhynchosaurs, with the ancient claim
Of beak-herbivory; the early rush

Prosauropods, {{c|1740|Sauropos}}' first attempt
At the long-necked, long-tailed, four-legged form,
To be the thunder-lizards: these, exempt
From nothing, not from tooth or from the storm

Of {{c|1745|Coelos}}' pack descending in a wave
Of chirping, slashing, small-toothed predation
That bled the larger prey, took what they gave
In death by a thousand cuts—the station

Of small predators hunting what is large
Through numbers, speed, coordinated will.
And {{c|1732|Cruros}}' children, watching, kept their charge:
Rauisuchians and phytosaurs still

Held all the lowlands and the waterways—
But {{c|1745|Coelos}} and his pack ran in the dry
Uplands, the arid basins, and the haze
Of desert's edge, where greater lords passed by

Without a glance—for what was there to see
In packs of small and slender running things?
Nothing, they thought—and yet it was the key
To everything the coming future brings:

The greatest power is not tooth alone
But the bond between hunters, and the call
That says: together we are more than bone
And claw—together we can bring the tall

And heavy to the ground.

                              Honor the first
Pack-hunter, {{c|1745|Coelos}}, of the dinosaurs,
Who proved, in the {{x|Triassic}}'s heat and thirst,
That cooperation opens the doors

To evolution's sophistication—
That what one cannot do alone, a band
Of kin in hunting's coordination
Is able to achieve; upon this strand

Of social innovation, from the start,
The pack would grow, and with it, cunning's reach;
Future theropods would build terror's art,
And learn the lesson that the hunters teach.


# Chapter 94: The First Wings

Now hear of those who solved the oldest dream
Of every land-bound creature looking up:
{{c|1746|Pteros}}, who rode the thermal's rising steam
And drank the sky like water from a cup.

Not bird—for birds were dinosaurs, and these
Were something else: the children of a branch
Near {{c|1733|Avemeta}}'s root, who took the breeze
And stretched a single finger to a blanch-

White membrane, thin and strong, that caught the air
And held it—the fourth finger of the hand
Extended past all reason, and the rare
And living skin stretched from that finger-strand

To the body and the hind leg—a wing
Built not from feathers, but formed as a kite
Of skin, a bat-wing's cousin, ancient string
Of membrane that gave {{c|1746|Pteros}} his first flight.

He was the first vertebrate in the sky—
Not counting gliders in {{x|Permian}} trees,
The small and desperate lizard-forms that fly
A moment between branches in the breeze—

{{c|1746|Pteros}} achieved true powered flight: the beat
Of membrane wings against {{x|Triassic}} air,
The lift and thrust and banking that complete
Mastery of the third dimension's lair.

His bones were hollow—lighter than a thought,
Thin-walled as paper, filled with air-sacs that
Extended from his lungs, and these sacs brought
The oxygen of altitude to bat

Through every wingbeat's metabolic need.
Large-brained for his size, the cerebellum
Was swollen for the balance and the speed
Of reckoning in flight, on its vellum

Each point of the three-dimensional world
Mapped in neural tissue that the landlocked
Reptile had never needed—but unfurled
In the high sky, where any error mocked

With gravity's implacable demand.
The first of {{c|1746|Pteros}}' kind were sparrow-sized,
With teeth for catching insects on the strand
Of evening air, with wings not yet king-sized

But fit for the modest {{x|Triassic}} skies
Where no other vertebrate competed
For the aerial niche—{{c|1598|Neopter}}'s flies
And dragonflies held it, undefeated,

For some three hundred million years—but now
A backbone and a warm-ish body brought
A new competitor beneath the brow
Of each {{x|Triassic}} sunset, and the thought

Of vertebrate dominion in the air
Began with {{c|1746|Pteros}}' small and toothed patrol
Across the evening sky, catching his share
Of insects in the air's encircling bowl.

His children would grow large—enormous—some
With wingspans wider than a fighter plane—
{{c|1747|Quetzal}} of the {{x|Cretaceous}} would become
The largest thing that flew—but that refrain

Is for a later chapter. Here, the start:
Small, toothed, and membrane-winged, and insect-fed,
So {{c|1746|Pteros}} took the sky and played his part
In the {{x|Triassic}}'s grand trial, and led

The first invasion of the vertebrate
Into realms only arthropods had known—
And in the evening light, however late,
His silhouette against the sky was sown

As promise of the wings to come.

                                   Two ways
The vertebrates would find to powered flight:
{{c|1746|Pteros}}' own membrane, and the feathered sprays
Of {{c|1736|Deinos}}' later children—but tonight,

In the {{x|Triassic}}'s fading light, but one
Existed: membrane wing, the finger-kite,
The pterosaur ascending toward the sun
And banking in the thermal's lifting height.

Honor first fliers—{{c|1746|Pteros}} and his kin
Who dared the third dimension's world above
The ground where every other creature's been,
And found in empty sky a kind of love

That only those who fly can understand:
The freedom of the air, the lift, the soar,
The world below becoming merely land—
And sky, the sky, becoming something more.


# Chapter 95: The Eve of the Second Dying

{{x|Triassic}} days were good. Not perfect—none
Is perfect in the wake of greatest death—
But earth's recloathing in green had begun,
The sea's belated clearing, like a breath,

And radiation of the newer forms
Into every empty niche had made
A world that worked again: the coastal storms
Fed rain to forests where conifers swayed,

The {{c|1726|Ichthyos}} hunted the {{p|Tethys}} deep,
The {{c|1729|Nothros}} paddled in the shallow seas,
And on land {{c|1732|Cruros}}' children held their sweep
Of rivers; {{c|1736|Deinos}} grew by slow degrees.

A good world; and the late {{x|Triassic}} age
Saw it was full of life: three hundred kinds
Of marine reptile on the {{p|Tethys}} stage,
A thousand insects in the forest's rinds.

The great recovery was nearly through,
The scars the {{x|Permian}} had left near healed,
Discovery of ways of living new,
{{x|Mesozoic}} innovation, unsealed.

But earth keeps its appointments with the fire.
Beneath the floor that would in time become
The {{p|Atlantic Ocean}}, the entire
Mantle surged, and pressed, and would not succumb

Against the crust; and {{p|Pangaea}} was torn:
The {{x|Central Atlantic Magmatic}} swell,
The {{x|CAMP}} volcanism, rope-and-ring born
Of basalt in eruption that would well

From pole to pole along the growing rift—
And in {{x|Triassic}}'s last ten thousand years
The earth gave its second terrible gift
Of volcanic excess, which now appears:

Carbon dioxide and the sulfur flowed
Into the greenhouse air, already warm—
The ocean's chemistry, its hide, now showed
Its shifting underneath the acid storm

As it had shifted once before; the same
Script played again: warming, and then acid,
Then oxygen's decline, the ancient game
Of volcano and of ocean, placid

Upon the surface, choking in the deep.
The phytosaurs saw first—the river lords
Who had mimicked the crocodilian's creep
And ruled the waterways; their ancient hordes

Grew thin, for water's chemistry had changed.
Rauisuchians on the plains found less
To hunt as numbers of the grazers ranged
Toward zero in the climate's growing stress.

And {{c|1732|Cruros}}' dynasty—the elder son
Of {{c|1681|Archon}}, holder of {{x|Triassic}} reign
For forty million years—was now undone.
The world was changing; it would not sustain

Those who had grown too large, too specialized,
Too locked in lowland and in the river—
Those who could not move, could not be revised,
Could not become something new—the giver

Of extinction is always one: the loss
Of what you need while keeping what you are.
And {{c|1732|Cruros}}' children could not bear the cross
Of the changed world—not all, not every star

Within his constellation dimmed: the strain
Of crocodiles, survivors of his house,
Endured, small and amphibious, the plain
Civilian and not soldier, and the mouse

And not the lion of his kingly pride—
The modest crocodile-forebears who kept
By water's edge, and ate the scraps supplied
By the world's dying—and these small ones crept

Through the extinction, just as {{c|1673|Cynos}} passed
The last one: by being small, by being
Undemanding, by covenant held fast
Between the survivor and the seeing

Another morning.

                   But the great ones fell.
Rauisuchians, phytosaurs, the tall
Heavy lords of {{c|1732|Cruros}}' {{x|Triassic}} spell
Were gone beneath the {{x|CAMP}} eruptions' pall.

And as the elder brother's kingdom burned,
The younger brother's children—{{c|1736|Deinos}}' small
And humble dinosaurs—looked up and learned
The empty niches beckoned, one and all.

It is the eve. Tomorrow, the dying.
Tonight the world still breathes, the rivers run,
And the last phytosaur is still trying
To hold his kingdom underneath the sun.

Honor the eve—the last good night before
The fire; for every living, growing thing
That breathed {{x|Triassic}} air wove, to the core,
Its own end, unaware of morning's sting.


# Chapter 96: The Second Dying

Then the {{p|Atlantic}} opened, and the fire
Ran north and south along the cracking seam
Of {{p|Pangaea}}'s body; the entire
Long central rift erupted in a steam

And basalt flood that rivaled, in its reach,
The {{p|Siberian}} at {{x|Permian}}'s close—
The {{x|CAMP}} volcanism, another breach,
A Stygian catastrophe that rose

Ablaze across eleven million square
Kilometers of flood basalt—the earth
Repeated what it knew: the deep heat's flare
Of magma rising through convection's girth

It found each cut and weakness in the crust
And poured on through. The script was all too known:
First carbon, then the warming; as it must,
The sulfur in the poisoned blue was sown,

And acid rain that burst upon the trees
Just healed from the {{x|Permian}} acid bath—
The forests browned again, by swift degrees
To nothing, and the carbon cycle's math

Collapsed again, in thirty million years.
And in the sea the acid came again—
The pH falling, and the ancient fears
Of carbonate dissolving, and the pain

Of creatures building shells from that same stone
That acid water melts: the corals, and
Brachiopods: the funeral, once known,
Played out again on the reef-builders' strand,

{{x|Permian}} morals lost upon an earth
That cannot learn, but simply, always, does
Whatever mantle's heat dictates—the birth
And death of worlds is geology's buzz

Of a planet that does not think.

                                  On land,
