Confident, not aggressive; rich, not vain;
And pious, but not monumental; good
In letters, and the finest in its reign.

The Twelfth moved north, and set its throne up high
At {{p|Itjtawy}}, between the two lands, free;
The first {{c|2026|Amenemhat I}}, {{c|2027|Senusret I}},
{{c|2028|Senusret III}}, {{c|2029|Amenemhat III}}.

They drained and watered the {{p|Faiyum}}'s wide field,
And pushed down into {{p|Nubia}}, and spread
Their rule; and arts and letters, made to yield,
Grew finer than the pyramid age bred.

And then was {{p|The Tale of Sinuhe}} set down:
A noble fled the court, and lived among
The {{p|Amorites}} in {{p|Canaan}}, won renown,
And wed a princess of the foreign tongue,

And longed for {{p|Egypt}}, and to lie at last
Among his fathers in his native ground;
And so came home, his years of exile passed,
And with {{p|Egyptian}} burial was crowned.

{{p|The Shipwrecked Sailor}}, cast upon an isle
Where a great serpent spoke, and told its woe,
And sent him home with gifts, and with a smile,
Back to his king, to tell what he would know.

{{p|The Eloquent Peasant}}, cheated, then came
Before the court, and spoke nine times of right;
The king, delighted, held his case the same,
Delaying, that he'd speak, by day and night.

{{p|The Instruction of Amenemhat}} I, where
The murdered king's ghost warned his son of guile;
And {{p|Merikare}}'s, for princes; and the rare
Man who argued with his ba, whose trial

Was whether life was worth the living; and
{{p|The Satire of the Trades}} mocked the pains
Of barber, washer, laborer, to stand
The scribe above them, and the scribe's own gains.

{{c|1166|Osiris}}, who was once the king's alone,
Was opened to the nobles, then to all
Who had the rites; and each could be his own
{{c|1166|Osiris}} at his death, and hear the call.

The {{p|Coffin Texts}} were written on the wood
To guide the dead below; the heart was weighed
Against the feather of {{c|2030|Ma'at}}, the good;
For all, not kings alone, the scales were laid.

And traded to the {{p|Levant}}, and the south
To {{p|Nubia}}, and {{p|Punt}}, for myrrh and scent,
And with the {{p|Minoans}}, from the {{p|Nile}}'s wide mouth
To {{p|Crete}}, and back the painted wares they sent.

And to the eastern {{p|Delta}} came the folk
Of {{p|Canaan}}, sons of {{c|1876|J}}, and settled there,
As herders, farmers, merchants; and the yoke
Was light, and they were welcome everywhere.

But in the {{p|Thirteenth Dynasty}} the kings
Came quick and short; the {{p|Nile}} ran low; and then
The east went its own way; and, as fate swings,
The {{p|Hyksos}} ruled at {{p|Avaris}}, strange men.

So honor {{p|Egypt}}'s classic age, restored:
The tales, the wisdom, and the soul made free
To be {{c|1166|Osiris}}; and the scribe, the lord
Of letters, and the kingdom's harmony.


# Chapter 154: Jacob, Joseph, and the Hyksos

And now the tale turns to one family:
{{c|2019|Jacob}}, {{c|635|Isaac}}'s son, {{c|1308|Abraham}}'s own seed,
Whose twelve sons would become the tribes; and he
Had wrestled with the angel in his need

At {{p|Peniel}}, and dreamed the ladder high
At {{p|Bethel}}, served his uncle {{c|2034|Laban}} long,
Made peace with {{c|2035|Esau}}; loved, as they grew by,
{{c|245|Rachel}}'s sons more than {{c|2036|Leah}}'s, all the throng.

And {{c|2031|Joseph}}, {{c|245|Rachel}}'s son, his brothers sold
To the {{p|Ishmaelite}} traders, who went down
To {{p|Egypt}}; there to {{c|2037|Potiphar}}, of gold
And rank, they sold him, servant of the crown.

He rose within the house; and, falsely blamed
By {{c|2037|Potiphar}}'s own wife, was bound in jail;
Read two prisoners' dreams; and so was named
Before the pharaoh, to read his dream's tale:

Of seven fat cows, and lean, and of ears,
Full ears and withered ones; and so he said:
Full years of plenty, then of famine years;
The king made him vizier, at the head

Of all the land, to store the grain; and when
The famine came, had {{p|Egypt}} bread enough;
And {{c|2019|Jacob}}'s sons came down to buy; and then
He knew them, though they knew him not; then, rough,

Hard testing, he made known himself, and wept,
And brought his father's house to {{p|Goshen}}'s grass,
The eastern {{p|Delta}}, where the herds were kept;
And so did {{c|2019|Jacob}}'s house to {{p|Egypt}} pass.

For in those days the {{p|Hyksos}} held the land,
{{c|2038|Heka-khasut}}, the foreign kings, held sway,
Sons of {{c|1908|J2}}, of {{p|Canaan}}'s tongue and band,
And joined their {{c|2039|Baal}} and {{c|2040|Anat}} with {{c|308|Seth}}'s way.

They brought the chariot, the horse, the bow
Of compound make, the bronze; and took the east
Of {{p|Delta}}, and at {{p|Avaris}}, below,
Their {{p|Fifteenth Dynasty}} had throne and feast.

The {{p|Theban}} kings ruled south, and for a span
The land was two; and {{c|2031|Joseph}}'s pharaoh, he
Was {{p|Hyksos}}, of his kin, a {{p|Canaan}} man,
Who gladly raised a {{p|Canaanite}} to be

His vizier, and welcomed all the sons
Of {{p|Canaan}} to the {{p|Delta}}; and the kings,
{{c|2042|Salitis}} and {{c|2043|Apophis}}, and the ones
Named {{c|2044|Khyan}} and {{c|2045|Apepi}}, kept the things

Of {{p|Egypt}}, temples, scribes, and every rite,
And kept their own as well, both ways in one;
They ruled not as destroyers, but by right,
And under them the land's affairs were done.

The twelve: {{c|2047|Reuben}}, {{c|2048|Simeon}}, {{c|2049|Levi}}, and
{{c|2050|Judah}} and {{c|2051|Issachar}}, {{c|2052|Zebulun}}, {{c|2053|Dan}},
{{c|2054|Naphtali}}, {{c|2055|Gad}}, and {{c|2056|Asher}}, {{c|2031|Joseph}}'s hand,
{{c|2057|Ephraim}}, {{c|2058|Manasseh}}; {{c|2059|Benjamin}}; the clan.

And {{c|2019|Jacob}}, old, within his tent, blessed each:
{{c|2050|Judah}} the lion, {{c|2031|Joseph}} fruitful bough,
{{c|2053|Dan}} judging his own people, and the reach
Of {{c|2052|Zebulun}} beside the sea, and how

{{c|2059|Benjamin}} was the ravening wolf; and then
Old {{c|2019|Jacob}} died, and was embalmed, and laid
Back into {{p|Canaan}}, to lie with the men,
With {{c|1308|Abraham}} and {{c|635|Isaac}}, in the shade

Of {{p|Machpelah}}'s cave at {{p|Hebron}}; and so
The fathers of the house were gathered in,
And {{c|2019|Jacob}}'s sons in {{p|Goshen}} stayed, to grow
Into a people, multiplied from kin.

So honor {{c|2019|Jacob}}, {{c|2031|Joseph}}, and the sons,
The {{p|Hyksos}}' welcome in the {{p|Delta}}'s grass,
The tent, the blessings, and the chosen ones
Who came to {{p|Egypt}}, saw the famine pass.


# Chapter 155: The Aryan Migration

While in the west the {{p|Hyksos}} took the {{p|Nile}},
Out of the east another people came:
The {{p|Aryans}}, the noble ones, whose style
And blood were {{c|1928|R1a}}'s, the steppe's own name.

For Aryan means noble, what they called
Themselves, of warriors; and from the plain
Of {{p|Central Asia}}, where their herds were stalled,
They came, by {{p|Bactria}}, in a long train.

Some went southwest, into {{p|Iran}}'s high land;
And some southeast, across the {{p|Hindu Kush}},
Down through the {{p|Khyber}}, where the passes stand,
Into the {{p|Punjab}}, like a river's push.

And there the {{p|Indus}} cities had grown still:
The {{p|Sarasvati}} had dried, the rains had turned,
{{p|Harappa}} emptied; and they came to fill
A land already changing, and not burned.

They did not slay, but joined the houses there,
The {{c|1874|H}}, the {{c|1878|L}}, the {{c|2061|R2a}}, the old;
And from the two came one; and everywhere
The blood was mingled, as the years unrolled.

They sang the {{p|Rig Veda}}, the oldest songs
Of all their kin: to {{c|2062|Dyaus}}, father sky,
To {{c|2063|Indra}} of the storm, to whom belongs
The thunder, and to {{c|2064|Agni}}, fire on high,

And soma's drink, and sacrifice of horse;
{{c|2062|Dyaus}} is {{c|101|Jupiter}}, is {{c|2066|Tyr}}, is {{c|2065|Zeus}},
One sky-father, the steppe's own, at the source
Of all their gods, the eldest in their use.

Then the {{c|2069|Dasas}} and the {{c|2068|Dasyus}}, they
Who dwelt there first, were sometimes foes, but more
Were joined with them, and served, and in their way
Kept their own god, the god they'd known before:

For {{c|2070|Rudra}}, wild god of the storm and hill,
Was {{x|Pashupati}}, lord of beasts, the old
God of the {{p|Indus}} seal; and he is still
{{c|1340|Shiva}}, one of the three great gods, all told.

And four the orders were: the {{p|Brahmin}}, priest;
The {{p|Kshatriyas}}, the warriors; and then
{{p|Vaishyas}}, merchants, farmers; and the least,
The {{p|Shudras}}, servants: so they ordered men.

Their tongue became {{p|Sanskrit}}, the holy speech,
From which {{p|Hindi}}, {{p|Urdu}}, {{p|Bengali}} came,
And {{p|Punjabi}} and {{p|Gujarati}}; each
A daughter; and a billion know that name.

And in the south the older tongues remained,
{{p|Dravidian}}: {{p|Tamil}}, {{p|Telugu}}, more,
{{p|Kannada}}, {{p|Malayalam}}, all maintained
As the old {{p|Indus}} speech had been before.

So honor them, the noble ones who came
Down from the steppe, and joined the {{p|Indus}} kin,
And sang the hymns, and kept the sky-god's name,
And {{c|1340|Shiva}} too, and made one land therein.


# Chapter 156: The New Kingdom

{{c|2060|Ahmose}} drove the {{p|Hyksos}} out, the son
Of {{p|Thebes}}, and finished what {{c|2073|Kamose}} began;
He took {{p|Avaris}}; when the war was done,
And {{p|Sharuhen}} fell, besieged for three years' span,

Then {{p|Egypt}} was again one land, and new:
It kept the chariot and bow it learned
From those it drove away, and outward grew,
To {{p|Canaan}}, {{p|Syria}}, where armies turned,

{{c|2074|Thutmose the First}} went to {{p|Euphrates}}' shore,
And south to {{p|Nubia}}; and so the throne
It ruled abroad, as never once before,
The first such rule it had, and all its own.

Then {{c|2077|Hatshepsut}} came, {{c|2074|Thutmose}} the First's own child,
The {{c|2076|Second}}'s wife; and when he died she reigned
As regent for the {{c|2078|Third}}, a boy; then, mild
No more, as pharaoh took the throne, ordained,

A woman pharaoh, twenty-two years long;
She sent her ships to {{p|Punt}}, and they came back
With myrrh and incense, beasts and gold; and strong
{{p|Deir el-Bahari}}, terraced, stack on stack.

Her statues bore the beard of kings, yet kept
A woman's face; and when at last she died,
{{c|2078|Thutmose III}} reigned, and her name was swept
From monuments; but still it would abide.

{{c|2078|Thutmose III}} went out on seventeen
Campaigns into the {{p|Levant}}, and he won
At {{p|Megiddo}}, against the kings between,
And held it till a century was done.

The spoils of conquest poured to {{p|Karnak}}'s door,
To {{c|2079|Amun-Ra}}'s great house; its priests grew great,
Until their wealth and power, more and more,
Became a rival to the king and state.

Then came {{c|1952|Akhenaten}}, the king, to reign,
Once Fourth {{c|2080|Amenhotep}}, the {{c|2081|Third}}'s son born;
He did what no king had: he took the gain,
The gold and gifts from all the houses; shorn

Of {{c|2086|Amun}}'s house and many houses more,
He gave them to one altar and one sun,
The {{c|2083|Aten}}, so the pouring, as before,
Was by his hand alone, the only one

Between the light and those who lived by it:
The same sun {{c|2079|Amun-Ra}} had always been,
The same hymns, a new house; and he would split
The priesthood's hold, and bring his own rule in.

He built {{p|Akhetaten}}, his seat, out where
The desert lay, and closed the temples' rest;
He took his court and all his household there,
And drove the priests, and took what they possessed.

In his own hand he wrote, to light the flame,
The {{p|Great Hymn to the Aten}}, to the sun
As maker of all life, the only name,
The god of all, the source, the only one.

And when he shut the house of {{c|2086|Amun}}, all
The altars but his own were closed: the rite
Of {{p|Canaanite}} households, and all the small
The household shrines of {{c|2019|Jacob}}'s sons in sight

Of {{p|Goshen}}, where they kept their fathers' way
As households do, lost altars with the rest;
And he who is praised as first, from that day,
To serve one sun, drove out the rite they blessed:

The fight was who would hold the altar, whose
Dead the houses honored, who poured the bread;
And those he drove would take, and never lose,
The name the one {{c|472|God}}'s rite most often said.

And when he died, his work was soon undone:
Young {{c|2087|Tutankhaten}} took {{c|2086|Amun}}'s own name,
And was {{c|2032|Tutankhamun}}, and back he won
The court to {{p|Thebes}}; and back the old cults came.

He reigned but briefly, and he died while young;
The {{p|Eighteenth}} closed; and then a general came,
{{c|2089|Ramesses I}}, and from his line there sprung
{{c|2090|Seti I}}, and the greater of the name,

{{c|2033|Ramesses II}}, for sixty-six years king,
Who fought at {{p|Kadesh}} with the {{p|Hittites}}' might,
Five thousand chariots, the greatest thing
Of chariot war; and after the fight,

He made the oldest treaty, peace, with one,
{{c|2092|Hattusili III}}, the {{p|Hittite}} lord,
And both their capitals kept it, when done,
On silver, in the house of {{c|2086|Amun}} stored.

He built at {{p|Abu Simbel}} in the stone
Four seated giants, sixty-five feet high,
The {{p|Ramesseum}}, and {{p|Karnak}}, {{p|Luxor}}'s own,
The last great builder, as the end drew nigh.

And at his end the {{p|Sea Peoples}} by sea
Came to the coast; the weather turned once more;
And under {{c|2093|Merneptah}}, his son, would be
The first great waves of those who came to war.

So honor {{p|Egypt}}'s kingdom: her who ruled,
{{c|2077|Hatshepsut}}; and {{c|2078|Thutmose III}}, strong at war;
And {{c|2033|Ramesses II}}, whose peace-treaty cooled
The wars; and {{c|2019|Jacob}}'s sons, who kept their lore.


# Chapter 157: The Hittites

North, past {{p|Canaan}}, {{p|Syria}}, and the sand,
Upon the high plateau where {{p|Turkey}} lies,
A kingdom rose to rival {{p|Egypt}}'s land:
{{p|Hittites}}, beneath {{p|Anatolia}}'s skies.

Of {{c|1942|R1b}}, kin of the steppe, they came
To {{p|Anatolia}} early, and spread
Across the central plain; {{p|Hatti}}, the name
Their kingdom bore; and so their line was led.

Their tongue was {{p|Hittite}}, the first tongue to be
Set down of all the steppe-born tongues; they wrote
In wedge-script that from {{p|Akkad}}'s scribes came free,
And thirty thousand tablets kept their note:

The letters of their kings, their laws, their deeds,
Their treaties, annals, myths, the god's own care;
A people of the scribe, of lists and screeds,
Who wrote it down, and kept it written there.

{{c|2095|Anitta}} first took {{p|Hattusa}}'s hill
And other towns, and founded {{p|Hatti}}'s throne;
{{c|2096|Hattusili I}} made it greater still,
With {{p|Hattusa}} his seat, his very own.

Then {{c|2097|Mursili I}} led his army south,
Across the {{p|Taurus}}, through {{p|Syria}}'s plain,
To {{p|Babylon}}, to the {{p|Euphrates}}' mouth,
And sacked it, ending {{c|1919|Hammurabi}}'s reign:

His line was finished; and they did not stay,
But took the plunder home; and in their wake
The {{p|Kassites}} came to {{p|Babylon}} to sway;
The {{p|Hittites}} home, a thousand miles to take.

Its kings: {{c|2098|Suppiluliuma}} the first,
{{c|2099|Mursili II}}, {{c|2100|Muwatalli II}} then,
{{c|2092|Hattusili III}}, and, last and worst
Of days, {{c|2101|Tudhaliya IV}}, king of men.

Theirs: the plateau, {{p|Syria}}'s north, the strand
Of the upper {{p|Levant}}; and to the south
Was {{p|Egypt}}; two great poles, each king, each land,
And {{p|Syria}} between, from coast to mouth.

And so they met at {{p|Kadesh}}, by the stream
Of the {{p|Orontes}}; there {{c|2033|Ramesses II}} came
Against {{c|2100|Muwatalli II}}; and the gleam
Of chariots was more than war could name:

Two thousand of {{p|Egypt}}'s; three thousand came
From {{p|Hatti}}; and the {{p|Hittites}} laid a snare:
{{c|2094|Ramesses}} rode ahead, too far, and flame
Chariots overran his camp, and there

He rallied what he had, and held the field
By nightfall; but there was no victory;
Each claimed it; neither one would ever yield,
Nor drive the other out; and so they'd be

At war for years, and then they made a peace:
{{c|2033|Ramesses II}}, {{c|2092|Hattusili III}}, swore
A pact of mutual aid, and release
Of those who fled; and war would be no more.

{{c|2092|Hattusili}}'s daughter wed the pharaoh, queen
Among his queens; on silver it was set,
The treaty, kept in both their seats, and seen
In both: the oldest peace that both kept yet.

They held it to the end: no war again
Between the two; the oldest peace of all
Was the first lasting one, kept by both men
And by their sons, until the {{p|Hittites}}' fall.

Their gods were of the steppe: the father sky,
The storm-god; and with them, the gods they found
In {{p|Hatti}}, {{p|Hurrian}} too; and thereby
They took them in, and kept them, all around:

{{x|Land of the Thousand Gods}}, they called their land;
For each town that they won, its god they kept,
And added to their own, and never banned
The local rite, where once the old gods slept.

{{c|2103|Teshub}}, storm-god, from the {{p|Hurrians}}, ruled;
The {{p|Arinna}} sun-goddess was his queen;
And mountains, rivers, kings who had been schooled
In rule, made gods; the fields; all that was seen.

So those they conquered took their rule with ease,
Because their gods were honored, not cast down;
They kept the household altars, and the trees,
The hill, the spring, the god in each one's town.

Their law, gentler than {{c|1919|Hammurabi}}'s code:
They rarely put to death, but made men pay
The one they wronged, or kin, the debt they owed,
And did not maim; and so they kept the way.

And when they fell, their kingdom did not die
Complete: in {{p|Syria}}, the towns held on,
{{p|Carchemish}} and {{p|Aleppo}}, {{p|Hamath}}, and nigh
To {{p|Sam'al}}, kept the {{p|Hittite}} ways, though gone.

For at the end, when the collapse came down,
Then {{p|Hattusa}} was sacked; the court was done;
They hid the archives in the shrines in town,
And so they lasted; and the folk, each one,

Fled, scattered; and the {{p|Sea Peoples}} then came,
The {{p|Kaska}} from the {{p|Black Sea}} coast rose too,
And famine with the weather's turn; the same
Fall took them all, but took the {{p|Hittites}} through.

{{p|Egypt}}, though less, lived; {{p|Assyria}} stood;
And {{p|Babylon}} remained, the {{p|Kassites}}' land;
But {{p|Hatti}} fell complete, as no one could,
Within a generation, all its band.

And still today we read the tablets kept,
And name their kings, and read their peace's word;
The archive in the temples, where it slept,
Still speaks; and {{p|Hatti}}'s voice again is heard.

So honor {{p|Hittites}}, {{c|1942|R1b}}'s own kin,
Who sacked great {{p|Babylon}}, who made the peace,
Who took the thousand gods of all within,
And wrote it all, that it should never cease.


# Chapter 158: The Mycenaeans

And in the west, upon the {{p|Greek}} land's tip
And on the isles of the {{p|Aegean}} sea,
A third great kingdom rose, of sword and ship:
{{p|Mycenaean Greece}}, as rich as could be.

{{p|Mycenae}} on its hill in {{p|Argolid}},
With walls of stone so great, unmortared, piled,
Called {{p|Cyclopean}} by men; and amid
Its peers it ruled, the strongest and least mild.

And {{p|Tiryns}}, {{p|Pylos}}, {{p|Athens}}, {{p|Thebes}}, they stood,
{{p|Orchomenos}}, and others, kings in each;
And while {{p|Egypt}}'s {{p|New Kingdom}} rose, they could
Grow great, and {{p|Hatti}} too, within their reach.

They were of {{c|1942|R1b}}, the steppe's own kin,
Who came to {{p|Greece}} in days long gone; their tongue
Was early {{p|Greek}}; they wrote it down therein
{{p|Linear B}}, from {{p|Linear A}} sprung,

The script of {{p|Crete}}; and on their tablets kept
Their lists: the sheep, the workers, and the tax,
The rations, and the arrows, where they slept
In armories, the wheat in all its stacks.

The palace kept the count of all its land,
Each worker's share of grain, each bronze-head spear;
The scribes kept all of it beneath their hand,
And so the house ran on from year to year.

But they were warriors above all: their lords
Were buried with their boar's-tusk helms of war,
With golden masks upon their faces, swords
Of bronze, and jewels, in the shaft-graves' store.

They loved the fight, the loot, the honored name,
The gift that bound one war-band to the next;
They were the heroes, those of later fame,
The first {{p|Greek}} lords, by sword and honor vexed.

At first they learned from {{p|Crete}}, the island's style,
The lesser of the two in wealth and lore;
But when {{p|Thera}} had burst, after a while,
They came across and took the {{p|Cretan}} shore:

They took the palaces at {{p|Knossos}}, wrote
Their {{p|Linear B}} on the {{p|Cretan}} clay,
And kept the {{p|Cretan}} ways, the bull, the note
Of goddess and of maze, and kept their sway.

But where the {{p|Minoans}} painted fields and sea,
The {{p|Mycenaeans}} painted war and hunt;
And so the two were joined, the island's free
Rich grace, and the steppe's war-bands, the spear's front.

And they grew rich: their pots went out to all,
{{p|Egypt}}, {{p|Cyprus}}, {{p|Anatolia}}'s shore,
To {{p|Sicily}}, and {{p|Sardinia}}'s wall;
They brought back copper, tin, and ivory's store,

And gold from {{p|Egypt}}, cedar from the hills
Of {{p|Lebanon}}; they sent out oil and wine
And cloth; their {{p|Aegean}}, a lake that fills
With ships, and palaces that taxed each line.

And at the end of this, there came the war,
The war of {{p|Troy}}, the city on the strait,
{{p|Wilusa}}, {{p|Ilios}}, stood before
The {{p|Greeks}}; and all the kings of {{p|Greece}}, the great,

Were led by {{c|1337|Agamemnon}}, the high king
Of {{p|Mycenae}}; for {{c|2114|Paris}}, {{p|Troy}}'s own son,
Had taken {{c|2113|Helen}}; and so they would bring
Their ships across, and fight till it was done.

{{c|2110|Achilles}} fought, and {{c|2111|Hector}} fought, and fell;
{{c|2112|Odysseus}} of wiles was there; and when
Ten years had passed, the city fell as well,
And {{p|Troy}} was burned, and taken by the men.

And then a generation passed, no more,
The {{p|Mycenaean}} palaces were burned:
{{p|Mycenae}}, {{p|Tiryns}}, {{p|Pylos}}, whose clay store
Of tablets baked, and so the lists were learned.

{{p|Sea Peoples}} came; the servants rose; the rain
Failed; and the trade that held the world was done;
In twenty years, the palaces were slain,
And no one built them up again, not one.

And {{p|Greece}} went dark: the script was lost, the trade,
The palaces, the towns; the people dwelt
In villages, and farmed; and what they made
Was songs, the heroes' songs, which still they felt:

{{c|2110|Achilles}} and {{c|2112|Odysseus}}, their tale,
The boar's-tusk helm, the list of each great ship,
The names, the places: so the songs prevail,
From mouth to mouth, and never lose their grip.

{{c|1991|Dionysus}}, the god of wine, went east,
And led his army to {{p|India}}'s land,
And set his rite there, and his dance and feast,
And then came home to {{p|Greece}}; and so the hand

Of {{p|Greece}} reached out to {{p|India}}; the two
Were joined in song, the west, the east, as one;
For {{p|Greece}} spoke with {{p|Hatti}}, with {{p|Egypt}} too,
And {{p|Syria}}, the lands beyond the sun.

Honor the {{p|Mycenaeans}}, kings of war,
{{c|1337|Agamemnon}}'s realm, the foe of {{p|Troy}}'s wall,
Who took {{p|Crete}}, and who sailed to each far shore,
Whose songs are sung of heroes, after all.


# Chapter 159: The Ramayana

In {{p|Ayodhya}}, the city of the north,
{{c|2125|King Dasharatha}} had three queens, and four
Sons: {{c|2009|Rama}} first, the eldest; and then forth
{{c|2127|Bharata}}, {{c|2119|Lakshmana}}, {{c|2128|Shatrughna}}, more.

And {{c|2009|Rama}} was the heir, and learned the bow
And rule; and with sage {{c|2129|Vishwamitra}} went
To guard the rites from demons, high and low,
And reached {{p|Mithila}}, where his steps were bent

To {{c|2130|Janaka}}'s high court; and {{c|2118|Sita}} there,
The king's own child, found in a furrow's earth
At ploughing time, was promised to the heir
Who strung great {{c|1340|Shiva}}'s bow; and he, of worth,

Not only strung it, but he broke it through;
And they were wed, and to {{p|Ayodhya}} came;
And {{c|2126|Dasharatha}}, old, would make him, too,
King in his place, and give the throne his name.

But {{c|2131|Kaikeyi}}, the second queen, was stirred
By {{c|2132|Manthara}}, her maid, and claimed two boons
The king had sworn her once: and at her word
Her {{c|2127|Bharata}} was crowned; and fourteen moons

Of years, {{c|2009|Rama}} must go to forest wild;
The king was bound, and gave it; and his son
Went out without a word, the faithful child;
And {{c|2118|Sita}} would go with him, as would one,

{{c|2119|Lakshmana}}; and the three went through the wood
Of middle {{p|India}} for years; and then
A golden deer drew {{c|2009|Rama}} where he stood,
And {{c|2120|Ravana}} took {{c|2118|Sita}} from the glen.

He was the king of {{p|Lanka}}, with ten heads
And twenty arms, a scholar and a priest
Of {{c|1340|Shiva}}, wise and learned in his threads,
A worthy king, and yet his lust released

His ruin; for he took her to his isle,
And kept her in his garden, and she stayed
Faithful; and {{c|2009|Rama}} and his brother, while
They searched, met {{c|2121|Hanuman}}, who came to aid:

The monkey-lord, the wind-god's son, whose might
Could change his size; he leapt across the sea
To {{p|Lanka}}, found her faithful, and by night
He set the city burning, and was free,

And came back to report; then {{c|2009|Rama}} raised
His host: {{p|Vanaras}}, with {{c|2133|Sugriva}}, king
Of monkeys, whom he'd helped, and bears; and praised
Was {{c|2121|Hanuman}}, the chief of everything.

They marched to {{p|India}}'s south shore, and made
A stone bridge across the sea, {{p|Ram Setu}};
It lies there still, the shoals; and unafraid
They crossed to {{p|Lanka}}, and the war broke through.

The demon generals fell beneath the sun;
{{c|2119|Lakshmana}} slew {{c|2134|Indrajit}}, the king's son;
And {{c|2009|Rama}} met {{c|2120|Ravana}}, the great one,
And fought him, and the battle was begun:

His heads grew back, his arms held arms divine;
But {{c|2009|Rama}} took the arrow that was blessed
By {{c|2135|Agastya}}, of {{c|1952|Brahma}}'s own design,
And pierced the demon king in his own breast.

So {{p|Lanka}} fell, and {{c|2118|Sita}} was restored;
But {{c|2009|Rama}} asked if she had been beguiled;
She said that she was not; and he, the lord,
Asked proof; and she walked in the flame, and smiled,

For {{c|2064|Agni}} would not burn her, and she came
Out whole; and so they went back home, and he
Was crowned in {{p|Ayodhya}}; and his reign's name
Was {{p|Rama Rajya}}, just as rule could be.

But still the people talked; and so the king
Sent {{c|2118|Sita}} out again, into the wood,
To {{c|2136|Valmiki}}, the sage; and there, the thing
He did not know, she bore two sons, and good:

{{c|2137|Kusha}} and {{c|52|Lava}}; and in years to come
He met them, and he knew them for his own;
And {{c|2118|Sita}}, proven true, would then become
One swallowed by the earth, her mother's throne.

And {{c|2009|Rama}} ruled until his days were done,
And walked into the {{p|Sarayu}}, then home
To {{c|2072|Vishnu}}, whom he was: the seventh one
Of {{c|2072|Vishnu}}'s comings, come to earth to roam,

To slay the king no god could slay; for he
Had won a boon that no god could, and so
A man must do it; and his dharma, free
Of fault, the rule of right, would always show:

The king, the husband, warrior, and son,
Who did what duty asked, and paid its cost;
And wise {{c|2120|Ravana}}, by his lust undone;
And {{c|2118|Sita}}, faithful, twice tried, and twice lost.

And still today his name is sung: the kings
Of {{p|Siam}} take {{c|2009|Rama}}'s name, as kings will;
In {{p|Java}} shadow puppets dance the things
He did; and at {{p|Angkor}} his war stands still.

So honor {{c|2009|Rama}}, {{c|2118|Sita}}, and the one,
{{c|2121|Hanuman}}, the devoted; and the wise
Proud {{c|2120|Ravana}}, by his own want undone;
And {{p|Ayodhya}}, from which the great kings rise.


# Chapter 160: Exodus, Trojan War, Bronze Age Collapse

And then the world of bronze was overthrown:
In fifty years, the palaces and towns
Of all the eastern sea were burned, or flown,
Abandoned; and the kings put down their crowns.

{{p|Hattusa}}, {{p|Hatti}}'s seat, burned to the ground;
And {{p|Ugarit}}, the trading town, was razed;
Its last king wrote for help, and none was found;
His letter in the kiln was left unglazed.

{{p|Mycenae}}, {{p|Tiryns}}, {{p|Pylos}}, {{p|Thebes}}, the same;
{{p|Knossos}} on {{p|Crete}}; and {{p|Troy}}, the town, was done;
{{p|Emar}}, {{p|Alalakh}}, {{p|Kadesh}}, {{p|Gath}}: the flame
Took {{p|Canaan}}'s cities, {{p|Cyprus}}' too, each one.

And {{p|Egypt}} lived, but less, and lost its lands
Abroad; {{p|Assyria}} waned; and the throne
Of {{p|Babylon}} was weak in {{p|Kassite}} hands;
And {{p|Elam}} shook; and few came through alone.

{{p|Linear B}} was lost; the {{p|Hittite}} hand
In wedge-script died with {{p|Hattusa}}'s fall;
The letters that the kings sent, land to land,
Were ended; and the trade was ended, all:

The roads that tied {{p|Mycenae}} to the {{p|Nile}},
To {{p|Ugarit}}, to {{p|Cyprus}}, and away
To far {{p|Sardinia}}: they broke; the while
The people fell, nine-tenths in some, they say.

For five things came at once: the first, the drought,
From twelve hundred fifty, a hundred years,
The worst the age of bronze had known; without
The harvests, famine came, and with it fears.

The second, earthquakes, shook the towns, and brought
The walls down, with the burning, or before;
The third, the peasants, who for grain had wrought
For lords, rose up when there was grain no more.

The fourth, the peoples moving in their waves,
The {{p|Sea Peoples}}, a host of raiders, came,
And {{c|2140|Ramesses III}}, the last who saves
{{p|Egypt}}, fought twice, and won, and carved their name

At {{p|Medinet Habu}}, upon the stone:
The {{p|Shekelesh}}, the {{p|Tjeker}}, {{p|Peleset}},
The {{p|Denyen}}, {{p|Sherden}}, {{p|Weshesh}}, and their own
{{p|Lukka}} from {{p|Lycia}}, in battle met.

The {{p|Sherden}} were {{p|Sardinia}}'s; and those
{{p|Shekelesh}}, {{p|Sicily}}'s; the {{p|Denyen}}, they
Were {{p|Danaoi}}, the {{p|Greeks}}; for when the blows
Fell on {{p|Mycenae}}, they too sailed away,

And raided, settled; and the {{p|Peleset}},
The {{p|Philistines}}, from the {{p|Aegean}} shore,
Took {{p|Canaan}}'s southern coast, and settled, set
Their pots and halls as at their home before.

The fifth: the whole was tied, and each one stood
Upon the rest: the tin, the copper, grain;
{{p|Ugarit}} leaned on {{p|Hatti}}, as it should,
And {{p|Hatti}} on the {{p|Levant}}'s grain, or wane;

So when one fell, the next fell, one by one,
And none could raise the whole; and so it broke,
The greatest falling that was ever done,
Of all the kingdoms, all the palace folk.

And out of it came iron, which was found
In many lands, and could not be held tight;
And out of {{p|Canaan}} came the letters, sound
By sound, the alphabet, that all could write;

And small towns, leagues of tribes, and peoples came:
{{p|Phoenicians}}, {{p|Arameans}}, {{p|Israel}}'s line,
The {{p|Hittite}} towns of {{p|Syria}}, the same;
And {{p|Greeks}} in dark, that waited for their sign.

And in those years did {{c|1006|Moses}} lead the sons
Of {{c|2019|Jacob}} out of {{p|Egypt}}, from the land
Of {{p|Goshen}}, where the king had bound the ones
Who kept their fathers' altars, by his hand.

The plagues came down on {{p|Egypt}}; and they fled;
The sea of reeds, the {{p|Yam Suph}}, parted wide;
They crossed it, and the chariots, instead,
Were drowned behind them, in the closing tide.

At {{p|Sinai}} then the covenant was made;
And forty years they wandered in the waste;
Then {{c|2141|Joshua}} led them in, unafraid,
To {{p|Canaan}}, where the falling towns were placed.

And {{c|2093|Merneptah}}, the son of {{c|2033|Ramesses}}, set
A stone, and wrote that {{p|Israel}} was laid
Low by his hand; and so in {{p|Canaan}} yet
Was {{p|Israel}}, a people, and it stayed.

They were not all who left; for many came
To {{p|Canaan}} in the breaking of the world;
But theirs the story of the house, the name,
Of {{c|2019|Jacob}}'s sons, when their flag was unfurled.

And in those years the {{p|Trojan War}} was fought,
The last great sailing of the {{p|Greeks}}; for when
The war was won, and {{p|Troy}} was burned to naught,
The kings came home, and lost their homes again:

Then {{c|1337|Agamemnon}}'s own {{p|Mycenae}} burned
Within a generation of the war;
{{c|2112|Odysseus}}' isle, where he had returned,
Grew small and dark, and was a king's no more.

So three things happened in the age's end:
The breaking, and the war, the going out;
And from the ruin, kingdoms that would mend
Into small nations, with new gods about.

The god-kings fell, because the house they ruled
Was broken, and no palace held the rite;
And so the rite went out, no longer schooled
By kings, to households, and to those who write.

So honor those who lived when bronze was done:
{{c|2140|Ramesses III}}, who held the sea at bay;
The sons of {{c|2019|Jacob}}, {{c|1006|Moses}}' own, each one;
And {{p|Troy}}, and those who burned and sailed away.


# Chapter 161: Fall of Shang

And while the west was breaking, in the east
The {{p|Shang}}, who ruled the {{p|Yellow River}}'s plain
Six hundred years, would fall, its glory ceased,
And from the west the {{p|Zhou}} would come to reign.

At {{p|Yin}}, the last seat, at {{p|Anyang}}, ruled
The {{p|Shang}} kings, and they buried with their dead
The bronze, the jade, the silk, the lacquer, tooled
With care, and hundreds, slain to go ahead.

The king's work was to speak with those before,
His fathers, who would speak to {{c|2147|Shang Di}}, high,
The {{c|2148|Lord on High}}; and so he'd ask, and pour,
And write his question, and await reply

On oxen's shoulder-blades and turtle shells,
Which then were heated till they cracked, and read;
The {{p|Oracle Bone Script}}, whose writing tells
Of hunts and wars, the weather, dreams, the dead.

The king was not a god, but stood between;
His calendar of rites was the state's frame;
His steppe-born chariots, of bronze, were seen
With warriors in their hundreds when war came.

But {{c|2149|Di Xin}}, the last king, grew cruel and vain:
He made a lake of wine, a wood of meat,
And made his foes walk on a greased bronze chain
Above the coals, to fall into the heat;

And he and {{c|2151|Daji}}, whom he loved, would laugh;
For {{c|2151|Daji}} was a fox-spirit, who wore
A woman's body, and she led him half
To ruin, and he ruled by her, and more.

His taxes and his labor crushed the land;
His wars were lost; the rites he did not keep;
And on the west, beneath the {{p|Shang}}'s own hand,
The {{p|Zhou}} grew strong, while {{p|Shang}} was half asleep.

The {{p|Zhou}} held the {{p|Wei River}}'s vale, and they
Had ties to western peoples, to the {{p|Qiang}};
But took {{p|Shang}}'s writing and {{p|Shang}}'s rites, their way,
And kept their own: and from {{c|2152|Hou Ji}} they sprang,

The {{c|2153|Lord of Millet}}, father of the grain;
And {{c|2154|King Wen}}, the {{c|2155|Accomplished King}}, would bind
The lords against the {{p|Shang}}, but did not strain
To war; his son, {{c|2156|King Wu}}, was of war's mind.

And {{c|2157|Jiang Ziya}}, the fisherman, the sage,
Whom {{c|2154|King Wen}} found beside the river, rose
The greatest strategist of all the age;
His {{p|Six Secret Teachings}} told how war goes.

They bound the lords of {{p|Shang}} who were aggrieved,
And kept a name for virtue, and waited;
And when the time was right, as they believed,
{{c|2156|King Wu}} marched forth, at the moment fated.

At {{p|Muye}}, close by {{p|Yin}}, the two armies met;
The {{p|Shang}} men turned their spears and joined the {{p|Zhou}};
{{c|2149|Di Xin}} fled to his palace, and there set
It all aflame, and he died with it too.

And so the {{p|Shang}} was ended; and {{c|2156|King Wu}}
Came into {{p|Yin}}, and honored those who fell,
And founded {{p|Zhou}}, the longest house, and true,
That ruled eight hundred years, and ruled them well.

{{c|2156|King Wu}} died young; his brother, {{c|2160|Duke of Zhou}},
Was regent for his son, and he made known
The {{p|Mandate of Heaven}}, why rule was due
To {{p|Zhou}}, and not by force of arms alone.

The god {{c|2161|Tian}} was {{c|2147|Shang Di}}, the {{p|Shang}}'s own sky,
One Lord, two names; the fight was for the rite:
Which house would make the offering, and why,
To {{c|2162|Heaven}}; for the house that held it, right

Was with it. And the {{p|Shang}}'s own dead were fed:
{{p|Zhou}} gave {{p|Song}} to {{p|Shang}}'s heirs, so they could set
Before their fathers still the wine and bread;
The {{p|Shang}} was gone; its dead were honored yet.

For {{c|2162|Heaven}} gives the house that governs well
The leave to rule, but only while it's good;
When it grows harsh, the leave is lost; they fell,
The {{p|Shang}}, because they ruled not as they should.

So {{p|Zhou}} was not a thief, but heir by right:
The mandate passed from {{c|2149|Di Xin}}'s line to theirs;
And so a house that falls has lost the light,
And one that rises has it, and is heirs.

The {{p|Zhou}} king gave out lands to kin and lords,
Who ruled as vassals, owing grain and war
And rites to him; {{p|Fengjian}}, by its cords,
Held well for many years, and many more.

And with the {{p|Zhou}} the rites were all set down:
The {{p|Book of Rites}}, the {{p|Book of Songs}}, and then
The {{p|Book of Changes}}; and calendar's crown,
The feasts, the harvests, sacrifices, when

The seasons turned; the writing was made one;
And {{p|Zhongguo}}, the {{p|Middle Kingdom}}, there stood
The center of the world, beneath the sun,
And round it, {{p|Rong}}, {{p|Di}}, {{p|Yi}}, {{p|Man}}, the wild wood:

For any folk could take its rites, and be
Within; or keep away, and stay without;
And {{p|Zhou}} was center, and the rest could see
Their place by it, the world spread round about.

Honor {{c|2154|King Wen}}, {{c|2156|King Wu}}, the {{c|2160|Duke of Zhou}},
And {{c|2157|Jiang Ziya}}, the fisher by the stream;
And {{p|Shang}}, whose dead were fed by those who slew
Their king; and {{c|2162|Heaven}}'s mandate, and its gleam.


# Chapter 162: The Bantu Expansion

And while the west was broken, to the south
A people moved, as great as any known:
The {{p|Bantu}}, out from {{p|Cameroon}}'s green mouth,
{{c|1949|E1b1a}}'s, {{p|Nigeria}}'s own;

The house of {{c|1861|E}}, which stayed at home, and grew;
They spoke the {{p|Niger-Congo}} tongue; and they
Grew yams and the oil palm, and made pots too,
And iron came to them from the north's way.

With iron they could clear the forest wide,
With iron they could fight, and raid, and hold;
With farms and iron, they went far and wide,
And moved out east and south, the young and old.

East, by the {{p|Congo}} forest's southern rim,
They came into the {{p|Great Lakes}}, lake and shore:
{{p|Victoria}}, {{p|Tanganyika}}'s brim,
{{p|Malawi}}; and they met the folk before:

The {{p|Cushites}}, {{p|Nilotes}}, and the {{p|Khoisan}}'s band;
And they would trade with them, and they would wed,
And sometimes fight; but most, the farming hand
Outgrew the bands of foragers, and spread.

Their villages had children, many more
Than roving bands; the first folk joined with them,
Or went to forest, desert, mountain, or
Were lost; and so it went, from root to stem.

And south they went, around the {{p|Congo}}'s wood,
Or up its rivers, to {{p|Angola}}'s land,
{{p|Zambia}}, {{p|Zimbabwe}}, where cattle stood,
And {{p|Botswana}}, to the {{p|Limpopo}}'s sand.

And so they went three thousand miles, and on
For thousands of years; and today they are
Four hundred million, and their tongues are drawn
From one: {{p|Swahili}}, {{p|Zulu}}, near and far,

{{p|Xhosa}}, {{p|Shona}}, {{p|Lingala}}, {{p|Kikuyu}},
{{p|Ganda}}, {{p|Kirundi}}, {{p|Luba}}, {{p|Kongo}}, more,
{{p|Setswana}}, {{p|Sesotho}}, {{p|Chichewa}}, true
Kin tongues from the one {{p|Bantu}} tongue before.

{{c|1949|E1b1a}}'s men came, took to wife
The women of the lands to which they came;
And so the father's house ran through the life
Of all, the mothers many, as the same

By {{c|1928|R1a}} in {{p|India}}, and by
The steppe in {{p|Europe}}; so the farmers spread;
And yet the first folk did not wholly die:
The {{p|Khoisan}} kept their clicks, the oldest said;

The {{p|Pygmies}} of {{p|Ituri}} kept the wood,
The hunt, the forest ways from long before;
The {{p|Nilotes}} of the {{p|Rift}} kept cattle good;
The {{p|Cushites}} kept the {{p|Horn}}; and many more.

They took new crops: the cattle in the east;
And from isles beyond the {{p|Indian}} sea
Banana came, and made the {{p|Great Lakes}}' feast,
And there the people grew, dense as could be.

And iron was their craft: their furnaces
Drew air themselves, and burned hot with small fuel;
The smith was priest as well, whose work it is
To change the stone to metal, by the rule

Of rite; and so the smiths were set apart,
A caste, with gods of their own, for the change
Of ore to iron was a holy art,
A making, like the world's, and like it strange.

Their gods: a high creator, far away;
Their dead, who stay among them, near and strong;
The spirits of the tree, the hill, the bay,
The cave; diviners, healers, those whose song

Brings rain; and over all the bond of kin,
{{p|Ubuntu}}: I am, for we are; the hand
Of hospitality, the peace within;
From the first homeland carried through the land.

So honor them, the {{p|Bantu}}, who went far,
With yam and iron, children, and the rite;
And those they met, who still are where they are,
The {{p|Khoisan}}, {{p|Pygmies}}, keeping their own light.


# Chapter 163: Zarathustra

Upon {{p|Iran}}'s high plateau, there, between
The {{p|Caspian}} and the {{p|Hindu Kush}}, came
A prophet such as none before had seen:
{{c|2146|Zarathustra}}, or {{c|2165|Zoroaster}} by name.

Of {{c|1928|R1a}}, the steppe's own kin, whose speech
Was that of {{p|Iran}}; and he was a priest
Of the old rite of flame, the rite that each
Of those kin kept, in {{p|India}}, the east.

He sang the {{p|Gathas}}, seventeen hymns, in
The old {{p|Avestan}}, close to {{p|Vedic}} speech:
That all the world's a field where good and sin
Must fight, and every soul must choose for each

Thought, word, and deed: {{c|2170|Asha}}, the truth and right,
Or {{c|2171|Druj}}, the lie; and that the choice is real;
That {{c|2166|Ahura Mazda}}, the {{c|2167|Wise Lord}}, light,
Made all things good, and good is his whole seal;

But {{c|2168|Angra Mainyu}}, spirit that destroys,
Is lie and dark and ruin; and the two
Contend; the world's the field; and all the noise
Of good and ill is theirs, the old and new.

No ill comes from {{c|2166|Ahura Mazda}}'s hand;
The ill is all the other's; so the one
Is wholly good; and men, who take their stand
With him, will help him win, till all is done.

And at the end, the good will win; and then
A judgment comes, and those who chose the right
Go up to paradise; the wicked men
To torment; and at last, made clean and bright,

The world is made anew, and all restored.
He taught them less of slaughter at the shrine,
And more the flame that burns before the lord,
Kept always lit, of {{c|2170|Asha}} the true sign;

And good thoughts, and good words, and good deeds, three,
Were all the rite. The steppe's old gods kept form:
{{c|296|Mithra}} and {{c|2172|Anahita}} bowed to be
Beneath the {{c|2167|Wise Lord}}, with the sun and storm,

Or were {{p|Amesha Spentas}}, holy, the same.
And {{c|2063|Indra}}, whom the {{p|Vedic}} hymns put high,
Was called a {{c|2174|daeva}}, given a worse name,
A demon, and a servant of the lie.

So {{p|Sanskrit}} {{c|2173|deva}} names a god of light;
In {{p|Avestan}}, {{c|2174|daeva}}, a foe. The fight
Was not between two faiths: it was one rite,
One flame, one tongue, one holy drink, one night

Of pressing, and two priesthoods at one shrine,
And what they fought about was whose lords drank;
One family split its flame, but kept its line:
The plateau's folk kept his, and closed their rank;

The east, {{p|Indo-Aryan}} folk, refused,
And kept their {{c|2173|deva}}, fed the {{p|Vedic}} feast;
Each kept the same old flame, and each one used
A worse name for the other's lords, at least.

At first his people would not hear him; so
He went out, seeking one who would; and found
{{c|2175|King Vishtaspa}}, eastward, who let him go
Before his court, and heard, and so was bound

To {{c|2166|Ahura Mazda}}; and all his court
Took up the word; and from {{c|2176|Vishtaspa}}'s land
It spread across the plateau, by report
And priest, and flame, from hand to waiting hand.

And still today the flame of his is fed
By {{p|Parsis}} and by those of {{p|Iran}}'s own;
And still the judgment, and the rising dead,
And good's last winning, are the seeds he'd sown.

So honor {{c|2146|Zarathustra}}, who made plain
The {{c|2167|Wise Lord}}'s good, the lie's dark, and the choice;
Who kept the flame, and split it, and the twain
Kept one rite still, though each had its own voice.


# Chapter 164: David

And back to {{p|Canaan}}, where, among the hills,
The sons of {{c|2019|Jacob}} settled, small and spread,
In villages with four-room houses, mills,
With no pig in the pot, no king their head.

The {{c|2187|Judges}} led them, and then {{c|2188|Saul}} was king,
The first of {{p|Israel}}; and then there came,
Of {{p|Judah}}, {{c|2198|Jesse}}'s youngest, who would sing,
A shepherd, ruddy, {{c|1956|David}} was his name.

He played the lyre; and {{c|2199|King Saul}} was sore pressed
By a dark spirit; and they brought the boy
To play for him, and give the king his rest,
And {{c|1956|David}} came to court, the king's own joy.

The {{p|Philistines}}, who came in from the sea,
Were {{p|Israel}}'s great foe; their chosen one,
{{c|2200|Goliath}}, giant, called for one to be
His match; and {{c|1956|David}}, young, the shepherd's son,

Too small for armor, took a sling and stone,
And struck him in the forehead, and he fell;
The {{p|Philistines}} fled; and {{c|1956|David}}, alone,
Was hero, more than {{c|2188|Saul}}, and loved as well.

And {{c|2188|Saul}} loved him, and gave him {{c|2201|Michal}}, wife,
His daughter; and yet feared him; and would try
To kill him, then relent, then seek his life;
And {{c|1956|David}} fled, an outlaw, to the dry

The {{p|Judean}} wilds, with outcasts at his side;
And twice he had {{c|2188|Saul}} in his hand, and twice
He spared him, for the {{c|295|Lord}}'s anointed; bide
He would, and wait, and not pay that dark price.

He served a while the {{p|Philistine}} of {{p|Gath}},
And ate his bread, and made, as he was bade,
His raids on others, never on the path
Of {{p|Israel}}; he lied, and so he stayed.

{{c|2188|Saul}} and his sons fell on {{p|Gilboa}}'s height,
And {{c|2203|Jonathan}}, whom {{c|1956|David}} loved, was slain;
{{c|2188|Saul}} fell on his sword; and {{c|1956|David}}, that night,
Sang: How the mighty fall, the weapons vain!

The love of {{c|2203|Jonathan}} for him was great,
Passing the love of women, so he sang;
A love so deep, it bore a grief whose weight
Through all the years since then has always rang.

Then {{c|1956|David}} became king, at {{p|Hebron}}, first
Of {{p|Judah}}; and then, when {{c|2204|Ish-Bosheth}} fell,
Of all of {{p|Israel}}; and he, who durst,
Took {{p|Jebus}}, no tribe's town, its citadel,

{{p|Jerusalem}}, he named it, made it his;
The {{p|Ark of the Covenant}} brought inside,
And danced before it, as a king's joy is,
Though {{c|2201|Michal}} scorned him, watching, in her pride.

He fought the {{p|Philistines}}, and {{p|Moab}} next,
{{p|Ammon}}, {{p|Edom}}, {{p|Aram}}, and grew the land;
And then, when he was great, his heart was vexed:
{{c|2205|Bathsheba}}, bathing, whom he took in hand,

The wife of {{c|2105|Uriah the Hittite}}, one
Of his most faithful men, away at war;
And when she was with child, then it was done:
He set {{c|2206|Uriah}} in the front, before

The hardest fighting, so he'd die; he died;
And {{c|1956|David}} married her. Then {{c|2207|Nathan}} knew,
The prophet, and he told him, at his side,
A tale: a rich man, and a poor man's ewe;

And {{c|1956|David}}, angry, cursed the rich; and then
Said {{c|2207|Nathan}}: You're the man. And {{c|1956|David}} wept,
And fasted, and repented, before men,
And sang for mercy; but the curse was kept.

The child he had of her died young; his son
{{c|2208|Amnon}} forced {{c|2209|Tamar}}, his half-sister; then
{{c|2210|Absalom}} killed {{c|2208|Amnon}}; when that was done,
Rebelled, and drove his father out; and when

They fought, in {{p|Ephraim}}'s wood, his hair was caught
Up in an oak tree, and {{c|2211|Joab}} stabbed him there,
Though {{c|1956|David}} said to spare him; and the thought
Of {{c|2210|Absalom}} was {{c|1956|David}}'s worst despair:

O {{c|2210|Absalom}}, my son, my son, would I
Had died for thee! So {{c|1956|David}} cried; and none
Would hide the grief of kings, or tell it why;
It stands as it was cried, my son, my son.

Then {{c|2212|Sheba}} rose; and {{c|1956|David}}, old, was hemmed
With plots; {{c|2205|Bathsheba}}, {{c|2207|Nathan}}, won the throne
For {{c|2189|Solomon}}, her son; and they condemned
{{c|2213|Adonijah}}'s claim; the crown his alone.

And {{c|1956|David}} died, and in his city lay,
{{p|Jerusalem}}, his city and his name;
And from his line a king would come, they say,
To gather {{p|Israel}}, and spread his fame.

He was no god-king, but a man who stood
Beneath his {{c|472|God}}, and sinned, and knelt, and could
Be told by prophets that he was not good,
And so repented, as a true king should.

So honor {{c|1956|David}}, shepherd, harper, king,
The giant-slayer, outlaw, sinner, son
Of {{c|2198|Jesse}}, father, mourner, who would sing
His psalms; and kneel; and grieve: my son, my son.


# Chapter 165: Classical Greece, Part One

Four hundred years, the {{p|Greeks}} lived in the dark,
In villages, with writing lost, and trade
Grown small; and yet they kept the songs, the spark
Of heroes, and the world they'd known, unmade.

And then the dawn came quickly: from the shore
Of {{p|Phoenicia}} came letters, and they wrote;
And {{c|1957|Homer}} set the {{p|Iliad}}'s old war,
The {{p|Odyssey}}, in writing, note by note.

They founded the {{p|Olympic Games}}; they made
{{p|Delphi}} the shrine of all the {{p|Greeks}}; they went
To found new towns by every sea, and trade,
Around the {{p|Black Sea}} and the {{p|Middle}} sent.

The {{p|polis}} was their way: the city-state,
Each one its own, with laws and gods and speech,
Its calendar, its fields; and small or great,
Its citizens, the {{p|demos}}, ruled in each.

Some ruled by few, some ruled by one, by all;
But each man's name was of his town: he'd be
{{p|Athenian}} or {{p|Spartan}}, and his call
Was to his {{p|polis}}, though all {{p|Greeks}} were free.

And each one strove to beat the rest: in feast,
In temples, games, in war, in schools of thought;
And one rich man, by building, as the least
Of towns was small, could change what his town sought.

Two poles: {{p|Athens}} and {{p|Sparta}}. With strong hand,
In the {{p|Peloponnese}}, {{p|Sparta}} made
{{p|Messenia}}'s {{p|Helots}} till all its land,
And then became a warrior caste, arrayed

By laws {{c|2217|Lycurgus}} gave: at seven, boys
Were taken to the barracks, trained, made hard,
The {{p|agoge}}; and men ate in common, poise
And war their only work, the {{p|Helots}}' guard.

Their women, freer, trained their bodies well,
To bear strong sons; two kings from two lines ruled,
With elders and the people; and they fell
Like stone on any field, their phalanx schooled.

At {{p|Thermopylae}}, three hundred there stood
Against great {{c|1985|Xerxes}}' host, and still today
They are the heroes' stand; and yet the good
Of letters they gave up, and war's the way.

But {{p|Athens}} went the other way: at first
Its nobles ruled, {{p|Eupatridae}}; and then
Then {{c|2218|Solon}} cancelled debts, so none were cursed
To slavery, and opened rule to men

Of every birth, though ranked by wealth; and then
{{c|2219|Peisistratos}} ruled as a tyrant, one
Who ruled alone, but well; and after, when
{{c|2220|Hippias}}, his son, was cast out and done,

{{c|2222|Cleisthenes}} then made ten tribes by where men dwelt,
To break the noble houses, and the {{c|2223|Boule}},
Five hundred chosen by the lot; and dealt
The {{p|Ecclesia}}, the people's highest rule.

And so the {{p|demos}} ruled, the people's sway;
The men who were its citizens would go
Themselves to speak, and vote, and judge; and they
Had need of speech, to sway, to win, to show;

The {{p|Sophists}} came, and taught for pay the art
Of speaking, logic, and the way to win;
And {{p|Athens}} grew, of all the world, the heart
Of making, all the thinking pressed within.

There {{c|2224|Aeschylus}} the playwright wrote, and then
{{c|2225|Sophocles}} and {{c|2226|Euripides}}; the jest
Of {{c|2227|Aristophanes}}; and the two men
Of history, {{c|2183|Herodotus}} the best,

And {{c|2228|Thucydides}}; and then {{c|2229|Phidias}} made
His {{c|1995|Athena}} and his {{c|2065|Zeus}}, the far-famed;
{{c|2230|Ictinus}} built the {{p|Parthenon}}'s arcade;
{{c|2231|Pericles}} spoke, whose speech the city claimed;

And {{c|2232|Socrates}}, who asked, and asked again,
And would not stop, until the asking won;
All in one town, in one long age of men,
Some thousand citizens, beneath one sun.

But first, in {{p|Ionia}}, on the shore
Of {{p|Anatolia}}, {{p|Miletus}}, came
The first who asked what all things are, before
The gods, what stuff they're made of, what their frame:

{{c|2233|Thales}} said that all is water, which can flow
As ice and steam, and feeds all things that live;
{{c|2235|Anaximander}} said the boundless; and so
{{c|2236|Anaximenes}} said air; and all would give

Their answers: of the {{p|apeiron}}, of air,
Of number, and of being, and of flame;
They asked, by reason and by looking there,
What all things were, and how they change and came.

{{c|2238|Pythagoras}} left {{p|Samos}} for the sun
Of {{p|Croton}}, and he founded there a band
Of thought and rite: that number is the one
True stuff; and music's ratios he scanned;

And souls, he taught, go on from life to life.
{{c|2239|Heraclitus}} at {{p|Ephesus}} said all
Things flow, and all is held in stress and strife,
And none can step twice in one stream at all;

And {{c|2240|Parmenides}} said: no, there is no change;
That being does not move; and so the two
Would set the argument, in all its range,
That those who think since then must still go through.

{{c|2243|Herodotus}} went journeying, and wrote
{{p|Egypt}}, {{p|Persia}}, {{p|Scythia}}, and the rest,
The customs and the tales of all of note,
And told them kindly, east as well as west.

And {{c|2228|Thucydides}} wrote later, hard and cold,
Of why men war, and gave his speakers speech;
And at {{p|Melos}} the {{p|Athenians}} told:
The strong do what they can; the weak, beseech.

And all of this was set against the war
With {{p|Persia}}: first {{c|2178|Darius}} sent his host;
At {{p|Marathon}} it fell; {{c|2244|Miltiades}}' corps
Of {{p|Athens}}, {{p|Plataea}}, held the coast.

Ten years, and {{c|2245|Xerxes}} came, the greatest host
The world had seen; with boats he bridged the strait;
{{p|Leonidas}} held, and died at his post;
And {{p|Athens}} burned; but the {{p|Greeks}} lay in wait

At {{p|Salamis}}, with {{c|2246|Themistocles}}, broke
The {{p|Persian}} fleet; at {{p|Plataea}}, then,
The {{p|Greeks}} by land; and {{c|1985|Xerxes}}, with his folk,
Went home; and {{p|Greece}} was free, of its own men.

And so they said: we are not {{p|Persians}}; we
Do not bow down; we rule ourselves; and from
That saying, and that war, and being free,
Their golden age of making was to come.

Honor {{p|Greece}}'s first age: the {{p|polis}}, strong;
And {{p|Sparta}}'s spear; and {{p|Athens}}' people's rule;
{{c|2233|Thales}}' water, and old {{c|1957|Homer}}'s written song;
And {{p|Salamis}}, where {{p|Greeks}} kept their own school.


# Chapter 166: Assyria and Babylon

But east once more, before the {{p|Greeks}}' bright day:
On {{p|Tigris}}, {{p|Assyria}} rose again,
And three long centuries it held its sway,
With iron, siege, and terror over men.

Its kings kept armies, engines, iron's store
In heaps, and made a law of fear: the town
That rose was razed; its chiefs were flayed; and more:
Their skins on walls; and stakes; and hands cut down;

And all the rest were carried far away,
So none could rise again; and this they wrote
In their own words, and boasted of the day;
And all the east, in fear, would read the note.

Yet they were builders too: at {{p|Nimrud}}, high,
{{p|Dur-Sharrukin}}, and {{p|Nineveh}}, their halls
Were carved with lion hunts, and wars, the sky
Of courts; their reliefs ran along the walls.

And {{c|2249|Ashurbanipal}} gathered, in his hall
At {{p|Nineveh}}, a library of clay,
Tens of thousands of tablets, keeping all
Old songs, {{c|1913|Gilgamesh}}, {{p|Sumerian}} way.

{{c|2250|Ashurnasirpal II}} then moved the seat
To {{p|Nimrud}}; {{c|2251|Shalmaneser}} then went west,
At {{p|Qarqar}} fought, and {{c|2252|Ahab}} he would meet,
{{p|Samaria}}'s king, there among the rest.

Then {{c|2253|Tiglath-Pileser III}} made it strong:
A standing army, provinces, and those
Who were deported, all the peoples' throng;
{{c|1986|Sargon II}} took the north, and dealt it blows:

It fell: the ten tribes were carried off, lost
Among the lands; and others, brought instead,
Were mixed with those who stayed, and at that cost
{{p|Samaritans}} were made, from those who'd fled.

And only {{p|Judah}} stood, beneath the yoke;
{{c|2254|Sennacherib}} came down, and took and burned
Its forty-six towns, and, with flame and smoke,
{{p|Zion}} was ringed; and {{c|2255|Hezekiah}} turned

To {{c|472|God}}; and in a night, an angel slew
A hundred eighty-five thousand, his host;
{{c|2254|Sennacherib}} went home, and never drew
His sword against the city; so the most

Of {{p|Judah}} held that {{c|472|God}} would keep his own,
His city, that no host could take his hill.
{{c|2256|Esarhaddon}} took {{p|Egypt}}'s very throne;
And {{c|2249|Ashurbanipal}}, the last king, held still

From {{p|Egypt}} to the {{p|Zagros}}, wise and learned;
But war with {{c|2257|Shamash-shum-ukin}}, his own
Brother in {{p|Babylon}}, drained it; it turned
To ruin after him, and soon was flown.

The {{p|Medes}} came from the {{p|Zagros}}; from the south
{{c|2258|Nabopolassar}}'s {{p|Babylon}}; they fell
On {{p|Nineveh}}, and burned it, and the mouth
Of the great library was buried well

In ash; {{c|2260|Sinsharishkun}} died in the flame;
At {{p|Harran}} the last were crushed; and in one
Short generation, all the fear and name
Of {{p|Assyria}} was gone, terror done.

And {{c|2261|Nahum}} sang: Woe to the bloody town,
Of lies and robbery! Who'll mourn, who'll yearn?
And all the peoples, when it was brought down,
Rejoiced, and {{p|Judah}} too, to see it burn.

Then {{c|2259|Nebuchadnezzar II}} ruled, and won
There at {{p|Carchemish}} against {{c|2262|Necho}}, and held
The west; and {{p|Babylon}}, beneath the sun,
He built again, the greatest; and it swelled:

Its walls were vast; the {{p|Ishtar Gate}} was blue
With shining tiles, and beasts in gold; and there
{{p|Hanging Gardens}} rose for {{c|2263|Amytis}}, who
Missed her mountains in the {{p|Median}} air.

Two hundred thousand dwelt there; and its priests
Watched all the stars for centuries, and made
The zodiac, and reckoned moons and feasts,
And how the planets move, and where they strayed.

The week of seven days, for seven lights,
The {{p|Sun}}, the {{p|Moon}}, five wanderers that roam;
The circle's degrees, sixty-fold; the rites
Of sixty minutes: these we keep at home.

But {{p|Judah}} rose against him; and he came,
And took {{p|Jerusalem}}, and took its king,
{{c|2270|Jehoiachin}}, the nobles, and the same
Craftsmen to {{p|Babylon}}; and, rebelling,

Then {{c|2271|Zedekiah}} rose again; eighteen
Months long the siege; and then the city fell;
The temple {{c|2189|Solomon}} had built was seen
In flames, its gold and bronze borne off as well;

{{c|2271|Zedekiah}} watched his sons slain, and then
His eyes were put out, and in chains he went;
And all the city's people, all its men,
To {{p|Babylon}} were carried, and were spent.

The line of {{c|1956|David}} broke; the temple fell;
And by all reckoning, the folk should be
Lost like the northern tribes, as nations tell;
But {{p|Judah}} was not lost; they kept, though free

Of land and temple, all their law and rite;
They dwelt together on {{p|Babylon}}'s plain;
{{c|2272|Ezekiel}}, {{c|1922|Jeremiah}}, gave them light:
That {{c|472|God}} was not defeated, but again

Would bring them home; for they had strayed, and so
Not leaving, but correction for their sin;
And there they gathered, that the law might go
With them, the prophets' words, the tales within,

To keep them anywhere they were; and then
The house of {{c|2019|Jacob}} could not die, but stayed
Alive by word and law, among all men.
{{c|2024|Nebuchadnezzar}} died; his line decayed;

And {{c|2273|Cyrus}} came, of {{p|Persia}}, and he took
{{p|Babylon}} with ease; its folk, who had borne
A hated king, received him; and he shook
The exiles loose for home, no more to mourn.

Honor them: {{p|Assyria}}'s great clay hall,
And {{p|Babylon}}'s blue gate, its stars, its week;
And {{p|Judah}}, which, in exile, after all,
Kept its own law, and lived by what they speak.


# Chapter 167: The Babylonian Exile and the Birth of Monotheism

In {{p|Babylon}} the house of {{c|2019|Jacob}} dwelt,
Far from its land; and there its word grew new:
For once they'd said their {{c|472|God}} was great, and knelt
To him alone, though other gods were true;

Who is like you among the gods? they'd sung,
And had no other gods before his face;
But in the exile, from the prophet's tongue,
There came a word that gave no others place:

I am the first, I am the last; there's none
Beside me; and the idols are but gold
And silver, hands' work, mouths that speak to none,
And eyes that do not see; they are not old,

Not gods at all. And so {{c|472|God}} was the one
Of all the nations, though they did not know;
And all of history beneath the sun
Was his, and all the world's right, high and low.

For gods then had their lands; and to be borne
Away from home was leaving one's god there;
And so the exiles chose: had {{c|2021|Marduk}} torn
Them from their {{c|472|God}}? Or was he everywhere,

In {{p|Babylon}} as much as {{p|Zion}} too?
And they said: everywhere. And {{c|2021|Marduk}}'s shrine,
And {{c|2275|Nabu}}'s, {{c|1976|Ishtar}}'s, all the gods they knew,
Were wood and stone, the work of hands, no sign.

And some went over, as the exiled do;
But those who stayed said why: the gods are naught.
And from {{p|Iran}}, the {{c|2167|Wise Lord}}'s word came through,
One maker, and a judgment, and they caught

That word, and it was theirs, and back again;
And with the temple gone, the priests dispersed,
They gathered up their law, their tales, and then
The prophets' words, and wrote them down, and versed

Them all in one, to keep them as they went;
And where ten men could meet, they'd meet to read,
To pray, though there no altar's smoke was sent,
And so the house could live in any need.

Now, where the poem stands: it will not weigh
The one god and the many, nor the claim
Of rival faiths, as if they were; for they
Are one: a hundred names don't change the same

Offering: bread and cup and honoured dead.
The prophet said all worship is one rite
Confused about one god; what he has said
The poem keeps as its own word, by right.

The wars were fought for land, and for the crown,
And altar: who would hold the rite, and where;
One house, one shrine, its heirs at war, cast down
Each other at its one door, fighting there.

And yet the exiles did not, would not make
Their word for war; they made it to hold on,
When others held the altar, for the sake
Of rite, which would not fall when crowns were gone.

{{c|2272|Ezekiel}} the priest, at {{p|Babylon}}'s stream,
Saw {{c|472|God}}'s glory there, his chariot-throne
That moved across the heavens, like a dream,
{{c|472|God}} with the exiles, not {{p|Zion}} alone.

{{c|1922|Jeremiah}} wept: he warned, and they fell;
He saw the city burn; and he was borne
To {{p|Egypt}} by the fleeing, and he'd dwell
And die an exile, called by {{c|472|God}} to mourn.

The prophet of the exile sang the one
{{c|472|God}}, and the servant suffering, whose pain
Would heal the nations; {{c|2276|Ezra}}, when they'd won
Their way back home, read out the law again;

{{c|2277|Nehemiah}} built {{p|Jerusalem}}'s wall,
With {{p|Persia}}'s leave, and ruled, and kept it whole;
{{c|2278|Zerubbabel}}, of {{c|1956|David}}'s line, and all
With {{c|2141|Joshua}} the priest, raised up the goal:

The {{p|Second Temple}}, smaller than the first;
But not all came; for many stayed instead
In {{p|Babylon}}; and those who came, the worst
Of lands they found, with hostile neighbors spread:

The {{p|Samaritans}}, who kept {{c|472|God}} as well;
And no king ruled; the line of {{c|1956|David}} stayed
A hope; and so they waited, and would tell
Of one who'd come, and how the world was made

To end the evil age and bring the new.
So from the exile came the word: that one
{{c|472|God}} is, and he is everywhere; the true
Law in a book; the meeting; and the sun

Of hope; and all of it, our house's own,
Our rite, kept in the exile through the night
Of {{p|Babylon}}, when temple, land, and throne
Were gone, and still they kept the bread and light.

So honor them: the exiles, and the word
They kept by {{p|Babylon}}'s streams, where they'd roam;
{{c|2272|Ezekiel}} and {{c|1922|Jeremiah}}, who heard;
And {{c|2276|Ezra}}, {{c|2277|Nehemiah}}, who came home.


# Chapter 168: Confucius and Laozi

In {{p|China}}, while the {{p|Zhou}} king's rule grew thin,
And vassals fought as kingdoms of their own,
In {{p|Spring and Autumn}}, from the chaos in
The land, a hundred schools of thought were sown:

There were {{p|Confucian}}, {{p|Daoist}}, {{p|Legalist}},
The {{p|Mohist}}, and the {{p|School of Names}}, and more,
The {{p|Yin-Yang}}; and of all of them, the list
Was led by two, who stood at the root's core.

{{c|1958|Confucius}}, {{c|2296|Kongzi}}, {{c|2297|Master Kong}}, was born
In {{p|Lu}}, of noble blood, but fallen low;
His father died when he was three; and worn
By poverty, his mother raised him so.

He learned the {{p|Zhou}} rites; and he served in {{p|Lu}},
And rose, and was the minister of law;
But those he crossed were strong, and out he flew,
And fourteen years he wandered, and he saw

No ruler who would hear him; home he came,
And taught, and set the classics right; and died
Believing he had failed; and yet his name
Lives on, the teacher of the world's wide side.

His students wrote his sayings down; he said
That five ties make the world: the king and men,
The father, son; the husband, wife; the head
And younger brother; friends with friends; and then

Each one has his own duty: rule with {{p|ren}},
Benevolence; and serve with loyal heart;
The father nurtures; sons keep {{p|xiao}}; and when
Each does his own, the world is not apart.

But when the kings are cruel, and sons forsake,
The world falls into chaos; so the cure
Begins with the king's virtue, which will make
The rest grow good, as wind bends grass, and sure.

No god's command, no judgment after death,
Nor reason's rule alone, but ties of kin,
And learning, rite, and thought, with every breath,
Make the {{p|junzi}}, the gentleman within.

He is not born, but made: he learns the songs,
The rites, {{p|Book of Changes}}, and the {{p|Annals}};
And beauty's tied to goodness; and he longs
To shape his feeling through the old channels.

{{c|2144|Laozi}}, the {{c|2301|Old Master}}, kept the scrolls{{fn|Many historians doubt that Laozi was a single historical person, and date the Daodejing to the fourth century BCE or later.}}
Of the {{p|Zhou}} court, and older far than {{c|1958|Kong}};
{{c|1958|Confucius}} came to him; of all his goals
He told him: let them go; your wish so strong

To set the world right: drop it. Then he left
The court, which rotted, on a water-ox,
And rode out west; and at the mountain's cleft
The gatekeeper there, {{c|2302|Yinxi}}, by the rocks,

Knew him, and begged him: write it down. And so
Five thousand words he wrote, the {{p|Dao De Jing}},
And rode on west, and none would ever know
Where he had gone, or see him, or his thing.

The {{p|Dao}} that can be spoken of is not
The lasting {{p|Dao}}; the Way's beyond our speech;
And it moves by {{p|wu wei}}, without the knot
Of forcing; who would force, will fail to reach.

The soft things of the world will overcome
The hard; the water yields, and wears the stone;
And so the sage does little, and the sum
Is much; and so the king who rules alone

By force will fail, and rouse revolt; but he
Who rules but lightly, lets the people be,
Rules well: rule a great state as you would see
A small fish cooked, and do not stir it free.

{{c|1958|Confucius}} said: be good, and lead by deed;
{{c|2144|Laozi}} said: do nothing, let it flow;
And both grew from the {{p|Zhou}}'s same broken need,
And {{p|China}} kept them both, and kept them so:

In public, the {{p|Confucian}} rite and law;
In private life, the {{p|Daoist}} hill and stream;
The scholar served the court, and also saw
The mountain, and the tea, the empty dream.

The poem honours this. It keeps no score
Between the many gods and one; the way
Of {{p|China}}, keeping both, is that one door,
One house, which keeps two teachings, day by day,

Its own rites, both of them, in its own view:
Not things that clash, but parts, as they were meant;
Not rival faiths, but partners, are the two;
The ones who made them knew the way they went.

So honor them: {{c|1958|Confucius}}, who would teach
The ties, the rite, the {{p|ren}}, the {{p|junzi}}'s art;
{{c|2144|Laozi}}, of the Way beyond our speech;
Two poles of one house, never held apart.

---

# Gemini (7宮) - Days 169-196


# Chapter 169: The Persian Empire

{{c|2273|Cyrus the Great}}: a conqueror, and yet
The conquered thanked him; {{p|Judah}} named him blessed,
{{c|472|God}}'s own anointed; {{p|Babylon}}, in debt,
Hailed him as freer; and the {{p|Greeks}} confessed

That he was just; and from the {{p|Indus}} plain
To the {{p|Aegean}}, {{p|Caucasus}} to {{p|Nile}},
Some thirty million lived beneath his reign
And his heirs', many tongues, and every style.

At {{p|Anshan}} he was born, the son of one,
{{c|2279|Cambyses I}}, king of the {{p|Persian}} race,
Who served the {{p|Medes}}; his mother, so they've spun,
Was {{c|2280|Astyages}}' daughter, {{p|Median}} grace.

He took his father's throne, and then he rose
Against the {{p|Medes}}, and took {{c|2280|Astyages}}' land;
Then west, to {{p|Lydia}}, whose king, one knows,
Was {{c|2281|Croesus}}, rich; who'd asked, at {{p|Delphi}}'s hand,

If he should war on {{p|Persia}}; and it said:
Cross {{p|Halys}}, and a great realm will be lost;
He crossed; it was his own; at {{p|Thymbra}}, dead
Hopes; {{p|Lydia}}, {{p|Ionia}}, the cost.

Then east he went, and held the plateau wide,
And {{p|Central Asia}}; then, when these were won,
{{p|Babylon}} fell with little fight; inside,
Its priests, who scorned their king, welcomed this one.

And {{c|2180|Cyrus}} let the exiled peoples go
Back to their lands, and build their gods' own halls;
Not {{p|Judah}} only, all: he'd have them so,
Content and loyal, safe within their walls.

He wrote it on a cylinder of clay:
The gods restored, the peoples sent back home;
And then, against the {{p|Massagetae}}, one day,
He died in battle, far from where he'd roam.

His tomb at {{p|Pasargadae}}, of plain stone,
A gabled roof, still stands; and on it read:
O man, I'm {{c|2180|Cyrus}}, who made {{p|Persia}}'s throne,
The king of {{p|Asia}}: grudge me not this bed.

His son, {{c|2284|Cambyses II}}, then took the {{p|Nile}}:
{{c|2285|Psamtik III}} fell there; and, crowned anew,
{{c|2283|Cambyses}} ruled as pharaoh for a while,
And died; and then a crisis came in view:

For he'd had {{c|2286|Bardiya}}, his brother, killed
In secret; and a false {{c|2286|Bardiya}} rose;
{{c|2287|Darius}}, of the royal kin, and skilled,
With {{p|Persia}}'s nobles, cast him down, and those

Who rose against him, nine, he put them down,
And carved it high on {{p|Behistun}}'s cliff face
In three tongues, him above them, with his crown;
And then he ordered all the realm's wide space:

Twenty {{p|satrapies}}, each one ruled, and
A general apart, a scribe to tell
The court of both; one tax in all the land;
One weight and measure; the {{p|daric}} as well,

Of gold; and roads, the {{p|Royal Road}}, with posts
A day's ride each, from {{p|Susa}} to the sea
At {{p|Sardis}}; and {{p|Persepolis}}, whose hosts
Of columns in the {{p|Apadana}}, free;

And round it, carved, the peoples bringing gifts:
The {{p|Medes}}, {{p|Elamites}}, and {{p|Babylon}}'s band,
{{p|Egypt}}, {{p|Ionia}}, by turns, in shifts,
{{p|India}}, {{p|Scythia}}, and {{p|Arab}} land.

Each kept its tongue, its gods, its rulers, rite,
And paid its tribute, sent its troops, and bowed;
No mass deportments, no forced faith, no blight
Of terror like {{p|Assyria}}'s; the crowd

Lived well beneath. {{c|2287|Darius}} took the east,
The {{p|Indus}}, {{p|Thrace}} the west; but lost to {{p|Greece}}
At {{p|Marathon}}; and died, his reign's last feast
Thirty-six years; and {{c|1985|Xerxes}} found no peace

In {{p|Greece}}, but lost at {{p|Salamis}}; and then,
As {{c|2288|Ahasuerus}}, {{c|1985|Xerxes}} would wed
{{c|392|Esther}}, of {{p|Judah}}'s house, among his men
At {{p|Susa}}; and built where his father led.

And after him, the kings kept what they'd won:
{{c|2289|Artaxerxes}}, {{c|2290|Darius II}}, and more;
{{p|Egypt}} rose often, and was overrun;
And plots and bribes and hired troops grew sore.

And {{p|Aramaic}} was the common tongue;
The stars of {{p|Babylon}} went east and west;
{{p|Greek}} doctors, {{p|Phoenician}} sailors, among
Their servants; {{p|Judah}}'s scribes; and all the rest.

The kings bowed to {{c|2166|Ahura Mazda}}, but
They did not force their faith: in {{p|Babylon}},
{{c|2180|Cyrus}} served {{c|2021|Marduk}}; and in {{p|Egypt}}, what
The pharaohs did, {{c|2283|Cambyses}} did; and on

{{p|Zion}} the temple rose with royal gold;
For the {{c|2167|Wise Lord}}, the maker of all things,
Was served wherever right worship was told,
By any name; and so, as {{c|2167|Wise Lord}}'s kings,

They kept all rites: one rite, by many names,
One house, and many altars, and one lord;
And so the realm was home to all its claims,
And none were forced, and none put to the sword.

So honor {{p|Persia}}: {{c|2180|Cyrus}}, who set free;
{{c|2287|Darius}}, of the roads and of the coin;
The king who kept all rites, and let them be,
And let the many peoples, as one, join.


# Chapter 170: Classical Greece, Part Two

And {{p|Persia}} beaten, {{p|Athens}} rose: its fleet,
{{c|2246|Themistocles}}' own fleet, had won the day
At {{p|Salamis}}; its city, burned, complete,
Was raised again; and it would lead the way.

Formed the {{p|Delian League}}, on {{p|Delos}}' isle,
To guard against the {{p|Persians}}: ships and gold
From all, the fleet from {{p|Athens}}; and a while
It freed the {{p|Greeks}} the {{p|Persians}} still would hold.

But those who sought to leave were held by force;
The treasury was moved from {{p|Delos}}' shrine
To {{p|Athens}}, and it built, by that resource,
The {{p|Acropolis}}; so the league's design

Became {{p|Athens}}' rule; others paid it due;
And {{p|Sparta}} feared it, and her friends; and war
Would come of it. But first the golden few
Years, from four-sixty to four-thirty, bore

The richest fruit the world had seen: the rule
Of {{c|2231|Pericles}}; the men who were its own,
Some fifty thousand, met, and, by the rule
Of lot, held office; judged; and spoke alone

Upon the {{p|Pnyx}}; ten boards of ten; the courts
Of hundreds; war and treasure, voted through
By all; and {{c|2231|Pericles}}, of all its sorts,
Was general yearly, the city's due.

And at the graves of {{p|Athens}}' dead he said:
Our rule is called the people's, for it's held
Not by a few, but all; and so they led,
Free men, by laws they made, and so excelled.

At the {{p|Dionysia}} plays were made,
Each poet striving for the prize; and three
Great makers of the tragedies were weighed:
{{c|2224|Aeschylus}}, grand and mythic, first; and he

Wrote {{p|Oresteia}}: {{c|1337|Agamemnon}}, back
From {{p|Troy}}, slain by {{c|1336|Clytemnestra}}, his wife;
{{c|2359|Orestes}}, son, avenging; then the track
Of blood was judged by {{c|1995|Athena}}; the strife

Was ended by a court; the {{c|2360|Furies}} turned
To {{c|2361|Eumenides}}, kindly ones; and so
The vengeance of the clan for law was spurned,
And civic justice founded, long ago.

{{c|2225|Sophocles}}, next, wrote men of weight who fought
Their fate: {{c|2362|Oedipus}}, he who solved the {{c|2363|Sphinx}},
Yet killed his father, wed his mother, caught
Unknowing, and then blinded at the brinks;

{{c|2365|Antigone}}, who buried, though the king
Forbade it, her own brother, by the law
Of gods above the city's; and the thing
She did stands as the higher law we saw.

{{c|2226|Euripides}}, the last, more doubting, gave
A voice to women, slaves, the beaten side:
{{p|Medea}}, {{p|Bacchae}}, {{p|Trojan Women}}, brave
And harrowing; and later, far and wide,

Held greatest. And the comedy: the bite
Of {{c|2227|Aristophanes}}, whose wives withdrew
Their love in {{p|Lysistrata}} till the fight
Should end; in {{p|The Clouds}} his mockery drew

Old {{c|2232|Socrates}}, a basket in the air,
Who taught the worse to seem the better; and
The real one rose up in the crowd, and there
Stood, so they could compare him, where he'd stand.

{{c|2229|Phidias}} made {{c|2369|Athena}}, gold to see,
Forty feet high, with {{c|2370|Nike}} in her hand,
And the {{c|2065|Zeus}} at {{p|Olympia}}; and he
And his made the calm, balanced bodies grand.

The {{p|Parthenon}}: {{c|2230|Ictinus}} drew its plan,
{{c|2371|Callicrates}} too, and {{c|2229|Phidias}} its stone;
Its columns curved to fool the eye of man,
Its frieze the great procession, gods there shown.

The {{p|Sophists}} came to teach the art of speech
For pay: {{c|2372|Protagoras}}, he who said that man
Is measure of all things; and each to each
They taught both sides, and some feared what began.

And {{c|2232|Socrates}} would take no fee, and taught
No doctrine, but said only that he knew
He nothing knew; he asked, and those he caught
Found that the things they knew were never true:

What's justice? Courage? Piety? He'd ask,
And test what they would answer, till they saw
They did not know; he took it as his task
From gods, to make men know, and find their flaw.

And he made many foes: the mighty, shamed
In public; those who kept the rites, who would
Not hear a man who said a god, unnamed,
Spoke in him; and the quarrel, as it stood,

In three-ninety-nine it was brought to court:
It asked who held the city's altars, who
Might speak for {{p|Athens}}' gods, and of what sort;
Of impiety, they said, and new gods too,

And leading youth astray; and yet he knew
The gods he served were {{p|Athens}}' gods as well.
Five hundred judged him; and he told them true:
His work, a gift; they found him guilty; fell

The sentence: hemlock; and he drank it, calm,
And would not flee; and dying, said, to one,
{{c|2377|Crito}}: we owe {{c|2378|Asclepius}}, for his balm,
A rooster; pay it. And so he was done.

He wrote nothing; {{c|2376|Plato}}, who wrote him down,
Was his; the {{p|Academy}} was his own;
The forms, the threefold soul, the king whose crown
Was wisdom, and the soul, undying, shown.

And {{c|2376|Plato}}'s pupil, {{c|1081|Aristotle}}, turned
To things themselves: to logic, physics, life,
The soul, the good, the city; and he learned
And wrote of all of them, and ended strife.

But {{p|Athens}} and {{p|Sparta}} then went to war,
Four-thirty-one; for twenty-seven years;
And {{c|2231|Pericles}} died of the plague; and more,
The fleet at {{p|Syracuse}} was lost, in tears;

In four-oh-four, {{p|Athens}} gave in; its walls
Were torn down; and the {{p|Thirty Tyrants}} ruled
A while, till rule returned to people's halls;
But all were worn; and so the gold age cooled.
