So honor {{p|Athens}}: {{c|2231|Pericles}}'s rule,
The three who wrote of grief, the one who laughed,
The {{p|Parthenon}}; and {{c|2232|Socrates}}, no fool,
Who served his city's gods, and drank the draught.


# Chapter 171: The Buddha

Upon the {{p|Gangetic}} plain, the {{p|Brahmin}} priests
Kept up the {{p|Vedic}} rite of flame and gift,
And thought it held the world; but from the feasts
The {{p|Shramanas}} went out, to wander, shift

For their own freeing, without priest or shrine;
The {{p|Upanishads}} turned the rite within:
That {{c|2305|Atman}} is {{c|2306|Brahman}}; and {{p|karma}}'s line,
{{p|Samsara}}'s wheel, and {{p|moksha}}, freed from sin.

How can a man be free from pain, and death,
And birth again? The {{p|Jains}} would starve, and lore
Of {{p|Ajivikas}} said fate rules each breath;
The {{p|Charvakas}}: this life, and nothing more;

The {{p|Brahmins}} kept their sacrifice; and then
Into the field came one, {{c|2304|Siddhartha}}, born
At {{p|Lumbini}}, of the {{p|Shakya}} men,
{{c|2307|Shuddhodana}}'s, the chief's son; {{c|2308|Maya}}, torn

From life, his mother; and the son was raised
By {{c|2309|Mahapajapati}}; the sages said:
King, or teacher; and his father, amazed,
Kept him from grief, and sickness, and the dead.

At sixteen wed {{c|2310|Yashodhara}}, and had
A son, {{c|2311|Rahula}}; and at twenty-nine
He went outside the walls, and saw the sad
Four Sights: the old, the sick, the dead, the sign

Of one who wandered, seeking; and that night
He left his palace, wife, and son, and cut
His hair, and took the robe, and sought the light,
The way from pain; and every door was shut.

He learned from two great teachers, deep and wise,
Absorptions; but they did not end the pain;
Six years with five ascetics, under skies
Of cold and heat, he fasted, and would strain,

Breath held, so thin his spine could be felt through
His belly; and the freedom did not come;
He saw that self-torment, like pleasure, too,
Kept mind on body; and the middle sum

Was the way: he took from {{c|2315|Sujata}}'s hand
Rice pudding; and his five friends went away;
And at {{p|Bodh Gaya}}, where the fig trees stand,
He sat, and vowed he would not move till day

Had shown him what he sought; and {{c|2316|Mara}} came,
The lord of death and seeming, with delight
And fear, and said he had no right, no claim;
He touched the earth for witness; and the night

Was ended, {{c|2316|Mara}} beaten; and at dawn
He saw how pain arose, and how it ends;
The {{c|1959|Buddha}}, the awakened, from then on,
At thirty-five; and so his teaching wends.

There's suffering, {{p|dukkha}}: all that's made will pass,
And even joy is shadowed by its end;
Its cause is craving, {{p|tanha}}, grasp and grass
Of wanting, from not seeing; it can end:

{{p|Nirvana}}, blowing out, the flame's last fuel;
And there's a path, the {{p|Eightfold Path}}: right view,
Intention, speech, and action, as a rule,
Livelihood, effort, mindfulness, and true

Concentration; not pain nor pleasure, but
The middle way, for anyone to walk.
No self, {{p|anatta}}: and the door is shut
On any lasting self; the {{p|skandhas}}' stock,

The form, the feeling, sense, the shaping, mind,
Are flux, and none of them a self; and so,
In seeing through it, craving falls behind,
And there is no self saved, but self let go.

He taught for forty-five years; and he made
The {{p|sangha}}; kings and beggars, {{c|2317|Brahmins}}, came,
And those of no caste, and he did not grade
By caste; and women, at his nurse's claim,

And {{c|2318|Ananda}}'s; and spoke the common tongue,
Not {{p|Sanskrit}}; and to questions that were vain,
Is the world endless, is the self among
The body, would he live past death, he'd feign

No answer, but he said: a man is hit
With poisoned arrow, and he will not let
It out until he knows who shot, and it,
The bow, the feathers; he'll be dead, and yet

Not know. His care was pain, and how to free.
At {{p|Kushinagar}} he died, eighty, old;
All made things pass; strive on, with care, said he;
And left no book, no heir, but what was told

To the {{p|sangha}}, the {{p|Dharma}} as its guide;
And still today his path is walked by those
Some five hundred million, spread far and wide,
Who sit beneath the fig tree, as he chose.

He did not say there were no gods: on high
The {{p|devas}} live long in heavens, and turn
Upon the wheel as well, and they must die
And be reborn, and free themselves, and learn.

Our song: the gods are many, and live long,
None is the centre; and no second creed
Stands here beside our own; and all along
This book has said the same: the {{c|1959|Buddha}}'s seed

Is our own rite; the middle way's our road,
And his the fig tree, and the dawn he'd see;
Kept under names his country's tongue bestowed.
So honor him, the one who woke, and free.


# Chapter 172: Classical Greece, Part Three

And {{p|Athens}} lost the war; and yet the {{p|Greeks}}
Went on, less strong, but sharper in their thought;
The fourth age brought the two whose wisdom speaks
The loudest: {{c|2376|Plato}}, and the one he taught.

{{c|2376|Plato}}'s early dialogues asked, as he,
Old {{c|2232|Socrates}}, had asked, what justice is,
Or courage, piety, and left, unfree
Of doubt, the asker: {{p|Euthyphro}}, and his

The {{p|Laches}}, the {{p|Charmides}}; and then he made
His own: {{p|Republic}}, {{p|Phaedo}}, and the feast
Of the {{p|Symposium}}, {{p|Phaedrus}}; and laid
Out there the {{x|Forms}}: behind each thing, the least

Of beauties, justice, shapes, there is a Form,
The Beautiful itself, the Just, more true
And lasting than the thing; and reason, warm,
Not sense, can see them; and the wise man's due

Is climbing to them. In the {{p|Cave}}, he wrote,
Men sit in chains, and watch the shadows play,
And think them real; the wise man, freed, remote,
Climbs to the sun, and sees, and then the way

Back down, to free the rest, though they resist;
As {{c|2232|Socrates}} had done, and died for it.
{{p|Republic}}: let the wise, who've seen and kissed
The {{x|Forms}}, be kings; the many, who'd submit

Opinion, should not rule; the guards below,
And then the farmers, craftsmen, traders, each
To his own work; for {{p|Athens}}, he would know,
Had killed his teacher, by its vote and speech.

And later, in the {{p|Parmenides}}, he tried
His {{x|Forms}} again, and doubted; in his {{p|Laws}},
He gave the kings up, and a code supplied;
And in the {{p|Timaeus}}, sang the world's first cause.

And his {{p|Academy}} in {{p|Athens}} taught;
And there, a young {{p|Macedonian}}, came one,
{{c|1081|Aristotle}}, of {{p|Stagira}}, who sought
Wisdom with {{c|2376|Plato}} twenty years, till done.

Passed over, he went off to {{p|Lesbos}}' shore,
And studied living things; then was called home
To {{p|Macedon}}, to teach the young prince, before
He was king: {{c|1982|Alexander}}, who would roam.

And then to {{p|Athens}}, and the {{p|Lyceum}}, where,
Walking, he taught; and when the prince was dead,
They turned on him; to {{p|Chalcis}} he fled there,
And died there in the next year, it is said.

He wrote of logic, {{p|Organon}}; of all
Of nature, {{p|Physics}}, {{p|Heavens}}, weather, birth;
Of animals; the soul; and what we call
{{x|Metaphysics}}, after the physics' worth;

The {{p|Ethics}}: that the end of man is to
Flourish, {{p|eudaimonia}}, virtue's way;
{{p|Politics}}, and {{p|Rhetoric}}; and he knew
The {{x|Poetics}}, catharsis, and the play.

And there were other schools: the {{p|Cynic}} men,
Who scorned all rules; and {{c|2400|Diogenes}} lived there,
In {{p|Athens}}' market, in a jar; and then
The great {{c|2381|Alexander}} once came to where

He lay, and asked what he could do for him,
{{c|2401|Diogenes}} said: just stand out of my sun.{{fn|The meeting of Alexander and Diogenes is told by Plutarch and Diogenes Laertius, centuries later; historians doubt it happened as told.}}
The conqueror of all could not, by whim,
Give anything to one who needed none.

And {{c|2402|Pyrrho}} went with {{c|1982|Alexander}}'s host,
To {{p|India}}, and learned there, and came back
To teach that every claim, the least, the most,
Had arguments both ways; and so the track

Was to hold back, and live in peace; and then
{{c|2403|Epicurus}} then taught that pleasure, freed
Of pain and fear, is good; and that all men,
And gods, and death, are atoms; and the need

Is simple life, and friends, and not to fear
The gods or death. And all these schools would grow,
Each with its masters, texts, and fellows near,
And each from that one {{p|Greek}} root, long ago.

And {{c|2406|Philip II}} of {{p|Macedon}}, in the north,
Half-{{p|Greek}}, as some said, beat the southern towns
At {{p|Chaeronea}}; and the cities, forth
From then, served him, the {{p|League of Corinth}}'s crowns;

{{c|1406|Philip}} died; {{c|1982|Alexander}}, twenty, took
The throne, and crushed the risings one by one,
He turned on {{p|Persia}}, as his father's book
Had planned; and so the free towns' age was done.

So honor {{p|Greece}}'s last age: {{c|2376|Plato}}'s cave,
And {{c|1081|Aristotle}}'s all; the {{p|Cynic}}'s jar;
The {{p|Skeptic}}'s pause; calm {{c|2403|Epicurus}} gave;
And {{c|1982|Alexander}}, setting out afar.


# Chapter 173: The Mahabharata

{{c|2328|Vyasa}}, the compiler, sage, was there,
And saw it, and he told it: for his own
Were {{c|2329|Dhritarashtra}}, {{c|2330|Pandu}}, and the heir
{{c|2331|Vidura}}; and from them the war was grown

Of cousins came, the {{p|Kuru}} house that ruled
At {{p|Hastinapura}}: {{c|2330|Pandu}}'s five sons
Called {{p|Pandavas}}; and hundred, who were schooled
As {{p|Kauravas}}, the blind king's many ones.

The blind one could not rule; and {{c|2330|Pandu}} reigned,
And died; the blind one ruled for all the young;
And then {{c|2332|Duryodhana}}, his eldest, strained
Against {{c|2124|Yudhishthira}}, the first among.

The five: {{c|2124|Yudhishthira}}, the righteous, true;
{{c|2333|Bhima}}, the strong; {{c|2334|Arjuna}}, with the bow;
{{c|2335|Nakula}} and {{c|2336|Sahadeva}}, the two
Twins, handsome; and one wife they'd share and know,

{{c|2337|Draupadi}}, won by {{c|2334|Arjuna}}; and when
Their mother {{c|2338|Kunti}} said: share what you've won,
Not knowing, she was wife to the five men.
And {{c|2332|Duryodhana}} envied them; and none

Of his attempts could kill them: house of lac
They burned; they fled; the poisoned sweet; the snare;
And then the dice: {{c|2339|Shakuni}}, at his back,
Played loaded dice; {{c|2124|Yudhishthira}} sat there,

Who would not turn a game down, and he lost
His kingdom, wealth, his brothers, and himself,
And {{c|2337|Draupadi}}; and she was dragged, the cost,
Into the hall, to strip her, like a shelf;

But {{c|2340|Krishna}} made her sari without end,
And none could strip her; but the deed was done.
They went to exile: twelve years, and to spend
The thirteenth hidden; and when that was run,

{{c|2332|Duryodhana}} would not give back their land;
And war came: at {{p|Kurukshetra}}, the field,
For eighteen days, and every house's hand
Was in it; and the dead lay, none would yield;

And on its eve, {{c|2334|Arjuna}} looked across
At cousins, teachers, kin, and sank in grief:
How could he kill them, bearing such a loss?
His driver: {{c|2340|Krishna}}, {{c|2072|Vishnu}}, come in brief

To earth; in the {{p|Bhagavad Gita}} sang:
The body dies, the soul does not; so fight;
Act, but let go the fruit, and do not hang
On gain or loss; give all as offering right;

The three paths: deed, and knowledge, and the love
Of god; and all are good. And then he showed
His form: all worlds, all beings, all, above
And under, eating warriors, past and owed,

The source of all, and where all things return;
And {{c|2334|Arjuna}} could barely bear the sight;
And then he took his bow up, with no turn
Of doubt; and so began eighteen days' fight.

Yet dharma there was hard: to tell a lie
To win? ({{c|2340|Krishna}} said yes.) And {{c|2348|Karna}}, born
A {{p|Pandava}}, raised by {{p|Kauravas}}: why
Should he leave him who raised him? So, forlorn,

He chose his friend, and died; and {{c|2349|Bhishma}}, old,
Bound by his oath to who would hold the throne,
Fought those he loved, and fell, as he was told,
On arrows, by {{c|2334|Arjuna}}'s hand alone.

And all were dead: {{c|2332|Duryodhana}} lay low,
His hundred brothers gone, the teachers, friends;
The {{p|Pandavas}} had won, and stood in woe
Over the field of kin, the bitter ends.

{{c|2124|Yudhishthira}} was crowned, and ruled for long,
Thirty-six years; then left, with brothers, wife,
Up to the {{p|Himalayas}}; and the throng
Fell one by one, and left, along with life,

Him and a dog, which was the god of right;
He would not leave the dog, and he went in
To heaven; there he found, in that strange light,
{{c|2332|Duryodhana}}, and his own kin in sin

Below; and that was the last test; for good
Does not make sure of joy, and judgment's thin
Before the world. And {{c|2349|Bhishma}}, as he could,
Had taught him, dying, peace and law within.

And {{c|2340|Krishna}} was {{c|2072|Vishnu}}, come down to earth,
As he would come when right was threatened: fish,
{{c|1550|Matsya}}; {{c|2350|Kurma}}; {{c|2351|Varaha}}, the boar's birth;
{{c|2352|Narasimha}}, man-lion; dwarf, by wish,

{{c|2353|Vamana}}; {{c|2354|Parashurama}}; the king
{{c|2009|Rama}}; {{c|2340|Krishna}}; and the {{c|1959|Buddha}}; and last,
{{c|2355|Kalki}}, who comes to end the dark age' ring:
The god comes down to us, and holds us fast.

So honor them: the five, the hundred, all,
{{c|2337|Draupadi}}, {{c|2348|Karna}}, {{c|2349|Bhishma}}, arrow-laid;
And {{c|2340|Krishna}}, at the chariot, the call,
Who sang the {{p|Gita}}, and the war was made.


# Chapter 174: Alexander the Great

Great {{c|2407|Alexander}} of {{p|Macedon}}, the third,
In thirteen years, from {{p|Greece}} to {{p|Indus}}' shore,
Took all the lands, and {{p|Persia}}'s throne, and stirred
The world; and died at thirty-two, no more.

His father, {{c|2406|Philip II}}, had made the north
A force: the phalanx, with its pikes held long,
The {{p|sarissas}}, and horse, and so went forth
To {{p|Thrace}}, {{p|Illyria}}, the southern throng,

And beat them at {{p|Chaeronea}}; and made
The {{p|League of Corinth}}; and he planned to go
Against the {{p|Persians}}, to repay the raid
Of {{c|1985|Xerxes}}; but he was slain there, and so,

At his own daughter's wedding, by his guard;
Some said {{c|2410|Olympias}} had willed it, or
Her son; and {{c|1982|Alexander}}, twenty, hard
And young, took up the throne, the host, the war.

The north rose, and he beat it; {{p|Thebes}} rose too,
And he destroyed it, slew and sold its folk,
And spared the house of {{c|2411|Pindar}}, poet; through
That terror, {{p|Greece}} was quiet, under yoke.

He crossed the {{p|Hellespont}} with thirty-five
Thousand, beat {{p|Persia}} at {{p|Granicus}}' stream,
Freed the {{p|Ionian}} {{p|Greeks}}; still alive,
{{c|2294|Darius III}} met him, like a dream,

At {{p|Issus}}, fled, and left his wife and girls
Behind; and {{c|1982|Alexander}} kept them well;
{{c|2287|Darius}} offered land, and gold, and pearls,
And a daughter; {{c|2412|Parmenion}} said: I'd sell,

If I were {{c|1982|Alexander}}. So would I,
He said, if I were {{c|2412|Parmenion}}. And south
To {{p|Tyre}}, which held its isle seven months; by
A causeway that he built from mainland's mouth

He took it, and he slew or sold its men;
And {{p|Gaza}} too; and {{p|Egypt}}, hating those
Who'd ruled it, welcomed him, and crowned him then
As pharaoh; and to {{p|Siwa}}, where there rose

The shrine of {{c|1426|Ammon}} in the desert sand,
He went, and there the oracle said: son
Of {{c|2413|Zeus-Ammon}}; and he held to it, and
He founded {{p|Alexandria}}, the one

The greatest of the cities of his name,
Where sea and {{p|Nile}} and {{p|Red Sea}} trade would meet.
And east, at {{p|Gaugamela}}, there he came
Against {{c|2287|Darius}}, many times his fleet

Of men, and beat him; and {{c|2287|Darius}} fled;
And {{p|Babylon}} and {{p|Susa}} opened wide,
And then {{p|Persepolis}}, where, as it's said,
For {{p|Athens}}' burning, or for {{p|Persia}}'s pride,

He let the palace burn. And {{c|2414|Bessus}}, then,
The satrap, slew {{c|2287|Darius}}, and was king;
And {{c|1982|Alexander}} caught him, killed him; when
He'd done it, he was heir, not foreign thing,

The {{p|Great King}}: and he took the {{p|Persian}} court,
Its ways, its wives, and bade his men wed too;
And {{p|Greek}} and {{p|Persian}} he'd join in one sort;
His {{p|Macedonians}} hated it; through

The plots, he slew {{c|2415|Philotas}}, and he then
Slew {{c|2412|Parmenion}}; and {{c|2416|Cleitus}}, who had saved
His life, he killed while drunk; and so, of men,
He grew afraid, and darker, and depraved.

He went on east: to {{p|Bactria}}, and wed
{{c|2417|Roxana}}; through the {{p|Hindu Kush}}; and down
The {{p|Indus}}; at the {{p|Hydaspes}}, there, he led
Against King {{c|2418|Porus}}, elephants, and crown,

And won; and asked him how he'd treat him, then;
Like a king, {{c|2418|Porus}} said; and he was made
A king again, his vassal. But his men
Would go no farther; and so there he stayed

At {{p|Hyphasis}}: they would not march; he sulked
Three days; and then turned back, and sailed the stream
To the sea; and marched, while thirst and dust skulked,
Through {{p|Gedrosia}}; thousands died, a dream;

And {{c|2419|Nearchus}} sailed beside; and back he came
To {{p|Babylon}}, and planned to take the west;
And bade the {{p|Greeks}} call him a god by name;
And drank, and fevered, and was laid to rest

At thirty-two; his body, borne away
To {{p|Alexandria}}, entombed, to lie.
His heir unborn, his generals took sway:
{{c|2265|Ptolemy}}, {{p|Egypt}}; {{c|2420|Seleucus}}, east, high;

{{c|2421|Antigonus}}, {{p|Macedon}}; and many more;
And {{p|Greek}} became the tongue from sea to sea,
In twenty {{p|Alexandrias}}, the store
Of all learning; and the {{c|1959|Buddha}} would be

Carved in the {{p|Greek}} way, in the east; and so
The roads he opened carried west and east.
So honor {{c|1982|Alexander}}: how he'd go,
And take the world, and found it, and the feast.


# Chapter 175: The Maurya Empire

When {{c|1982|Alexander}} turned from {{p|Indus}}' shore,
Out of the north of {{p|India}} there rose
A house that held the land as none before:
{{p|Maurya}}, from {{p|Bengal}} westward it goes,

From the {{p|Hindu Kush}} down to the {{p|Deccan}}:
{{c|2424|Chandragupta Maurya}} founded it,
And by his side, {{c|2426|Chanakya}}, the wise man
{{c|2427|Kautilya}}, whose book of rule was writ

Taught how to rule: the taxes and the spies,
The friends abroad, the plots, the risings crushed,
All cold and whole; and by it he would rise,
And cast the {{p|Nandas}} down, and all was hushed;

And at {{p|Pataliputra}} he set his seat;
And then {{c|2420|Seleucus}} came, to take the west
Of {{p|India}} back, and he met defeat,
Gave up {{p|Afghanistan}} and all the rest,

{{p|Balochistan}}, for elephants; and sent
{{c|2429|Megasthenes}}, who told of the roads and feasts,
Of wealth, of castes; and of the king, who spent
His nights in fear, and slept, as hunted beasts,

Changed beds each night, with women guards; and kept
Them close; and at the last he would lay down
His throne, and took the {{p|Jain}} way, and he stepped
Into the fast, {{p|Sallekhana}}, no crown.

{{c|2430|Bindusara}}, his son, took {{p|Deccan}}'s south;
The {{p|Greeks}} had named him {{c|2431|Amitrochates}}; sent
To {{c|2432|Antiochus}} for wine, figs, the mouth
Of a sophist; and the answer back went:

The wine and figs, yes; but our law forbids
That we should sell philosophers. And then
Came {{c|2320|Ashoka}}, who, as the story bids,
Slew brothers for the throne, and ruled like men

Before him, hard; and then made war upon
{{p|Kalinga}}, on the east coast; and he won;
A hundred thousand slain, and, carried on,
A hundred fifty thousand; and when done,

He saw the dead, and grieved; and he became
Follower of the {{c|1959|Buddha}}, and he made
The {{p|Dhamma}} his: no more war; and the same
Kindness to beasts; and meat no more was laid;

He founded hospitals, and dug the wells,
And planted trees along the roads; and stone
Pillars, with lions, wheels, whose writing tells
His {{p|Dhamma}}: be kind; honor elders; own

Respect for priests of every faith; for who
Speaks ill of others' faith, shames too his own;
And so he wrote, and thirty more stand true,
In his own voice, upon the pillars' stone.

He held the third great council, and sent out
The monks: across the strait went his own son
{{c|2435|Mahendra}}, {{c|2436|Sanghamitra}}, daughter, out
To {{p|Greeks}} and to {{p|Central Asia}}, each one;

And so the {{c|1959|Buddha}}'s way went out across
The world. His {{p|Dhamma}} was for all, not one
Faith only: right, and truth, and gifts, no loss
To any beast; and so the king's rule won

Its right by goodness, not by blood or sword;
And beasts had places where they were not slain.
And still today his wheel, his lion, ward
The land of {{p|India}}, on flag and plain.

He died; and after him the realm grew small,
Its governors their own; and, in a coup,
{{c|2439|Pushyamitra Shunga}} made the fall
Of the last {{p|Maurya}}; the {{p|Shunga}}'s new.

Honor them: {{c|2425|Chandragupta}}, and the cold
Wise {{c|2426|Chanakya}}; and great {{c|2320|Ashoka}}, who
Grieved for the dead of war, and then would hold
The world in kindness, and sent the monks through.


# Chapter 176: The Punic Wars

And in the west, two cities rose to fight
For all the sea: {{p|Rome}} on the {{p|Tiber}}'s bank,
Which {{c|1566|Romulus}} had founded; ruled by right
Of seven kings, till {{c|2453|Tarquin}}, proud, then sank,

Cast out; then the {{p|Republic}}: consuls, two,
Each checking each; the {{x|Senate}}, old and wise;
The people's votes; the tribunes, who could do
The veto for the poor; and so to rise

Through all of {{p|Italy}}: {{p|Etruscans}}, all
The {{p|Samnites}}, {{p|Sabines}}, {{p|Latins}}, and the {{p|Greeks}}
Of southern {{p|Italy}}; and then the call
Across the strait, where {{p|Carthage}} ruled the creeks.

For {{p|Carthage}}, from {{p|Phoenician}} {{p|Tyre}}, had grown
Upon {{p|Tunisia}}'s coast, and ruled the trade
Of {{p|Africa}}, {{p|Iberia}}'s ore, sown
{{p|Sardinia}}, {{p|Corsica}}; fleets were made

The greatest; and its tongue was {{p|Punic}}, kin
To {{p|Hebrew}}; and its gods, {{c|2454|Baal Hammon}} and
{{c|2455|Tanit}}; and in the {{p|tophet}}, laid within,
Were infants, given in crisis by land.

And {{p|Sicily}}, half {{p|Greek}} and half {{p|Punic}},
Was where they met; and three wars they would fight.
The first: {{p|Rome}} had no fleet, and, stubborn, quick,
Copied a {{p|Punic}} ship, and, with the might

Of {{p|corvus}}, boarding-bridge, made sea to land;
And won, and {{p|Sicily}} was {{p|Rome}}'s; and gold
Was paid; and while {{p|Carthage}}'s hired band
Rose, {{p|Rome}} seized {{p|Sardinia}}, and the hold

Of {{p|Corsica}}; {{c|2456|Hamilcar Barca}}'s son,
{{c|2457|Hannibal}}, swore at the altar, when young,
Undying hate for {{p|Rome}}; and Spain was won
By {{c|2458|Hamilcar}}, {{c|2459|Hasdrubal}}; and among

Them, {{c|2457|Hannibal}}; and then the second war:
He crossed the {{p|Ebro}}, {{p|Pyrenees}}, and {{p|Gaul}},
The {{p|Alps}} in winter, elephants, and more,
And came to {{p|Italy}} with half of all,

And won at {{p|Trebia}}; and by the lake
Of {{p|Trasimene}} ambushed a host and slew
{{c|2460|Flaminius}}; and then, at {{p|Cannae}}, he'd make
The center yield, the wings close round them, through;

Some fifty thousand {{p|Romans}} died that day;
And many allies went to him; but {{p|Rome}}
Would not give in; its {{x|Senate}} would not pay;
{{c|2461|Fabius}} would not fight, but kept at home

The war by waiting, cutting off his bread;
{{c|2462|Scipio}} took {{p|Spain}}; and {{p|Syracuse}} fell,
And {{c|2409|Archimedes}}, by a soldier, dead;
{{c|2464|Scipio}} took war to {{p|Carthage}} as well,

And at {{p|Zama}} beat {{c|2457|Hannibal}}; and lost
{{p|Carthage}}'s fleet, its lands abroad; it paid
A mighty sum; and {{c|2465|Cato}}, at all cost,
Ended each speech: {{p|Carthage}} must be unmade.

The third war: three years' siege; the city fell,
Was burned, and razed, its people sold, and salt
Sown in its ground; and {{p|Africa}} as well
Was {{p|Rome}}'s; and {{p|Punic}} {{p|Carthage}} came to halt.

And {{p|Rome}} was changed: a fleet, and lands abroad,
Grain from {{p|Sicily}}, {{p|Africa}}; and gold
From {{p|Spain}}; and generals great; and, overawed,
The farmers, ruined while away, were sold

Their land to rich men with their slaves; the throng
Of poor men crowded {{p|Rome}}; and then it turned
East: {{p|Macedon}}, and then {{p|Greece}}, were {{p|Rome}}'s ere long,
{{p|Seleucids}} at {{p|Magnesia}}; it learned

To call the sea its own. And he, the great
{{c|2457|Hannibal}}, exiled, went to foes of {{p|Rome}};
With {{c|2471|Prusias}}, when {{p|Rome}} came for him, his fate
Was poison, which he drank, far from his home.

So honor {{c|2457|Hannibal}}, who crossed the snow
With elephants, and won at {{p|Cannae}}'s field;
And {{p|Rome}}, which would not break, though brought so low;
And {{p|Carthage}}, which was razed, and would not yield.


# Chapter 177: Qin and Han

In {{p|China}}, seven warring states had fought
Two hundred years; then {{p|Qin}} took one by one:
{{p|Han}}, {{p|Zhao}}, {{p|Wei}}, {{p|Chu}}, {{p|Yan}}, {{p|Qi}}; and all was brought
To one, and {{p|Warring States}} at last were done.

Young {{c|2442|Qin Shi Huang}}, king at thirteen years, ruled
Through regents first, and then himself; and he
Was {{c|2441|First Emperor}}; thought his line was schooled
To last ten thousand ages; and decree

Made one the script, the {{p|small seal}}; weights, and coin,
And measures, and the axles of the carts;
He cast the old lords down, and made men join
His service by his choice, in all the parts;

He split the land in thirty-six, and set
Each with a governor, a guard, and one
To watch them; built the roads, canals; and yet
Joined the old walls, the {{p|Great Wall}}, northward run,

Against the {{p|Xiongnu}}; he burned the books
Not useful to his rule; buried alive
Four hundred sixty scholars; and he looks
To {{p|Legalism}}, the way that he'd thrive:{{fn|The burning of the books and burying of the scholars is told by Sima Qian, a historian of the Han, the dynasty that overthrew the Qin; some historians think the account exaggerated.}}

{{c|2444|Han Feizi}}'s way: that men are selfish, and
Hard laws, the same for all, with clear reward
And harsh reproof, alone can rule the land,
Not virtue in the king; and by that cord

He ruled, hard and exact. And he feared death,
And sent out men to find the deathless brew;
And took the mercury, to keep his breath,
Which killed him; and he built a tomb, and through

{{p|Lintong}}'s ground, and all around it stood
The {{p|Terracotta Army}}, thousands strong,
Each face its own, with horse and car, and good
To guard him in the dark; and still, the long

Ranks stand. He died at forty-nine, away;
{{c|2445|Li Si}} and {{c|2446|Zhao Gao}} hid his death, and killed
The heir, and set a weak one up; one day
Men rose; and in three years the land was filled

With war; the capital fell; so the line
That should have lasted ages lasted, all,
Just fifteen years. But roads, and law, and sign
Of script, and provinces, outlived its fall;

And then {{c|2447|Liu Bang}}, a peasant rebel, rose,
Fought {{c|2448|Xiang Yu}}, the noble, strong of arm,
Four years, and won by patience; and the blows
At {{p|Gaixia}} ended him; free from harm,

He was {{c|2449|Emperor Gaozu}} of the {{p|Han}};
And kept the {{p|Qin}}'s whole frame, but made it mild;
And {{c|2450|Emperor Wu}} made {{p|Confucius}}' plan
The rule, and chose by learning, not by child

Of noble birth; and sixty million souls,
A fifth of all the world, and {{p|Chang'an}}, great
As {{p|Rome}}; and {{c|2450|Wu}} sent armies, and their goals:
The {{p|Xiongnu}}, {{p|Nanyue}}, {{p|Korea}}'s state,

And west, to {{p|Ferghana}}, for heaven's horse;
And so the {{p|Silk Road}} opened; silk went west,
And glass and gold came east along its course,
And horses; and {{c|2300|Sima Qian}}, the best

Of histories, the {{p|Records}}, wrote, from the
{{p|Yellow Emperor}} down to his own day;
And steel was made, the finest there could be;
And still the {{p|Chinese}} call themselves, today,

The {{p|Han}}, from that same house. So honor them:
The {{c|2441|First Emperor}}, the wall, script, the clay
Ten thousand strong; and then {{c|2447|Liu Bang}}, the stem
Of {{p|Han}}; and {{c|2450|Wu}}, who sent the silk away.


# Chapter 178: Second Temple Period

From {{p|Babylon}}, back up to {{p|Zion}}'s height,
By {{c|2180|Cyrus}}' leave, the exiles came, and raised
The {{p|Temple}}, small; and then, by blood and right,
Who was a {{c|2510|Jew}}, was asked, and they were fazed:

They drew the line; {{c|2511|Samaritans}} were turned
Away; the mixed were cast out. {{c|2276|Ezra}} read
The {{x|Torah}} seven days, and all men learned,
At {{p|Water Gate}}; and {{c|2277|Nehemiah}} spread

The walls again; the priesthood was the core,
The high priest ruled; and under {{x|Persian}}, then
The {{x|Macedonian}} rule, {{p|Judea}} bore
Its quiet years. And {{c|1982|Alexander}}, when

He came, was shown the words of {{c|2512|Daniel}}, read
Of him, and spared {{p|Jerusalem}}; and then
The {{c|2514|Seleucids}} of {{p|Syria}} were head,
And ruled {{p|Judea}}, province of their men.

{{c|2515|Antiochus IV Epiphanes}} then came,
Who meant the {{x|Greek}} way kept; he banned the {{x|Law}},
And sacked {{p|Jerusalem}}, and in its name,
On the Lord's altar there the people saw

The Lord of Heaven under the king's name:
{{c|2065|Zeus}} of the heights; the same sky, and the sign
The same old altar; but his priests, his frame
Of rite, his swine, laid in the court; the line

The prophet wrote, there punning on that name,
Called the abomination; and the stand
Was at one altar, set in fear and shame:
Who'd stand before it, whose law rule the land.

And then {{c|2516|Mattathias}} the priest refused
To make the {{x|Greek}} rite, and he slew the one
Who came to make it; and his son, who used
The name of {{c|2518|Hammer}}, {{c|2517|Judas}}, was his son,

Made war from hills against the {{c|2519|Greeks}}, and won
The {{p|Temple}} back, and made it clean again;
And {{x|Hanukkah}} keeps the eight days begun
With oil for one day, burning eight days then.

{{x|Hasmoneans}} rose from that war, and were
Both king and high priest; and some held it wrong.
The {{c|2520|Essenes}} went out to {{p|Qumran}}, to stir
No more, but wait the end, and keep their long

Scrolls in the caves; the {{c|2521|Pharisees}} would teach
The oral law, the house of prayer, the home
Where each man read the {{x|Torah}}, each to each;
The {{c|2522|Sadducees}}, the priests, kept but the tome

Of written law, no rising of the dead;
The {{c|2523|Zealots}} wanted war with all who ruled;
And some wrote of the end, when {{c|472|God}}, they said,
Would break into the world, and all be schooled.

Then {{p|Rome}} came: {{c|2468|Pompey}} marched in, sixty-three
Before the era, walked into the place,
The {{p|Holy of Holies}}, and he could see
Nothing: no god, no image, and no face,

But empty room, where once the {{x|Ark}} had stood
Before {{c|2024|Nebuchadnezzar}}. And {{p|Rome}} set
{{c|2524|Herod the Great}}, the {{x|Idumean}}, who would
Build palaces, the {{p|Temple}} greater yet,

The grandest in the east; but he was mad
With fear, and slew his sons, his wife; and slew
The infants of {{p|Bethlehem}}; what he had
Was split; and {{p|Rome}} sent governors; and through

The poor and those in debt, the hope rose high:
When would the {{c|2526|Messiah}} come, the true son
Of {{c|1956|David}}, drive out {{p|Rome}}, and bring, nearby,
The kingdom back, as in the days long done?

And many claimed it: {{c|2528|Theudas}}, and the one
{{c|2529|Judas the Galilean}}, and then he
From {{p|Egypt}} on the {{p|Olivet}}; and none
Prevailed. And {{c|2531|John the Baptist}}, by the sea

Of reeds, the {{p|Jordan}}, preached: repent, and turn;
The kingdom's near; in camel-hair, he ate
The locusts and wild honey; and would burn
With words; and baptized many at the gate,

And {{c|1912|Jesus}} of {{p|Nazareth}}; and then lost
His head to {{c|2532|Herod Antipas}}, for he
Had cursed his wedding, and his law was crossed.
The kingdom seemed so near, the end so free.

For all agreed: one {{c|472|God}}, and not his face
In image; covenant, the {{x|Torah}}, rest
Of {{x|Sabbath}}, and clean food; and in each place
A faith that could be carried, east or west.

So honor them, who came back, and who kept
The law in every house, and waited long
For the anointed, while the {{p|Romans}} stepped;
And {{c|2531|John}}, who cried the kingdom in his song.


# Chapter 179: Rome

After {{p|Carthage}} fell, {{p|Rome}} stood
the master of the {{p|Middle Sea}},
and what had been a farmers' town
now ruled from {{p|Spain}} to {{p|Thessaly}}.

The {{x|Republic}} had been built for farms,
for citizen-assemblies small,
for consuls chosen year by year,
for {{x|Senate}} giving voice to all.

But empire cracked the ancient forms.
The legions served the generals now.
The conquered provinces sent wealth
that drowned the old {{p|Italian}} plough.

The {{c|2475|Gracchi Brothers}}, {{c|2476|Tiberius}}
and {{c|2477|Gaius}}, saw the danger clear:
the landless poor, the latifundia,
the veterans with naught to cheer.

{{c|2476|Tiberius}} proposed reform,
to give the soldiers land again.
The {{x|Senate}} killed him in the streets.
His brother fell the same way then.

The {{x|Republic}} learned that reason died
when wealth was threatened at its root,
and after that the path was set
toward civil war and bloody fruit.

{{c|1027|Marius}} reformed the legions whole,
made volunteers the fighting core,
tied soldiers' loyalty to their chief
and not the state they fought for.

{{c|2467|Sulla}} marched his legions in
upon the sacred city's ground,
the first {{p|Roman}} to make such war,
and dictator for life was crowned.

He purged his enemies with lists,
proscriptions stripping wealth and breath,
and when he thought his work was done
he calmly walked away toward death.

But what he'd done could not be back.
The precedent was set in stone:
armies belonged to generals now,
and politics meant swords alone.

{{c|2468|Pompey}} rose, the golden boy,
who cleared the pirates from the sea,
who conquered eastward to the {{p|Nile}}
and gave {{p|Judea}} subsequently.

{{c|2478|Crassus}} rose, the wealthiest man,
who crushed the {{c|2479|Spartacus}} revolt,
whose gold bought armies, bought the {{x|Senate}},
bought whatever he assault.

{{c|2469|Julius Caesar}} rose, the third,
who claimed descent from {{c|2480|Aeneas}},
who claimed descent from {{c|95|Venus}} herself,
and was the ablest of the three.

The {{x|First Triumvirate}} was formed,
unofficial, power-sharing pact.
They carved the {{p|Roman}} world between them
and ruled by this unwritten act.

{{c|2478|Crassus}} died in {{p|Parthia}}, shot
with arrows at the battle's close.
His head was used as stage-prop in
a {{x|Greek}} tragedy, or so it goes.

Then {{c|2468|Pompey}} and {{c|1983|Caesar}} turned to war.
{{c|1983|Caesar}} crossed the {{p|Rubicon}} small
with legions, saying "die is cast,"
and brought the {{x|Republic}} to its fall.

He chased {{c|2468|Pompey}} to {{p|Egypt}}, where
the boy-king {{c|2265|Ptolemy}} beheaded
the {{p|Roman}} general, thinking thus
{{c|1983|Caesar}}'s gratitude was threaded.

{{c|1983|Caesar}} wept. Then met {{c|2481|Cleopatra}},
who rolled inside a carpet's pack,
and made alliance with her bed
and put her on the {{p|Egyptian}} track.

He conquered {{p|Gaul}} across the {{p|Alps}},
wrote {{x|Commentaries}} on his war,
"veni, vidi, vici" at {{p|Zela}},
and dictator for life he bore.

The {{x|Ides of March}} came. {{c|2482|Brutus}} struck,
with {{c|2483|Cassius}} and the {{x|Senate}}'s knives.
"Et tu, {{c|2484|Brute}}?" — then {{c|1983|Caesar}} fell,
and {{p|Rome}} was torn among his wives.

{{c|2485|Mark Antony}} gave the funeral speech
("I come to bury, not to praise"),
roused the crowd against the killers,
and started civil war's new phase.

{{c|2486|Octavian}}, {{c|1983|Caesar}}'s grandnephew,
adopted as his heir by will,
revealed himself the cold-eyed one
with patience and political skill.

The {{x|Second Triumvirate}} formed:
{{c|2487|Antony}}, {{c|2486|Octavian}}, {{c|2488|Lepidus}}.
They hunted {{c|2482|Brutus}} down at {{p|Philippi}},
then turned upon each other thus.

{{c|2488|Lepidus}} was marginalized.
{{c|2487|Antony}} went east to {{c|2481|Cleopatra}}.
{{c|2486|Octavian}} stayed in {{p|Rome}} to build
his reputation bit by bit.

{{c|2487|Antony}} lost himself in {{p|Egypt}},
living as pharaoh with his queen,
alienating {{p|Roman}} sentiment,
the conqueror gone {{x|Alexandrine}}.

At {{p|Actium}} the fleets collided.
{{c|2486|Octavian}}'s admiral {{c|2489|Agrippa}} won.
{{c|2487|Antony}} and {{c|2481|Cleopatra}} fled,
and soon enough their lives were done.

She with the asp, the royal cobra,
the uraeus of {{p|Egyptian}} crown.
He with his sword, the {{p|Roman}} way.
The {{x|Ptolemaic}} line went down.

{{c|2486|Octavian}} stood the sole {{p|Roman}},
and took the title {{c|2490|Augustus}} then,
the "revered one," princeps, first,
and ruled for forty-five years again.

He said he'd restored the {{x|Republic}},
but everyone knew the truth:
the {{x|Senate}} met, the consuls served,
but emperor ruled, and that was sooth.

The {{x|Pax Romana}} had begun.
Two centuries of peace and law.
Roads, aqueducts, courts, and coins.
The greatest empire men ever saw.

From {{p|Britain}} to the {{p|Tigris}} reach,
from {{p|Rhine}} to the {{p|Saharan}} sand,
one law, one coin, one road-network,
one citizenship across the land.

The emperors came, some good, some mad:
{{c|2476|Tiberius}} grew dark on {{p|Capri}}.
{{c|2491|Caligula}} made his horse a consul.
{{c|2492|Claudius}} the limping one was wily.

{{c|2493|Nero}} burned and fiddled — or
perhaps that part was later slander.
But he killed his mother, killed his wife,
killed {{c|2494|Christians}}, killed with grand meander.

The {{x|Year of Four Emperors}} came
when {{c|2493|Nero}} fell upon his sword.
{{c|2495|Galba}}, {{c|2496|Otho}}, {{c|2497|Vitellius}}, {{c|2498|Vespasian}} —
four imperial purples poured.

{{c|2498|Vespasian}} stabilized the state,
built the {{p|Colosseum}} in {{p|Rome}},
and founded the {{x|Flavian}} dynasty
to give the empire fresh new home.

His son {{c|2499|Titus}} sacked {{p|Jerusalem}}
in seventy of the {{x|Common Era}},
destroyed the {{p|Second Temple}} whole,
and changed {{x|Judaism}}'s era.

The menorah was carried west
upon the {{p|Arch of Titus}}' face.
The {{c|2500|Jews}} were scattered through the empire.
The {{p|Temple}} cult had lost its place.

But {{p|Rome}} rolled on, the {{x|Five Good Emperors}}:
{{c|2501|Nerva}}, {{c|2502|Trajan}}, {{c|2503|Hadrian}},
{{c|2504|Antoninus Pius}}, and {{c|2505|Marcus Aurelius}},
who was both emperor and {{x|Stoic}} man.

{{c|2502|Trajan}} pushed to {{p|Dacia}}, took the gold,
reached the greatest extent of the realm.
{{c|2503|Hadrian}} pulled back to the walls,
built {{p|Hadrian's Wall}} across the helm.

{{c|2506|Marcus}} wrote his {{x|Meditations}}
in {{x|Greek}}, for his own private eye,
a {{x|Stoic}} emperor's private journal,
one of the great books that will not die.

"Begin the morning by saying to thyself:
I shall meet with the busybody, ungrateful,
arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial..."
and yet still serve them all, faithful.

He fought the {{c|2507|Marcomanni}} on the {{p|Danube}},
plague was ravaging the troops,
and when he died, the empire was
already starting to lose its loops.

His son {{c|2508|Commodus}} was the break.
He fought in the arena, thought himself {{c|2509|Hercules}},
was strangled by a wrestler in his bath,
and after him came crises.

{{p|Rome}} had reached its high plateau.
From here, the slow decline began.
But for two hundred years it held
the greatest empire made by man.


# Chapter 180: Jesus

When {{c|2525|Herod}} died, the {{p|Galilee}} rose high,
and Varus burned {{p|Sepphoris}} for its war;
a {{p|Roman}} soldier, Pantera, passed by,
and {{c|1399|Mary}}, young, was taken; and she bore

a son. The soldier was of {{p|Dan}}, the tribe
that never kept the Yahwist law, and so
no line is written for him, and no scribe
would write his fathers' names for us to know.

And {{c|1399|Mary}}, in her grief, went to a pool
and fell, and told herself the child was sent
as {{c|2146|Zarathustra}}'s seed, in waters cool,
the {{x|Saoshyant}}, the savior that was meant.

The {{x|Magi}}, three, came by, and when she told
them what had happened, one of them said yes:
it may be so; and so she was consoled,
and {{c|2031|Joseph}} took her, and the child, no less.

Through {{c|2031|Joseph}}, he was Jeconiah's heir,
the exilarchs' and {{c|2146|Zarathustra}}'s line;
and {{c|2537|John}} the Baptist was his cousin there;
they fled as refugees; that was the sign.

He had three fathers, as the old lines tell:
{{c|2031|Joseph}} who raised him, Pantera of {{p|Rome}},
and {{c|2182|Yahweh}}, who had chosen him as well;
and grew a {{c|2510|Jew}} in {{p|Nazareth}}, his home.

He worked with wood, displaced, a poor man's son;
a magus on the road heard all his tale
and took him through the world, the two as one,
to cities where the mysteries prevail:

He learned of {{c|1991|Dionysus}} and the vine,
and of the {{x|Saoshyant}} from priests of fire,
and knew himself beyond Messiah's line,
beneath his cousin {{c|2537|John}}, who stood higher.

At thirty or so, he left his home,
went to {{c|2537|John}} at the {{p|Jordan}}'s flow,
was baptized, heard a voice from heaven:
"You are my beloved son, I know."

Then into the wilderness forty days,
tempted by whatever {{c|2538|Satan}} meant,
and afterward he began to preach
the kingdom's immanent advent.

"Repent, for the kingdom of {{c|472|God}}
is at hand." The same as {{c|2531|John the Baptist}}.
But where {{c|2537|John}} had preached apocalypse,
{{c|1912|Jesus}} spoke of mercy as the rest.

Five years he and his cousin went as one,
and preached to Gentiles, to the nations near;
he called himself the Lord, the Savior, Son
of {{c|472|God}}, the titles Caesar wore, to jeer.

He called twelve disciples, fishermen,
tax collectors, a zealot too,
and traveled through {{p|Galilee}} preaching
in synagogues and open view.

His teaching had three main features:
parables, beatitudes, love commands.
The parables told stories without resolution,
leaving thought in the listener's hands.

The prodigal son, the good {{x|Samaritan}},
the mustard seed, the sower of fields,
the lost sheep, the lost coin, the lost son,
the pearl of great price, the treasure it yields.

The beatitudes inverted the world:
"Blessed are the poor in spirit,
blessed are those who mourn, who hunger,
who are persecuted for my merit."

The love commands were two and radical:
"Love {{c|472|God}} with all your heart and soul.
Love your neighbor as yourself."
On these two hung the {{x|Law}}'s whole.

But he added one that no one had said:
"Love your enemies. Pray for those
who persecute you. Be perfect as
your {{c|2539|Heavenly Father}} is, who bestows

sun and rain on the just and unjust both."
This was the new, the radical turn.
Not just mercy to your tribe or friend,
but mercy to those whose hate you earn.

He healed the sick, cast out demons,
raised {{c|2540|Jairus}}' daughter from the dead,
raised the widow of {{p|Nain}}'s son,
raised {{c|2541|Lazarus}} four days in the bed.

He walked on water in the storm.
He fed the five thousand with few loaves.
He turned the water into wine.
He calmed the sea with breath he blows.

The {{x|Gospels}} frame these miracles as signs,
as breakings-in of the kingdom new,
as demonstrations that death and demon
were not the final word, it's true.

He chose twelve for the twelve tribes of {{p|Israel}},
symbolic of restoration complete.
He taught the disciples to pray "Our {{c|2542|Father}},"
giving the kingdom's prayer to recite.

He kept his sharpest words, though, not for those
Who sinned, the thieves and prostitutes he chose
To eat with, but for those who held the chair
Of {{c|1006|Moses}}, the {{c|2521|Pharisees}}, the scribes there:

"Woe to you, scribes and {{c|2521|Pharisees}},
hypocrites, who strain out a gnat
and swallow a camel. Who tithe mint
and cumin, but neglect the fat

weightier matters of the {{x|Law}},
justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
You whitewashed tombs, beautiful outside,
full of dead men's bones and ugliness."

In thirty, Herod's sword took {{c|2537|John}} away,
and {{c|2546|Pilate}}, whom this book does not forgive,
had nailed him up by {{c|2543|Passover}} that day,
the man who taught the poor that they would live.

He came up to {{p|Jerusalem}} to share
the {{c|2543|Passover}}, and in the {{p|Temple}} threw
the tables down, and rode a donkey there,
a Caesar mocked, as cheering crowds well knew.

It's better that one man of us should die
than {{p|Rome}} come down on all, so said the priest,
afraid of {{p|Rome}}, gave him to {{p|Rome}} to try;
and it was {{p|Rome}} that killed him at the feast.

{{c|2545|Judas Iscariot}} betrayed him
for thirty pieces of silver, paid.
He kissed him in the {{p|Garden of Gethsemane}}
and showed the soldiers where he stayed.

He was arrested, tried by the {{x|Sanhedrin}},
tried by {{c|2546|Pilate}}, tried by {{c|2547|Herod Antipas}},
sent back to {{c|2546|Pilate}}, who washed his hands,
and let the crowd choose {{c|2548|Barabbas}} instead.

The crowd chose {{c|2548|Barabbas}}. {{c|1912|Jesus}} was
scourged, crowned with thorns, made mocking king,
forced to carry his cross to {{p|Golgotha}},
the place of the skull, the ugliest thing.

Crucifixion was the {{p|Roman}} method
for rebels, slaves, the lowest of men.
He hung with thieves on either side
for six hours, and then spoke seven "amens":

"{{c|2542|Father}}, forgive them, they know not
what they do." "Today you shall be with me
in {{p|Paradise}}." "Woman, behold your son."
"My {{c|472|God}}, my {{c|472|God}}, why have you forsaken me?"

"I thirst." "It is finished."
"{{c|2542|Father}}, into your hands I commit
my spirit." And with these words he died.
The veil of the {{p|Temple}} was split.

Earthquake. Darkness. The centurion
who watched him die said "Truly this man
was the {{c|2549|Son of God}}." They took him down
at sunset, before the {{x|Sabbath}} ran.

Ten thousand thirty, Pisces twelve, the eve
of {{c|2543|Passover}}, the fourteenth of Nisan,
a Friday, when the lambs were killed; we grieve:
and he was killed among them as a man.

{{c|2550|Joseph of Arimathea}} provided
a new tomb, cut in rock, nearby.
They wrapped him in linen with spices,
and rolled a stone, and said goodbye.

On the third day, the women came
to finish the anointing at dawn.
The stone was rolled away. The tomb
was empty. His body was gone.

Ten thousand thirty, Pisces fourteen, dawn,
a Sunday, our third Easter, and the day
the women found the tomb, his body gone,
the morning that the stone was rolled away.

Angels said "He is not here, he is risen."
{{c|2551|Mary Magdalene}} met him in the garden
but did not recognize him at first.
He sent the twelve to make the kingdom's pardon

known to all nations, to baptize
in the name of {{c|2542|Father}}, {{c|2552|Son}}, and {{c|2553|Holy Ghost}},
teaching all he had commanded,
and he would be with them at the post

of every moment until the end.
Then he ascended to heaven's height,
with the promise that he would return
to judge the living and the dead in light.

This is the {{x|Christian}} claim, the core.
Not {{c|1912|Jesus}} the teacher only. Not {{c|1912|Jesus}}
the failed messiah, dead and done.
But {{c|1912|Jesus}} who rose, and reigns, and frees us.

Iry-Hor, first named, was kept for the few,
his name the first we know, a king's, alone;
but {{c|1912|Jesus}} keeps the many, he who knew
the poor, the dead unnamed, each one his own.

He left a son he never lived to see,
born on the day of {{x|Pentecost}}, the Just;
in {{p|Tarsus}} first, then {{p|Rome}}, where he was free,
and Petronilla married him, in trust.

So let his son have a good life, I say:
the father's road was horror all along;
his line ran down to {{c|3687|Theophylact}}'s day,
the corrupt popes, the punchline of the song.

A {{x|Jewish}} messianic sect went forth
into the {{x|Greco-Roman}} sea,
and merged with {{c|2554|Sol Invictus}} worship,
with mystery religions, gradually,

and became the faith of {{p|Rome}} itself
three centuries later under {{c|2555|Constantine}}.
But for now, a small community
in {{p|Jerusalem}} wondered what they had seen.

They met in upper rooms to pray.
They broke bread together and shared all things.
They waited for the return imminent.
And the spirit came on them on tongues' wings.


# Chapter 181: Buddhism Enters the Han

While {{c|1912|Jesus}} walked in {{p|Galilee}},
the {{c|2556|Han Dynasty}} in the {{p|East}}
was reaching its high mature phase,
and a strange new teaching entered its feast.

Emperor {{c|2557|Ming of Han}} dreamed a dream
of a golden man flying west-to-east,
and his advisors said: this is the {{c|1959|Buddha}},
the sage from {{p|India}}, the teaching priest.

He sent ambassadors down the {{p|Silk Road}}
to find the monks and the scriptures both.
They returned with two {{p|Indian}} monks,
{{c|2558|Kasyapa Matanga}} and {{c|2559|Dharmaratna}}, of both.

They brought scriptures, statues, and monks
on a white horse, the legend says,
and the first {{x|Buddhist}} temple in {{p|China}}
was the {{p|White Horse Temple}} of those days.

This was the first crossing — around
sixty-seven of the {{x|Common Era}}.
{{x|Buddhism}} entered the {{p|Han Empire}}
by imperial sponsorship without fear.

But centuries would pass before it grew
Its roots; the court gave the new shrine its due:
The old offering come by a western road,
Not yet in every household and abode.

It stood beside the {{c|2560|Daoists}}' altar, and
The two kept the same court and the same land.
They vied for the throne's gifts, and each one took
The other's words, as brothers share a book.

The translation problem was immense.
How translate "nirvana" into {{x|Chinese}}?
How translate "dharma," "karma," "anatta"?
The monks did their best to seize.

They used {{x|Daoist}} "wu wei" for "nirvana,"
"dao" for "dharma," and hoped it stuck.
Later, better translators came who
coined new terms with better luck.

Meanwhile, to the east, in {{p|Korea}},
a different strand of the Eastern story:
the legend of {{c|2562|Heo Hwang-ok}}, princess
of {{p|Ayodhya}}, sailed for coastal glory.

The legend says she was a princess
of the {{p|Kingdom of Ayuta}} in {{p|India}},
who sailed across the sea to {{p|Korea}}
in the first century, to marry plenty.

She married {{c|2563|King Suro}} of {{p|Geumgwan Gaya}},
became queen of that small kingdom,
bore him ten sons, and two took her surname,
founding the {{x|Kimhae Heo}} lineage wisdom.

Whether the legend is literal or
symbolic of cultural connection made,
the maritime links between {{p|South Asia}}
and {{p|East Asia}} were already there, unafraid.

The {{x|Kimhae Heo}} and {{x|Kimhae Kim}} clans
both trace descent from {{c|2562|Heo Hwang-ok}}.
Millions of modern {{c|2564|Koreans}} trace
their lineage back to this {{p|Indian}} shock.

{{x|Buddhism}} would later come to {{p|Korea}}
through {{x|Chinese}} channels, in the fourth century,
but already in the first, there were
threads of contact, mythic currency.

In {{p|India}} itself, {{x|Buddhism}} was
splitting into schools and lineages,
{{x|Theravada}}, {{x|Sarvastivada}}, {{x|Mahasanghika}},
the {{x|Vibhajyavada}} and other sages.

The {{c|2565|Kushan Empire}} under {{c|2566|Kanishka}}
in the second century united
{{p|Bactria}}, {{p|Gandhara}}, and northwest {{p|India}},
where {{x|Greco-Buddhist}} art ignited.

The {{p|Gandhara}} school carved {{c|1959|Buddha}} statues
in a {{x|Hellenistic}} {{x|Greek}} style,
with flowing robes like {{c|2567|Apollo}}'s,
with {{p|Mediterranean}} faces, for a while.

This is the origin of all {{c|1959|Buddha}} images.
Before {{p|Gandhara}}, the {{c|1959|Buddha}} was
represented only by symbols — wheel,
footprint, empty throne, the cause.

After {{p|Gandhara}}, the anthropomorphic
{{c|1959|Buddha}} with long earlobes, topknot, robe
spread across {{p|Asia}} from {{p|India}} east,
became the icon of the globe.

{{c|2566|Kanishka}} convened the {{x|Fourth Buddhist Council}},
where the {{x|Sarvastivada}} school was codified,
and missions went out across the {{p|Silk Road}}
to carry dharma to where it could hide.

{{x|Mahayana}} {{x|Buddhism}} was emerging,
"the {{x|Great Vehicle}}," with its new ideals:
the bodhisattva who forgoes nirvana
to save all beings, who feels what all feels.

The {{x|Lotus Sutra}}, the {{x|Heart Sutra}},
the {{x|Diamond Sutra}} were being written,
expanding the scope of the teaching from
the arhat path to the {{c|1959|Buddha}}'s wisdom.

{{x|Mahayana}} would be the form that traveled east
to {{p|China}}, {{p|Korea}}, {{p|Japan}}, {{p|Vietnam}}.
{{x|Theravada}} would survive in the south,
in {{p|Sri Lanka}}, {{p|Burma}}, {{p|Thailand}}, {{p|Cambodia}}'s psalm.

The {{p|Silk Road}} was the great conveyor.
From {{x|Kushan}} {{p|Gandhara}} eastward through
{{p|Tarim Basin}} oasis kingdoms,
monks and scrolls and statues flew.

{{p|Khotan}}, {{p|Kucha}}, {{p|Turfan}}, {{p|Dunhuang}},
the desert stations where caravans paused,
became centers of {{x|Buddhist}} translation,
cave monasteries where the great texts were housed.

{{p|Dunhuang}}'s caves would later shelter
the {{x|Diamond Sutra}}'s earliest print,
the world's oldest dated printed book,
from the ninth century, in preserved stint.

But that was later. For now, in the {{p|Han}},
The rite from the west trickled in, and ran
Beside the older altars, one more door
Into one house, not yet the river's roar.

The {{p|Han}} itself was showing strain.
The empress clans fought palace war.
The {{c|2568|Yellow Turbans}} rebelled in anger.
The {{p|Han}} would fall in the third century, raw.

But that's the next chapter. For now,
mark the crossing: the teaching of
the {{c|2569|Shakyamuni}} had crossed the mountains,
had entered {{p|China}}, the second love.

Two great transmissions. Two great streams
flowing out from the {{p|Indian}} source:
{{c|2320|Ashoka}}'s missions south and west;
these silk-road missions east, of course.

The dharma was becoming world-religion,
no longer just an {{p|Indian}} way.
The {{c|1959|Buddha}}'s "middle path" had proved
capable of crossing every sway.


# Chapter 182: The Fall of Han

While {{p|Rome}} was under the {{c|2684|Severans}} strained,
the {{c|2556|Han Dynasty}} in {{p|China}} fell apart.
The eunuchs fought the Confucian scholars.
The {{c|2568|Yellow Turbans}} rose with fervent heart.

{{c|2685|Zhang Jue}} and his brothers led
the {{c|2686|Yellow Turban Rebellion}} in 184.
{{x|Taiping Dao}}, the {{x|Way of Great Peace}},
promised a new heaven, a new core.

{{c|2685|Zhang Jue}} claimed healing powers, faith
cures, magical ceremonies, bean counting.
When plague and famine struck the peasants,
his followers numbered hundreds of thousands mounting.

The {{x|Han}} court raised armies, crushed the revolt,
but the generals became too strong thereby.
{{c|2687|Dong Zhuo}} marched into the capital,
controlled the boy emperor, made him cry.

{{c|2687|Dong Zhuo}} was assassinated. The warlords
carved up {{p|China}} like meat on the bone.
{{c|2688|Cao Cao}}, {{c|2689|Liu Bei}}, {{c|2690|Sun Quan}} emerged
as the three great regional powers alone.

{{c|2688|Cao Cao}} held the north, controlled the emperor,
ruled through the {{x|Han}} name though he was king.
{{c|2689|Liu Bei}} claimed descent from {{x|Han}} imperial blood,
built his base in {{p|Shu}}, the southwestern ring.

{{c|2690|Sun Quan}} inherited the south from his father and brother,
built his power along the {{p|Yangtze}}'s mouth,
{{p|Wu}} the eastern kingdom along the coast.
{{x|Three Kingdoms}}: {{p|Wei}}, {{p|Shu}}, {{p|Wu}}, facing drouth.

In two-twenty, {{c|2688|Cao Cao}}'s son {{c|2691|Cao Pi}}
forced the last {{x|Han}} emperor to abdicate.
The {{x|Han}} was formally dead. {{c|2691|Cao Pi}}
declared {{p|Wei}} dynasty at its birth date.

{{c|2689|Liu Bei}} declared {{p|Shu Han}} in response.
{{c|2690|Sun Quan}} declared {{p|Wu}} a few years later.
The {{x|Three Kingdoms}} period had begun,
lasting sixty years, never quieter.

The {{x|Han}} had lasted four hundred years.
Its fall was the end of classical Chinese order.
What followed was three centuries of division,
three centuries of warfare on every border.

The {{x|Three Kingdoms}}, then {{x|Jin}} unification briefly,
then the {{x|Sixteen Kingdoms}} in the north,
then the {{x|Southern and Northern Dynasties}} period,
three hundred years of {{p|China}} torn forth.

And in this time {{x|Buddhism}} took deep root:
as the old order failed, the people turned
to the one rite from {{p|India}}, its fruit
in sutras and in monasteries earned.

{{c|2692|Kumarajiva}} was brought from {{p|Kucha}} as hostage
to {{p|Chang'an}} where he translated sutras,
the {{x|Lotus}}, the {{x|Diamond}}, the {{x|Vimalakirti}},
setting the standard for Chinese Buddhist tutors.

{{x|Daoism}} also consolidated in this period
into an organized religion with clergy,
temples, canon, and liturgies modeled
on Buddhist forms they found analogously.

The {{c|2693|Celestial Masters}} had emerged
in the late {{x|Han}} as an organized church.
{{c|2694|Ge Hong}}'s alchemy sought immortality.
{{x|Daoism}} became institutional perch.

{{p|China}} would not be reunified until
{{c|2695|Sui Wendi}} in five-eighty-nine.
And then the {{c|2696|Tang Dynasty}} would build
on that foundation the greatest era fine.

But first, the {{x|Three Kingdoms}} would become
the great subject of Chinese historical imagination.
The {{c|2697|Romance of the Three Kingdoms}} novel
would make these warlords into every nation's creation.

{{c|2688|Cao Cao}}: the cunning, ruthless antihero.
{{c|2689|Liu Bei}}: the virtuous, righteous claimant.
{{c|2698|Zhuge Liang}}: the brilliant strategist advisor.
{{c|2699|Guan Yu}}: the loyal sworn brother, servant of heaven's pavement.

Their stories would shape Chinese culture
for fifteen centuries to come,
like the {{x|Mahabharata}} for {{p|India}},
like the {{x|Iliad}} for classical Greek home.


# Chapter 183: Jimmu to Jingū

In the island kingdom of {{p|Japan}},
the legendary first emperor {{c|2708|Jimmu}}
is said to have descended from {{c|885|Amaterasu}}
through a line of gods at their minimum.

Six-sixty BCE is the traditional date
for {{c|2708|Jimmu}}'s eastern expedition from {{p|Kyushu}}
to the {{p|Yamato}} plain, where he founded
the imperial line that {{p|Japan}} would issue.

Historically, the date is far too early.
The {{x|Yayoi}} rice-culture people had barely arrived.
The {{p|Yamato}} state would not coalesce
until several centuries after this contrived.

But the myth sets the frame: the imperial line
descends from the sun goddess through her grandson
{{c|2709|Ninigi}} who came down to {{p|Mount Takachiho}}
carrying the {{x|Three Sacred Treasures}} begun:

the mirror {{x|Yata no Kagami}},
the sword {{c|2710|Kusanagi}} (taken from the tail
of the eight-headed serpent {{c|2711|Yamata no Orochi}}
by {{c|2712|Susanoo}} in myth's oldest detail),

and the jewel {{x|Yasakani no Magatama}}.
These three still exist, kept in the shrines' stead,
as the imperial regalia of {{p|Japan}},
passed down through seventy centuries' tread.

{{c|2708|Jimmu}}'s great-grandfather was {{c|2709|Ninigi}}.
{{c|2708|Jimmu}}'s grandmother was {{c|2713|Toyotamahime}},
daughter of the sea dragon god, who bore
{{c|2714|Ugayafukiaezu}}, {{c|2708|Jimmu}}'s father, extremely.

So {{c|2708|Jimmu}} has divine lineage both through
the sun goddess {{c|885|Amaterasu}} above
and through the sea dragon gods below.
He is sky and sea, embraced by both's love.

He marched east from {{p|Kyushu}}, subduing
local chieftains, defeating rivals as he went.
At {{p|Kashihara}} in the {{p|Yamato}} plain
he founded the capital, his tent.

He ascended the throne there, we are told,
on February 11 of 660 BCE.
This date became {{p|Japan}}'s {{x|National Foundation Day}},
a holiday ever since, at least in theory.

For centuries after, the emperors listed
are largely legendary or semi-so.
The tenth emperor {{c|2715|Sujin}} may be
the first with some historical glow.

The twelfth, {{c|2716|Keikō}}, had a son {{c|2717|Yamato Takeru}},
the culture hero who conquered the eastern {{c|2718|Emishi}},
who killed his brother in his father's bathroom,
was sent to die on difficult missions barely.

He received {{c|2710|Kusanagi}} from his aunt
{{c|2719|Yamatohime}}, priestess of {{c|885|Amaterasu}} at {{p|Ise}}.
He used it to cut grass in a fire trap set by enemies,
saving his life, naming the sword "grass-cutter" in simplicity.

His son or nephew (accounts vary) {{c|2720|Chuai}}
was the fourteenth emperor, who died young,
leaving his pregnant queen {{c|2721|Jingū}} to rule.
She is the great semi-historical warrior tongue.

{{c|2722|Empress Jingū}} led an invasion of {{p|Korea}}
while pregnant with the future emperor {{c|2723|Ojin}}.
She held the birth back three years by
tying stones to her waist, the legend's imagine.

She conquered the Korean kingdoms (or received
their tribute), returning triumphant
to bear {{c|2723|Ojin}}, who would be deified as
{{c|2724|Hachiman}}, god of war, the most welcomed triumphant.

Modern historians are skeptical of {{c|2721|Jingū}}'s
Korean invasion. But there was certainly
contact with Korean kingdoms {{p|Baekje}}, {{p|Silla}}, {{p|Gaya}},
trade, migration, cultural transfer apparently.

From Baekje came writing, {{x|Confucianism}}, {{x|Buddhism}}
into {{p|Japan}} — {{x|Buddhism}} officially in 538 or 552,
though private transmission was earlier.
From Gaya came iron, craftsmen, immigrant troops.

The {{c|2725|Yamato}} court was consolidating
in the fourth and fifth centuries, building
the massive {{c|2726|kofun}} burial mounds,
the largest tombs in the world, filling.

The {{c|2727|Daisenryō Kofun}} attributed to
emperor {{c|2728|Nintoku}} is longer than the {{p|Great Pyramid}},
though lower — a 486-meter keyhole shape
of earth and stone, for the imperial pyramid.

These burial mounds mark the emergence
of a centralized state in the Japanese archipelago,
absorbing Korean immigrants, Chinese influence,
building toward what would become emperor {{p|Yamato}}.

Two clans, one court. The {{c|2729|Soga clan}} would raise
the Buddha's hall beside the kami's days;
and the {{c|2730|Mononobe clan}} would keep the rite
in its own hands, and both would go to fight.

In five-eighty-seven the {{c|2731|Soga}} won,
and court and temple and the shrine were one:
the Buddha and the kami of the sun,
{{x|Shinto}} with {{x|Buddhism}}, a rite begun.

The {{x|Kofun}} period was ending. The {{x|Asuka}} period
beginning. The constitution of {{c|2732|Prince Shōtoku}}
in 604 would organize the state
along Chinese lines — the shape we still see.


# Chapter 184: Elagabalus

The {{x|Severan}} dynasty held {{p|Rome}}
in the early third {{x|Common Era}},
and produced one of the strangest emperors
that ever held imperial ear.

{{c|2570|Elagabalus}}, aged fourteen, was made
Emperor in two-eighteen, and conveyed
From {{p|Emesa}} the rite he served by birth
To {{p|Rome}}, the sun his city kept on earth.

He was the high priest by descent of one,
{{c|2571|Elagabal}}, the city's god, the sun,
A black stone in a temple. {{p|Rome}} had known
The same sky under {{c|101|Jupiter}}'s own throne,

With {{c|97|Mars}}, the {{x|Capitoline}} three. The fight
Was whose priest held it, and whose house, whose rite.
He brought the stone to {{p|Rome}} itself, to stand
Above the other altars of the land.

He tried to marry it to {{c|1995|Athena}}.
When that failed, he tried {{c|2572|Astarte}}.
He held processions with the stone
in a chariot, barefoot, sweaty, hardly.

He is alleged — with what truth we
do not fully know — to have done many things:
married a {{x|Vestal Virgin}}, violating
the sacred celibacy that the office brings;

married several times to women,
married a charioteer in woman's dress,
preferred to be called "lady" by servants,
sought surgeons to perform a change of sex.

These accounts are true at heart,{{fn|The accounts of Elagabalus come from Cassius Dio and Herodian, who were hostile to him, and from the later Historia Augusta, which is often unreliable.}}
though hostile pens had spun
them after the fall, and the life
shines through what the enemies had done.

Some see in {{c|2570|Elagabalus}}
an early transgender figure,
the first recorded ruler who
sought physical transformation with rigor.

Others see only slander, the
standard tropes of {{p|Roman}} invective
used to destroy reputations
of rulers who proved ineffective.

The poem notes: whatever was the truth,
The quarrel was not gods but priests: the youth
Who set his city's priesthood over all
Of {{p|Rome}}'s own priesthoods was the one to fall.

The senate's houses, those who held the rites
Of {{p|Rome}}'s own altars, would not bear the slights.
The {{x|Praetorian Guard}} slew him, eighteen,
Dragged him through streets, and threw him, as unclean,

Into the {{p|Tiber}}, with his mother, laid
The sewer for a tomb. The stone, conveyed
Back home to {{p|Emesa}}, left {{p|Rome}}'s own sun
In {{p|Rome}}'s own priests' hands: the same rite, still one.

But something had been planted: one sun's rite
From {{p|Syria}}, had held the throne's own light
Briefly: one sun at the empire's head,
Kept by one {{x|Syrian}} house in {{p|Rome}}'s stead.

This was the first attempt to make
solar monotheism {{p|Rome}}'s state cult.
It failed under {{c|2570|Elagabalus}}.
It would succeed under {{c|2573|Aurelian}}'s result.

{{c|2573|Aurelian}} fifty years later,
after the {{x|Crisis of the Third Century}},
would make {{c|2554|Sol Invictus}} the state god,
the "{{c|2574|Unconquered Sun}}" of imperial sanctuary.

That syncretic sun-cult would merge
with mystery religions and with others,
would become the cultural matrix
into which {{x|Christianity}} hovers.

December twenty-fifth was {{c|2554|Sol Invictus}}'
birthday, the winter solstice celebration,
the "dies natalis {{c|2575|Solis Invicti}},"
the unconquered sun's inauguration.

{{c|2494|Christians}} would later fix their {{x|Christmas}}
on this same date, adopting the feast,
merging the birth of the {{c|2576|Son of Man}}
with the rebirth of the {{c|99|Sun}} in the {{p|East}}.

This is not accidental. The {{c|2554|Sol Invictus}}
cult and the {{c|1497|Christ}} cult were cousins,
sharing iconography, festivals, theology,
the rayed halo, the midwinter reasons.

The feast of the {{c|2574|Unconquered Sun}}, that night
the longest, was the feast of {{x|Aster Day}},
the same, kept under every name of light;
and {{x|Christmas}}, after, kept it the same way.

Three strands had been converging now
toward what would become monotheistic {{p|Rome}}:
{{x|Jewish}} exilic covenant-monotheism,
{{x|Persian}} dualistic cosmic home,

{{x|Egyptian}} {{c|1952|Akhenaten}}'s old {{c|2083|Aten}}
(a lost current but not forgotten),
{{x|Syrian}} solar-theologies rising,
{{x|Platonic}} philosophy unforgotten.

All were feeding into the stream
that would break through under {{c|2555|Constantine}}
and become the official faith of {{p|Rome}}
and then of {{p|Europe}}, clean and clean.

But we are not there yet. The third century
still held the old gods in their frame.
{{c|2570|Elagabalus}} was the weird episode
that {{p|Rome}} tried hard to forget by name.

His memory was damned, "damnatio memoriae,"
his name scratched out, his image defaced.
But history remembered him as
the strangest emperor {{p|Rome}} had faced.


# Chapter 185: Romance of the Three Kingdoms

The novel by {{c|2700|Luo Guanzhong}}
in the fourteenth century brought alive
the {{x|Three Kingdoms}} war with such vividness
that fact and fiction no longer survive

as separate things. What "everyone knows"
about this period comes from his book.
The historical {{c|2701|Chen Shou}}'s {{x|Records of Three Kingdoms}}
is less read, less fun, less took.

The opening line: "The empire, long divided,
must unite; long united, must divide.
Thus it has ever been." The novel begins
with the {{x|Peach Garden Oath}} on a riverside.

{{c|2689|Liu Bei}}, {{c|2699|Guan Yu}}, and {{c|2702|Zhang Fei}}
swore brotherhood in a peach garden,
pledging to die on the same day, to
restore the {{x|Han}}, to share every burden.

{{c|2689|Liu Bei}} claimed descent from the {{x|Han}} imperial line,
but sold straw sandals and mats to live.
{{c|2699|Guan Yu}} was a fugitive for avenging
a local bully who would not forgive.

{{c|2702|Zhang Fei}} was a butcher and wine-seller,
brash, brave, violent, loyal as stone.
Together they raised a volunteer army
against the {{c|2568|Yellow Turbans}} on their own.

{{c|2698|Zhuge Liang}} joined {{c|2689|Liu Bei}} later,
the {{c|2703|Sleeping Dragon}}, the brilliant strategist,
visited three times at his thatched cottage
before he would consent to be a lobbyist

for {{c|2689|Liu Bei}}'s cause. He devised the strategy
of the tripod: three kingdoms balancing,
{{p|Shu}} allied with {{p|Wu}} against {{p|Wei}},
the weaker two against the one advancing.

The {{c|2704|Battle of Red Cliffs}} in two-oh-eight
was the great set piece. {{c|2688|Cao Cao}}'s northern army
came south to crush the Wu-Shu alliance.
Eight hundred thousand troops, allegedly.

{{c|2698|Zhuge Liang}} borrowed arrows with straw boats
in the fog, ten thousand arrows from {{c|2688|Cao Cao}}'s
own archers fired at what they couldn't see.
Fire ships were prepared, east wind-blowings owed.

The Taoist {{c|2705|Zhuge}} summoned the east wind,
or predicted it, the novel is ambiguous.
The fire ships slipped into {{c|2688|Cao Cao}}'s fleet
chained together, and the conflagration was continuous.

{{c|2688|Cao Cao}}'s navy burned. His army fled
along the {{p|Huarong Road}} through marsh and mud.
{{c|2699|Guan Yu}} let him escape at the narrow pass,
repaying old debt of favor, blood.

(This was not in the histories. {{c|2700|Luo Guanzhong}}
invented the {{p|Huarong Road}} release
to show {{c|2699|Guan Yu}}'s righteousness, his sense
of honor even to foes, sense of peace.)

{{c|2699|Guan Yu}} became the god of war,
of loyalty, of brotherhood, of merchants,
worshipped across {{p|China}} and Chinese diaspora
as {{c|2706|Guandi}}, in temples of gold and servants.

{{c|2698|Zhuge Liang}}'s {{x|Six Campaigns}} against {{p|Wei}}
ended in his death at {{p|Wuzhang Plains}}.
"The heavens will not let me succeed,"
he said. {{p|Shu}} collapsed from his absent pains.

{{p|Shu}} fell to {{p|Wei}} in two-sixty-three.
{{p|Wei}} was replaced by the {{c|2707|Jin Dynasty}} in two-sixty-five.
{{p|Wu}} fell to {{x|Jin}} in two-eighty.
The empire was briefly reunified alive.

But {{x|Jin}} would not last. Barbarian invasions
from the north would push the {{x|Jin}} south,
the {{p|Northern and Southern Dynasties}} would begin.
{{p|China}} would be divided with famine in its mouth.

Yet the {{x|Three Kingdoms}} tales endured.
{{c|2689|Liu Bei}} as the righteous rightful heir.
{{c|2688|Cao Cao}} as the cunning realist.
{{c|2698|Zhuge Liang}} as wisdom incarnate there.

The novel's influence is vast.
Every Chinese child knows these names.
East Asian games, operas, films retell them.
Military strategy manuals cite their games.

"Hard as it is to conquer the world,
harder it is to keep what's conquered."
"Victory and defeat are common in war,
but the determined man's not deflowered."

The novel's worldview is deeply Confucian:
loyalty above survival, righteousness above success.
{{c|2689|Liu Bei}}'s cause is just though it loses.
{{c|2688|Cao Cao}}'s victory is tainted, a mess.

The deflationary polytheist sees here
the Chinese counterpart to epic,
the narrative matrix that shapes
moral imagination, subsonic and sceptic.


# Chapter 186: The Sassanid Empire

In {{p|Persia}}, the {{c|2593|Parthians}} fell
to {{c|2594|Ardashir I}} in two-twenty-four,
who claimed descent from {{c|2595|Sasan}}, a priest,
and founded the {{c|2596|Sassanid}} rule once more.

The new dynasty revived old glory,
the vision of {{x|Achaemenid}} days,
and made {{c|2597|Zoroastrianism}} state religion,
with {{c|2598|Kartir}} as high priest of ways.

They centered on {{p|Ctesiphon}} their seat,
on the {{p|Tigris}} near old {{p|Babylon}}'s ground.
They warred with {{p|Rome}} for four centuries,
locked in a struggle without bound.

{{c|2585|Shapur I}} captured {{c|2586|Valerian}},
defeated three {{p|Roman}} emperors in field,
carved his triumph on {{p|Naqsh-e Rustam}}'s cliffs,
where {{x|Achaemenid}} tombs were sealed.

{{c|2599|Mani}} arose in {{c|2600|Shapur}}'s court,
the prophet of {{c|2601|Manichaeism}},
blending {{x|Zoroastrian}} dualism with
{{x|Buddhist}}, {{x|Christian}}, and {{x|Gnostic}} idealism.

{{c|2599|Mani}} named every prophet in a chain:
{{c|2146|Zarathustra}}, the {{c|1959|Buddha}}, {{c|1912|Jesus}}, each
one light sent down to every age again;
a seal of prophets {{x|Islam}} came to teach.

The religion spread from {{p|Persia}} east
to {{p|Central Asia}} and to {{p|China}} past,
west to {{p|Rome}}, where {{c|2384|Augustine}} embraced it
for nine years, before he broke fast.

{{c|2600|Shapur}} let {{c|2599|Mani}} preach; {{c|2602|Bahram}} instead
had {{c|2599|Mani}} put in chains till he was dead,
and {{c|2598|Kartir}} struck at every rival flame:
the {{c|2603|Manichaeans}}, {{c|2500|Jews}}, {{c|2494|Christians}}, all one claim.

But what he taught no prison chain could hold:
it ran to {{p|Harran}} and the {{p|Uyghur}} east,
and {{x|Islam}}'s prophets, later, kept its mold,
and {{c|2598|Kartir}}'s {{c|2604|Avesta}} served the crown's priest.

{{c|2605|Khosrow I}} brought the golden age,
reformed taxation, built canals,
received {{x|Greek}} philosophers fleeing
{{c|2383|Justinian}}'s {{p|Athens}} shut locales.

He commissioned translation of
{{x|Indian}}, {{x|Greek}}, and {{x|Syriac}} books
into {{p|Middle Persian}}, preserving learning
that otherwise would have been shook.

The game of chess arrived from {{p|India}}
to his court, where it was refined.
The {{x|Pancatantra}} was translated
as {{x|Kalila wa Dimna}}, combined

with {{x|Persian}} wisdom, and later became
the source of fables across the world.
{{c|2606|Aesop}}'s cousins, {{c|2607|Uncle Remus}}' kin,
traveled through {{c|2608|Khosrow}}'s court unfurled.

{{c|2609|Khosrow II}} would fight the last great
war with {{p|Rome}}'s Eastern continuation,
capture {{p|Jerusalem}} and take the {{x|True Cross}},
nearly destroy {{p|Byzantium}}'s foundation.

Then {{c|2610|Heraclius}} would counter-strike,
marching into {{p|Persia}}'s heartland,
recovering the {{x|Cross}}, ending the war,
exhausting both empires first-hand.

Both empires were spent. The stage was set
for the {{x|Arab}} conquest sweeping north.
Within a decade of that war's end,
the {{x|Sassanid}} realm would be going forth

to its destruction. {{c|2611|Yazdegerd III}},
the last shah, would flee across the land,
murdered by a miller at {{p|Merv}}.
The fire temples would cease their stand.

But the cultural inheritance endured.
{{x|Persian}} language, literature, art
would resurface under {{x|Islamic}} rule
and shape the {{x|Islamic}} world's heart.

The {{x|Shahnameh}} of {{c|2612|Ferdowsi}} would
preserve the pre-Islamic past in verse.
The {{c|2613|Zoroastrians}} who fled to {{p|India}}
became {{c|2614|Parsis}}, their faith's unsquashed reverse.


# Chapter 187: The Third Century Crisis

After {{c|2570|Elagabalus}} was killed,
the empire stumbled for fifty years.
Fifty emperors in fifty years.
Plague. Inflation. Barbarian fears.

Historians call it the {{x|Crisis of the Third Century}}.
The imperial system nearly broke.
Legions acclaimed their generals,
who were killed by the next legion's stroke.

{{c|2577|Alexander Severus}} was killed.
{{c|2578|Maximinus Thrax}} was killed.
{{c|2579|Gordian I}} and {{c|2580|Gordian II}} died.
{{c|2581|Pupienus}} and {{c|2582|Balbinus}} were killed.

The names blur. The reigns were brief.
Emperors rose and fell like weather.
The coinage was debased, the silver
diluted to base metal's tether.

And then in two-fifty {{c|2583|Decius}} decreed
that every house burn incense at his shrine
and keep a paper proving it agreed.
The church said: the same incense, but at mine.

Many {{c|2494|Christians}} sacrificed, lapsed,
became the "lapsi" debated for years.
Others were martyred, {{c|2584|Cyprian}} of {{p|Carthage}},
the bishop, whose blood watered tears.

The {{p|Persians}} under {{c|2585|Shapur I}} captured
{{c|2586|Valerian}} the {{p|Roman}} emperor in battle,
used him as a footstool to mount horse,
then stuffed his body with straw for cattle.

The capture of a {{p|Roman}} emperor
was unprecedented, new,
and the skin hung in the temple
for the {{p|Roman}} envoys' view.

{{c|2587|Zenobia}} of {{p|Palmyra}} broke away,
ruled {{p|Egypt}}, {{p|Syria}}, {{p|Asia Minor}} east,
a warrior queen of legendary beauty,
until {{c|2573|Aurelian}} marched and seized.

The {{p|Gallic Empire}} broke off in the west,
ruled by {{c|2588|Postumus}} for years.
The empire was splitting three ways:
{{p|Gaul}}, {{p|Rome}}, and {{p|Palmyra}} in tears.

Then {{c|2573|Aurelian}} came. "{{c|2589|Restitutor Orbis}}."
The {{c|2590|Restorer of the World}}.
He reunited the three empires,
brought the eagle standards unfurled.

He defeated {{c|2587|Zenobia}} and took her
to {{p|Rome}} in golden chains to display.
He defeated the {{p|Gallic Empire}}.
He saved the state from decay.

And he made {{c|2554|Sol Invictus}} the state god.
The "{{c|2574|Unconquered Sun}}" became official.
The syncretic solar monotheism
was now imperial, not just unofficial.

This is the crucial step. The sun he crowned
at midwinter was {{c|1912|Christ}}'s own cousin, born
the very night that {{x|Aster Day}} comes round,
the longest dark, that turns toward the morn.

The old polytheism was still practiced.
The temples still stood. The priests still served.
But the emperor's personal faith
was focused on one divinity deserved.

{{c|2573|Aurelian}} was assassinated too.
But his work held. {{c|2591|Diocletian}} came
and restructured the empire entirely:
the {{x|Tetrarchy}}, four rulers, same aim.

Two {{x|Augusti}}, two {{x|Caesars}}, ruling
the four quarters of the empire wide.
{{p|Nicomedia}}, {{p|Milan}}, {{p|Trier}}, {{p|Sirmium}}
were the new capitals where power resides.

{{p|Rome}} itself was becoming peripheral.
The emperor rarely visited {{p|Rome}}.
Power was where the frontier armies were,
not in the old {{p|Italian}} home.

And in three-oh-three {{c|2591|Diocletian}} tore down
the churches, burned the books, and named it law:
the {{x|Great Persecution}}, so that the crown
would hold each altar the empire saw.

It failed. The church was too embedded.
Martyrs increased conversions, not decreased.
The persecution ended in three-eleven,
the next emperor's edict of peace.

{{c|2592|Galerius}} on his deathbed issued
an edict of toleration, saying
essentially, we've tried to crush them,
it hasn't worked, let them keep praying.

Then came {{c|2555|Constantine}}.

But before we get to him, mark this:
the third century was the civilizational near-miss.
The empire almost fell right then.
It was saved by {{c|2573|Aurelian}}'s fierce grip and kiss.

And saved in a form that was no longer
the old {{x|Republic}}'s civic-religion mode.
It was now a monarchical empire with
a near-monotheistic imperial code.

The groundwork was laid. The solar
monotheism of {{c|2573|Aurelian}} would
transition into the {{x|Christian}} monotheism
of {{c|2555|Constantine}}. One god would do.

Three centuries after {{c|1912|Jesus}},
the church had grown from twelve
to perhaps ten percent of the empire,
still a minority, but selective.

The bishops had become organized.
The creeds were being formulated.
The gospels had been canonized
and the writings of {{c|379|Paul}} disseminated.

The church was ready. The empire was ready.
What was needed was imperial blessing.
That would come in three-twelve, at
the battle of the {{p|Milvian Bridge}}, confessing.
