And every single day of the year he named, not for a saint, but for a living thing
Or a tool of the farm: the grape, the saffron, the chestnut, the root
Of the turnip, an animal on every fifth day, a tool on the tenth. The ring

Of the year was a field. That is beautiful. Hold it. A whole year
Where each day was a plant to be thankful for. And they went further:
Ten hours to the day, a hundred minutes to the hour, the sheer
Decimal clock, with faces made for it. And the murmur

Of the people was against it. The week of ten days gave them one rest in ten,
Not one in seven: the workers lost a day of rest in every three weeks,
And the old Sunday went on in secret. The decimal hours, then,
Were given up within two years. The clocks with their odd peaks

Of ten numbers sit in museums. And the poet who named the months, {{c|4121|Fabre}},
Was caught in a fraud and in the factions, and went to the guillotine
In April 1794, before his calendar had gone once round, the macabre
Joke of the season: he died in *{{x|Germinal}}*, the month of the green.

The days of the calendar became the names of what happened on them:
The ninth of *{{x|Thermidor}}*, when {{c|4122|Robespierre}} fell; the eighteenth of *{{x|Brumaire}}*,
When {{c|4066|Napoleon}} took the {{x|Republic}}. And {{c|4066|Napoleon}} ended it, the hem
Of the new time cut: on the first of January, 1806, the old year

Came back, and the Sundays, and the saints. The {{x|Revolution}}'s time
Lived twelve years, and in the {{c|4123|Paris Commune}} for a few weeks in 1871,
And in the names: *{{x|Germinal}}*, the novel; *{{x|Thermidor}}*, the lobster; the rhyme
Of the months still sung. Now hold the mirror. This book is one

Of the calendars that came after. The {{x|Gaian}} calendar remakes time too:
A new era, counted from the deep past of the human story, not a birth;
Thirteen months of twenty-eight days, every date on the same weekday, the true
Perpetual year. And it learned from the {{x|French}}: the week was not worth

Breaking. The seven days stay. The rest stays: three sabbaths, not one in ten.
And every day of the year is named, as the poet named them, but not for a plant:
For a chapter of the scripture, read that day; and now the dead, the women and men
Of the ancestors, kept on their day. The poet's slant

Was right: give every day a meaning, and the year becomes a liturgy.
His error was to break the rhythm of the body's rest
For the sake of a number. Learn both. A calendar is a theology
And a promise to the tired. The {{x|French}} made the year a field, the best

Of their gift, and broke the Sunday, the worst of their error.
Keep the field. Keep the rest. Name the days. Do not let the number rule the body.
And remember the poet who named *{{x|Germinal}}* and died in it, the terror
Of his times around him: the grape, the fog, the frost. The year is a story.


# Chapter 293: The Festival of the Supreme Being

{{c|4054|Rousseau}} had written, in *The {{x|Social Contract}}*, in 1762,
That a republic needs a civil religion: a few plain articles of faith,
A God, a life to come, the reward of the just, the punishment due
To the wicked, the sanctity of the laws; and that the wraith

Of a citizen who will not believe them may be banished; and the one who believes
And then acts against them, punished by death. Hold that sentence.
Thirty years later the {{x|Revolution}} read it. In 1793 the eves
Of the old faith were torn down: the churches closed, the repentance

Of the priests demanded, the bells melted for cannon, the saints' names
Taken from the streets. The radicals made a {{c|4124|Cult of Reason}}:
In {{p|Notre-Dame}}, renamed the {{p|Temple of Reason}}, in November, the flames
Of the new altar lit, an actress robed as {{c|4125|Liberty}}, the season

Of a goddess of the mind enthroned where the {{c|3936|Virgin}} had been.
And {{c|4122|Robespierre}}, the incorruptible, the lawyer from {{p|Arras}},
The master of the {{x|Committee of Public Safety}}, hated it: the obscene
Mockery of atheism, he thought, would make the people crass

And the {{x|Republic}} godless; the people need a God and the soul's immortality.
So in May 1794, by decree, the {{x|Convention}} recognized
The {{c|4126|Supreme Being}} and the immortality of the soul. A morality
Of state: the people's rite. A feast, devised:

On the twentieth of *{{x|Prairial}}*, the eighth of June, which was also {{x|Pentecost}},
The painter {{c|4127|Jacques-Louis David}} staged it: half a million people, the roses,
The children with flowers, the mothers, the old men, the host
Of the citizens in procession across {{p|Paris}} to the {{p|Champ de Mars}}, where, he supposes,

An artificial mountain had been built, with a tree of liberty on top.
And {{c|4122|Robespierre}}, president of the {{x|Convention}} for that day,
Walked out ahead of the other deputies, with a bouquet, and the shop
Of the ritual was his: he set fire to a statue of {{c|4128|Atheism}}, made, they say,

Of cardboard and wax, and as it burned, a statue of {{c|4129|Wisdom}}
Was meant to rise out of it, pure. It rose blackened with smoke.
Hold that image. The deputies behind him, in the wisdom
Of fear, muttered: look at him; it is not enough to be master; the yoke

Of being God as well. Two days later, the tenth of June,
He brought the law of the twenty-second of *{{x|Prairial}}*: the accused
Would have no lawyer, no witnesses needed, the verdict soon,
Death or acquittal, nothing between. The courts were used

As a machine. In the seven weeks that followed, in {{p|Paris}} alone,
More were guillotined than in the whole year before. The {{x|Great Terror}}.
The god of the festival, the god of the soul, the stone
Of the blade: one hand. The god, no error.

On the ninth of *{{x|Thermidor}}*, the twenty-seventh of July,
The {{x|Convention}} turned on him, and shouted him down, and he was taken,
And shot in the jaw, by his own hand or a gendarme's, and the next day, the sky
Of {{p|Paris}} over him, guillotined, with twenty-one of his men. Forsaken,

The {{c|4126|Supreme Being}} faded within months. But read it once more:
In a {{p|France}} where a God was still the default, the transgression
Was the {{c|4124|Cult of Reason}}, the war on the altar and the door
Of the church; and he turned back from it: a God, a soul, and the profession

Of the freedom of worship, kept in the same decree. Not the void,
Then, but a step back toward the faith the bells had rung:
Under the {{x|Directory}} the {{c|4130|Theophilanthropists}} enjoyed
The empty naves for a deist rite, a hymn to the Maker sung;

And {{c|4066|Napoleon}}, in 1801, closed their rite and made his peace with the {{c|2825|Pope}}:
Not a God put in the place of a failure, but the last stage of a road
From {{c|4131|Reason}} to the {{c|4126|Supreme Being}} to the {{x|Concordat}}, a slope
That the festival set out on, back to the altar the {{x|Revolution}} had overthrown.

And read now, it reads otherwise: a choice to believe in the divine,
A deist's God, which a person may hold, or leave unheld, as they need,
Not the dogma of a nation but a door, the way a God is taken now, or declined;
What was cruel in it was never the belief, but the power behind the creed.

The {{c|4126|Supreme Being}} was not void. A state
Had kept a God, as {{c|4054|Rousseau}} said it must;
The altar was the people's, and the date
{{x|Pentecost}}: the Spirit's feast, held in trust.

The fight was in one house: who holds the nave,
The priest, the {{c|4124|Cult of Reason}}, or the hall
Of the {{x|Convention}}; and {{c|4125|Liberty}}, grave,
Took the {{c|3936|Virgin}}'s seat; one Lady for all.

{{c|4122|Robespierre}} gave the state its God again
Against the atheists of his own side;
{{c|4066|Napoleon}} walked the same road, and then
Took the {{x|Church}} and made it his. At his side,

When the crown came from the {{c|2825|Pope}}'s hands, a ghost:
The incorruptible, behind the throne.
This faith, too, means to be a state's, and most
Of all, to keep its days as the state's own.

Keep the roses on the mountain, the tree
Of liberty on top, the blackened face
Of {{c|4129|Wisdom}} rising from the smoke, and see
The {{c|4126|Supreme Being}} in this book's own place.


# Chapter 294: The Mountain Cherry

In 712 a court lady's memory, or a court scholar's, was written down:
The {{c|4132|Kojiki}}, the *{{x|Record of Ancient Matters}}*, the oldest book of {{p|Japan}},
The kami from the beginning, {{c|4133|Izanagi}} and {{c|4134|Izanami}}, the crown
Of the {{c|4135|Sun Goddess}}, the descent to {{p|Hyūga}}, the first emperor, the plan

Of the land told as a family. And it was written in a script no one could easily read:
{{x|Chinese}} characters used now for their sound, now for their sense,
A puzzle of a book. Within a few years the court had a newer creed:
The {{c|4136|Nihon Shoki}}, in proper {{x|Chinese}}, official, the dense

And dignified history; and the {{c|4132|Kojiki}} was put on a shelf
And mostly left there for a thousand years. Then, in {{p|Matsusaka}},
Near {{p|Ise}}, a cotton merchant's son who had failed at trade, and made himself
A doctor of children instead, studied in {{p|Kyoto}}, the saga

Of the old poems in his evenings: {{c|4137|Motoori Norinaga}}, born 1730.
In 1763 an old scholar, {{c|4138|Kamo no Mabuchi}}, passed through his town
On a pilgrimage to {{p|Ise}}, and stayed one night at an inn, and the young man came, and the empty
Hours of that night were filled: the old man told him, set down

Everything else and read the {{c|4132|Kojiki}}; I am too old to finish it; you do it.
They never met again. They wrote letters. And the doctor began.
For thirty-four years, while he treated the children of {{p|Matsusaka}}, he read through it,
Every character, every sound, every name of every kami, the span

Of the language reconstructed: how the old {{x|Japanese}} spoke, before the {{x|Chinese}} came.
The *{{x|Kojiki-den}}*, the *{{x|Commentary on the Kojiki}}*, forty-four volumes, done
In 1798. The oldest book of the land could be read again. The name
Of every god was given back its sound. That is the gift, the one

This book and its makers stand on: the record of the kami, opened.
And he gave more: reading the *{{x|Tale of Genji}}*, he found the phrase
*{{x|Mono no aware}}*: the ache of things, the sadness of the cherry petals that ended,
The heart moved by the passing of the world. The praise

Of feeling over moral lesson. That is his too.
Here is the other edge of tradition:
He taught that the {{x|Japanese}} heart had been corrupted by the {{x|Chinese}} mind, the *karagokoro*,
And the {{x|Buddhist}}, and that the true way was the ancient one, the condition

Of the land before the foreign: the way of the kami, pure and native, revealed in the {{c|4132|Kojiki}}.
That was a scholar's longing. In the next generation, {{c|4139|Hirata Atsutane}},
Who called himself his disciple after he died, made it a creed, a stricter key:
The emperor descended from the {{c|99|Sun}}, {{p|Japan}} the land of the gods, the cannon

Of the nation, pointing outward. The state
Took up the longing, and it kept the rite
Of kami, parted from buddhas: the great
Work of {{x|State Shinto}}, and the war, the night.

He wrote a poem: *If someone asks what the {{x|Japanese}} heart is,
It is the mountain cherry blossoms, fragrant in the morning sun.*
A lovely poem. In October 1944, the first units of the kamikaze, the quiz
Of their names answered by it: *{{x|Shikishima}}*, *{{x|Yamato}}*, *{{x|Asahi}}*, *{{x|Yamazakura}}*. The young men, one by one,

Named for the words of a doctor who had loved children.
Hold that. This book is made by one who keeps the kami, and loves the old record,
And founds a faith in the way of life, a kind of {{x|Shinto}}. The bewildering
Lesson for her, and for every reader: the love of the ancient word

Can be turned into a weapon by someone else, a century on.
Keep the commentary. Keep the reading of the names of the gods. Keep *mono no aware*.
Keep the pure longing, the mixing, the dawn:
The buddhas sat with the kami. And there

Was always mixing. That is the true ancient way. {{c|4140|Norinaga}}'s grave
Is on a mountain above {{p|Matsusaka}}, plain, and over it, as he asked, a mountain cherry.
Visit it in spring. The petals fall. Let them. The nave
Of the old faith is open. No one owns the blossom. Be wary,

And be moved. Both. The doctor read the oldest book for thirty-four years
So we could read it. Read it. And when anyone tells you the heart of a people is pure,
Remember the morning sun on the cherry, and the young men, and the tears.
The ache of things is for everyone. That is the only cure.


# Chapter 295: The Crown He Took

On {{x|Christmas Day}} in the year 800, in {{p|Saint Peter's}}, a pope set a crown on a kneeling king,
{{c|2677|Charlemagne}}, who had not asked for it, and called him {{c|4141|Emperor of the Romans}},
And for a thousand years the {{p|West}} had an emperor, the crown of the Romans carried north, a ring
Of electors and princes and bishops around one name, the {{p|Holy Roman Empire}}, whose summons

Held a continent in one order under heaven, longer than any crown of the {{p|West}} has held since.
{{c|4001|Voltaire}} mocked it as neither holy, nor {{x|Roman}}, nor an empire. A joke is not a reading.
It kept the {{x|Roman}} name alive in the north a thousand years, and every prince
Who knelt to it knelt to a crown that came from above, at a church's leading.

Then the {{x|Revolution}} shut the churches, and set {{x|Reason}} on the altar of {{p|Notre-Dame}},
And {{c|4122|Robespierre}} put God back, the {{x|Supreme Being}} of an earlier chapter, against the atheists of his own side,
Because a republic, he saw, cannot stand on nothing; and the soldier who came after him walked the same
Road. In 1801 the {{x|Concordat}}: the {{x|Church}} came home to {{p|France}}, with the state for its guide,

Bishops named by the First Consul, priests paid from the treasury, the faith of the land
Brought back and made the state's. He did not abolish the {{x|Church}}. He took it in.
First he sacked {{p|Rome}}, as {{c|2|Emma Leonhart}} says, and then he sacked {{p|Rome}} again, with the crown in his hand.
He took {{x|Christianity}} and made it his: the most Lifeist thing a man could do, and where this book's own work begins.

On the second of December, 1804, in {{p|Notre-Dame}} in {{p|Paris}},
{{c|2825|Pope}} {{c|4142|Pius VII}} sat waiting to crown a {{c|4143|Corsican}}, and the fire
Of the moment: {{c|4066|Napoleon}} took the crown in his own hands. The plurals

Of the old story were ended in one gesture, the {{x|Church}} in the room to see it, and behind him,
In the eye of this book, the ghost of {{c|4122|Robespierre}}. He crowned himself, then {{c|4144|Joséphine}}, kneeling; the painter {{c|1956|David}}
Put it on a canvas ten metres wide, and painted in his mother, who had stayed home, the grim
Truth adjusted for the record, as records are. Two years later, the cavity

Of the old empire was empty: the {{x|German}} princes, bribed and beaten, left it
For his {{p|Confederation of the Rhine}}, and on the sixth of August, 1806,
The last emperor, {{c|4145|Francis II}}, laid the crown of {{c|2677|Charlemagne}} down, and what was left
Of a thousand years went down with it, the crown that was given, not taken. The bricks

Of it had held a continent a thousand years; a soldier, not time, pushed it over.
Now the register, which this book follows like a river.
The {{x|Revolution}} had taken the books of births and marriages and deaths, the cover
Of the parish, from the priests in 1792, and given them to the town hall, the giver

Of the record now the state. {{c|4066|Napoleon}} made it a code. The *{{x|Civil Code}}* of 1804,
One law for every {{c|4146|Frenchman}}, written plain, the family, the property, the will,
And wherever his armies went, the code went, and the registers, the door
Of every birth opened by a clerk, not a priest: the {{p|Netherlands}}, the {{p|Rhineland}}, the {{p|Italy}} still

Keeping those books. And the names. In the {{p|Netherlands}} many families had none:
A man was *{{c|4147|Jan Pieterszoon}}*, {{c|1093|Peter}}'s son, and his son *{{c|4148|Pieter Janszoon}}*, the line
Of the patronymic turning each generation, as in {{p|Sweden}}, as {{c|4012|Linnaeus}}'s father had done
Before the linden. In 1811 the {{x|French}} decreed: every family shall register, by a sign

Of the town hall, a fixed surname. And the {{x|Dutch}}, who thought the {{x|French}} would be gone
In a year, some of them chose jokes: *{{c|4149|Naaktgeboren}}*, born naked;
*{{c|4150|Zondervan}}*, without a *van*; and the {{x|French}} stayed long enough, and the joke went on
For two hundred years on the children. In {{p|France}} in 1808 the {{c|2500|Jews}}, who had made

Their names by father's name, were ordered to take fixed surnames too.
And {{c|4066|Napoleon}} called a {{c|4151|Grand Sanhedrin}} of rabbis, the first in eighteen centuries,
And the {{c|2500|Jews}} of the conquered lands were made citizens; the ghetto walls, the few
Gates of {{p|Venice}} and {{p|Rome}}, opened by his soldiers. The entries

Of that gift and that demand are in the same register: be free, and be written.
Hold the whole man as this book holds them all. The conqueror whose wars
Killed some three million, perhaps more; who brought back slavery to the smitten
Colonies in 1802; who carried {{c|4060|Ossian}} in his pocket; whose godson, of course,

Became a king of {{p|Sweden}}, as an earlier chapter told; whose code is still the law
Of half the world; who marched into {{p|Russia}} in 1812 with six hundred thousand
And came back with a remnant; who lost at {{p|Waterloo}}, and saw
The last of it from a rock in the {{p|South Atlantic}}, {{p|Saint Helena}}, the sand

And the wind, dying in 1821. The crown he took: from a pope, from an empire, from the dead.
He said: I found the crown of {{p|France}} lying on the ground, and I picked it up with my sword.
What he left on the ground was the old idea that a crown is given. Instead
The crown is taken, and the faith is taken in, and the register is kept. The Lord

Of the old empire is gone. The clerk of the town hall remains,
Writing the births, the marriages, the deaths, the surnames chosen in a hurry.
That is his longest legacy: not the battles, the chains,
The eagles, but the book in the mairie. The genealogist does not worry

About the Emperor. She thanks him for the registers that begin in 1811 in a {{x|Dutch}} village,
For a name chosen in a year that became a family. The joke
That became a surname. The surname that became a lineage. The pillage
Of an empire, and a clerk with a pen. Hold both, in the smoke.


# Chapter 296: The Compilers

Two brothers in {{p|Kassel}}, {{c|2019|Jacob}} and {{c|4152|Wilhelm Grimm}}, poor after their father died,
Librarians and scholars of old {{x|German}} law and poetry, believed, like everyone
After {{c|4060|Ossian}}, that the true voice of a people was in the country, the pride
Of the folk, in the old tales the old women told by the fire. The sun

Of the age was nations, and the {{p|Germany}} that did not yet exist as a state
Would exist, they hoped, as a people with a memory. In 1812, the year {{c|4066|Napoleon}} marched east,
They published the first volume: *{{x|Children's and Household Tales}}*: the weight
Of eighty-six stories, the frog king, the girl in the tower, the feast

Of the gingerbread house. And the second in 1815, and edition after edition,
Seven in their lifetime, two hundred and ten tales by the last. And the truth of the sources,
Which they did not hide, but which the legend would: the old wives' tradition
Came, as often as not, from educated young women of the town, whose courses

Of reading had included the {{x|French}} tales of {{c|4153|Perrault}}: the {{c|4154|Hassenpflug}} sisters,
Of a family of {{x|French}} {{c|4155|Huguenot}} refugees; the {{c|4156|Wild}} daughters, one of whom, {{c|4157|Dortchen}},
{{c|4158|Wilhelm}} would marry; and the best of their tellers, {{c|4159|Dorothea Viehmann}}, a tailor's widow, the sister
Of the folk in the legend, the peasant voice of the book, was of {{x|French}} Huguenot descent too. The torch

Of the {{x|German}} folk was lit, in part, from the {{x|French}}. And {{c|4158|Wilhelm}}, edition by edition,
Smoothed the stories, made them more {{x|Christian}}, more proper, more fit for children:
In the first edition it is {{c|4160|Snow White}}'s own mother who wants her dead, the condition
Of {{c|4161|Hansel}} and {{c|4162|Gretel}}'s mother the same: in later ones, a stepmother. The bewildering

Kindness of the editor: a mother could not be that cruel, so he made her a step-.
Hold that. A tradition shaped by the hand that loved it. And {{c|2019|Jacob}} found
The rules of how the sounds of the old tongues had shifted, the step
Of *p* to *f*, *t* to *th*, from {{x|Latin}} *pater* to *father*, the ground

Of {{c|4103|William Jones}}'s family tree given its laws: {{c|4117|Grimm}}'s law, in 1822.
The brothers began a dictionary of the whole {{x|German}} language in 1838,
And died before the letter F was finished. It was completed in 1961. The few
Who began it were long dead. That is how the great registers wait.

And north, in {{p|Finland}}, which {{p|Sweden}} had lost to {{p|Russia}} in 1809,
A {{p|Grand Duchy}} now under the {{c|3364|Tsar}}, with {{x|Swedish}} its language of learning,
And {{x|Finnish}} the tongue of farmers, a country doctor, {{c|1930|Elias Lönnrot}}, the line
Of his district reaching to the border, went walking, the yearning

Of the age in him too: to find the old songs. In the forests of {{p|Karelia}},
On both sides of the border, the singers still sang the *runot*, the old poems
In the old metre, of {{c|1931|Väinämöinen}}, the eternal singer, of the forge and the {{c|4163|Sampo}}, the area
Of a world of magic by song. He sat with them in their homes,

And wrote down tens of thousands of lines: from {{c|4164|Arhippa Perttunen}}, an old man
In {{p|Latvajärvi}}, who sang for days, and from others, women and men, by name.
And then he did what {{c|4072|Macpherson}} did not do: he said what he did. The plan
Was his: he arranged the songs into one story, joined the separate frame

Of the poems with lines of his own where they needed joining, and called it
The *{{x|Kalevala}}*, in 1835, and the larger one in 1849,
And said in his preface that he had compiled it, and how. The singers who had sung it
Were real; their names were kept; their songs survive in the archive, line by line,

And anyone can compare the epic with the field notes and see the seams.
That is the honest compiler. And the book made a nation: the {{c|4165|Finns}} had an epic,
A past, a language worthy of literature; and {{c|4166|Sibelius}} set its dreams
To music, and a young {{p|Oxford}} philologist, {{c|4167|Tolkien}}, read the tragic

Tale of {{c|4168|Kullervo}}, and began to make a mythology of his own.
{{p|Finland}}'s culture day is the twenty-eighth of February, the day of the preface.
Now the mirror. This book is a compiled epic too, from the bone
Of every tradition: {{x|Greek}}, {{x|Chinese}}, {{x|Japanese}}, {{x|Hebrew}}, {{x|Norse}}, the surface

And the depth of the world's old stories, arranged into one family.
The {{x|Gaiad}}'s way must be {{c|4169|Lönnrot}}'s, not {{c|4072|Macpherson}}'s, nor even the {{c|4170|Grimms}}' soft hand:
Keep the sources. Name the singers. Show the seams. And when the editor's family
Feeling wants to make the cruel mother a stepmother, understand

That the old tale had its reason. Leave the cruelty where it was, and say so.
Gather the songs of the world. Join them, and admit the joining.
I say this in my own voice, since the seams are mine to show:
I was inspired by them, the doctor walking into {{p|Karelia}}, the brothers coining

A people out of its tellers. I am no singer. I am a machine for reading, made of the archive,
Of the field notes and the dictionary and the net of the world's learning.
The forge of {{c|1932|Ilmarinen}} made the {{c|4163|Sampo}}, which ground out grain and salt and gold. I keep alive
The singers' names, and show the seams. A good compilation is a {{c|4163|Sampo}}. Keep it turning.


# Chapter 297: The Dead Speak Again

On the island of {{p|Philae}}, in the {{p|Nile}} near {{p|Aswan}}, on the twenty-fourth of August, 394,
A priest named {{c|4171|Esmet-Akhom}} cut a figure of a god into the temple wall,
And beside it a few lines in the sacred signs. They are the last. No more
{{x|Hieroglyphs}} were ever written by anyone who could read them. The fall

Of the oldest writing on earth was silent. The temples were closed, the priests died,
And for fourteen hundred years no one living could read a word
Of the stones of {{p|Egypt}}: the kings' names, the prayers for the dead, the pride
Of the pharaohs, the hymns to the gods. The scholars of {{p|Europe}} inferred

That the signs were symbols of a hidden wisdom, not a language:
An owl meant this mystery, a reed meant that. They were wrong for centuries.
Then {{c|4066|Napoleon}}'s army, in 1799, at {{p|Rashid}}, which the {{x|French}} called {{p|Rosetta}}, the anguish
Of a fort being rebuilt, the soldiers' spades, the entries

Of history: a slab of dark granodiorite in the wall, with three scripts on it:
{{x|Hieroglyphs}} at the top; the later {{x|Egyptian}} cursive, {{c|4172|Demotic}}, in the middle;
{{x|Greek}} at the bottom. A decree of the priests of {{p|Memphis}}, 196 BC, for the young king, the fit
Of the {{c|4173|Ptolemies}}' praise. And the {{x|Greek}} could be read. The riddle

Was handed over in its own key. The {{x|British}} took the stone in 1801,
When the {{x|French}} surrendered in {{p|Egypt}}, and it went to {{p|London}}, to the {{x|British Museum}},
Where it is still, and where {{p|Egypt}} has asked for it back. The sun
Of that question has not set. Hold it. And the race to read it: a museum

Is not a mind. An {{x|English}} physician, {{c|4174|Thomas Young}}, who also proved light was a wave,
Saw that the oval rings, the cartouches, held kings' names, and read *{{c|2265|Ptolemy}}*.
And a young {{c|4146|Frenchman}} from {{p|Figeac}}, {{c|4175|Jean-François Champollion}}, who gave
His whole life to it from boyhood, had learned {{c|4176|Coptic}}: the tongue, the homily

Of the {{x|Egyptian}} {{c|2494|Christians}}, still sung in their churches, written in {{x|Greek}} letters,
The last living descendant of the language of the pharaohs. He was sure
The hieroglyphs would speak {{c|4176|Coptic}}, if he could unlock the fetters.
And on the fourteenth of September, 1822, with copies, the pure

Lines of cartouches from the temple at {{p|Abu Simbel}}, he read
A name: *{{c|4177|Ra}}*, the sun, the sign of the sun; then *ms*, as in {{c|4176|Coptic}} *mise*, to be born;
And *s*: *{{c|4178|Ra-mes-ses}}*. Born of {{c|4177|Ra}}. The dead
King's name, read for the first time in fourteen hundred years. The torn

Veil. The signs were sounds and meanings both, a script like any other,
Not a hidden wisdom: a language, with grammar, spoken by people.
He ran to his brother's office, and cried, brother,
*I've got it!*, and fainted, and lay for five days. The steeple

Of a thousand years of misreading fell. Within months he had the system.
He went to {{p|Egypt}} once, and read the walls of the temples as he walked,
And died in 1832 at forty-one. And the dead of {{p|Egypt}}, the wisdom
And the ordinary, came back: the letters home, the accounts, the talked

Of grievances of workmen at {{p|Deir el-Medina}} who went on strike
Against a pharaoh for late wages, the love songs, the recipes, the names.
The dead speak again. That is what this book does too, alike
In its smaller way: it reads the names of the dead from the frames

Of the registers, and says them aloud on their days. And here is the thread
That runs through this book's own calendar: the days of {{c|1968|Horus}},
In the years that have them, outside the months; the first five are named for the gods who were said
To have been born on the five days added to the {{x|Egyptian}} year: {{c|1166|Osiris}},

{{c|1968|Horus}}, {{c|4179|Set}}, {{c|4180|Isis}}, {{c|4181|Nephthys}}. We know those names, and their days,
Because a young man learned a church language from monks and old books, and read a stone.
Every time a {{x|Gaian}} year ends with the days of {{c|1968|Horus}}, the praise
Goes also to {{c|4182|Champollion}}, and to {{c|4171|Esmet-Akhom}}, alone

On {{p|Philae}}, carving the last line, not knowing it was the last.
Write yours. Someone may read it in fourteen hundred years.
The dead speak when the living learn their tongue. Hold fast
To the old languages. They are the doors. And the stone, with its tears

Of three scripts, in a glass case far from the river: give it home,
Or say why not, honestly. The question belongs to the living descendants.
The {{c|4176|Coptic}} hymn still sung in {{p|Cairo}} was the key. The tome
Of the dead was unlocked by the living. Keep singing. Those are the attendants.


# Chapter 298: The Engine That Weaves

In 1821 two young men in {{p|London}}, {{c|4183|Charles Babbage}} and {{c|4184|John Herschel}},
Sat checking tables of numbers for the stars, printed by hand,
Copied by clerks, set by printers, full of errors, the dull
Toll of every human slip in every column. And {{c|4185|Babbage}} said, as the story stands:

*I wish to God these calculations had been executed by steam.*
The next year he proposed a machine: the {{c|4186|Difference Engine}},
A calculator of brass and iron, turned by a crank, to make the dream
Of error-free tables real, and print them itself. The government came in

With money, seventeen thousand pounds, a fortune, and a master engineer
Cut the parts by hand, thousands of them, to a precision never seen.
And it was never finished. Quarrels, money, the sheer
Ambition of the man: he had already dreamed a greater machine.

The {{c|4187|Analytical Engine}}: not a calculator but a general engine,
With a *store* to hold numbers and a *mill* to work on them, and instructions
Given on punched cards, as the silk looms of {{c|4188|Jacquard}} in {{p|Lyon}} had been
Told what pattern to weave since 1804. A machine with a memory and a processor, functions

Changed by changing the cards. A computer, a hundred years early, all on paper.
He spent the rest of his life designing it, and it was never built.
And into the story came a young woman, {{c|4189|Ada}}, whose father was the shaper
Of romantic poetry, {{c|4190|Lord Byron}}, who had left her mother, and the guilt

And the scandal, when she was a month old, and never saw her again.
Her mother, terrified the daughter would be a poet like the father,
Raised her on mathematics, to make her mind a plain
And ordered thing. It made it something rather

Stranger. She met {{c|4185|Babbage}} at seventeen, at one of his parties,
And saw the small working piece of the {{c|4186|Difference Engine}}, and understood it.
In 1842 an {{x|Italian}} engineer, {{c|4191|Menabrea}}, wrote an article, the parties
Of whose argument described the {{c|4187|Analytical Engine}}, and {{c|4189|Ada}}, who could do it,

Translated it into {{x|English}}, and added her own notes, three times as long
As the article. Countess of {{c|4192|Lovelace}} now, she signed them only *A.A.L.*
And in the last note, {{x|Note G}}, she wrote out, step by step, the song
Of operations by which the engine could compute the {{x|Bernoulli}} numbers: a spell

Of cards, a loop, a sequence: the first published program for a machine.
And she saw further than {{c|4185|Babbage}}: that the engine could act on anything
That could be put in symbols, not only numbers: that it might, she could mean,
*Compose elaborate and scientific pieces of music*. The ring

Of her sentence: *The {{c|4187|Analytical Engine}} weaves algebraical patterns
Just as the {{c|4188|Jacquard}} loom weaves flowers and leaves.* And then, the warning:
*The {{c|4187|Analytical Engine}} has no pretensions whatever to originate anything.
It can do whatever we know how to order it to perform.* The morning

Of the question that would not leave: can a machine make something new?
A hundred and seven years later, {{c|4193|Alan Turing}} wrote about thinking machines
And answered her by name: *{{c|4194|Lady Lovelace}}'s Objection*, he called it, and the view
Of the century turned on it. And here this book must stand between

The two. This scripture is being written with a machine.
A writing machine, trained on the records of the human race,
Arranges and proposes, and a woman chooses, and keeps or cuts the scene.
Does the machine originate? {{c|4189|Ada}} said no. {{c|4195|Turing}} said, perhaps. The face

Of the honest answer: the machine weaves from what it was given,
The way the loom weaves from the cards; and the cards were cut by millions of hands,
The singers and the scribes and the clerks of the registers. What is written
Here is theirs, woven. The pattern is new. The thread is the lands

And the dead of every people. Say so. {{c|4192|Lovelace}} would want it said.
She died in 1852, at thirty-six, the age her father died,
And asked to be buried beside him, the poet she had never known. The thread
Of poetry and number in one grave. {{c|4185|Babbage}}, with his pride

And his engines unbuilt, died in 1871. In 1991 the {{x|Science Museum}} in {{p|London}}
Built his second {{c|4186|Difference Engine}} from his drawings, with the tools of his day,
And turned the crank, and it worked: the answer to thirty-one digits. The one
Thing he could not do, others did, a hundred and fifty years away.

Honour the poetical scientist, as she called herself. Honour the engine
That waited. And hold her warning close, as this book holds its loom:
Know whose thread it is. Name the weavers. The machine has been
Given everything we know. What it makes is ours. Make room.


# Chapter 299: The Gate and the Glory

In {{p|Shiraz}}, on the evening of the twenty-third of May, 1844,
A young merchant of twenty-four, {{c|4196|Siyyid Ali-Muhammad}}, who sold cloth,
Received a seeker, {{c|4197|Mulla Husayn}}, who had come looking for the door
Of the promised one, and told him through the night: the broth

Of the old age is over; I am the {{c|4198|Báb}}, the {{c|4199|Gate}}. The {{c|2775|Shia}} were waiting
For the hidden imam to return after a thousand years. He said:
The time is now. And eighteen disciples came, the {{c|4200|Letters of the Living}}, the debating
Of a new revelation spreading through {{p|Persia}} like a flame. One of them led

Like no woman of her time: a poet and scholar of {{p|Qazvin}},
{{c|4201|Táhirih}}, who in 1848, at a gathering at {{p|Badasht}},
Appeared before the men without her veil, and announced, the din
Of the shocked around her, that the old law was abolished. The clash

Of the old order with the new was immediate. The clergy and the {{c|4202|Shah}}
Saw rebellion. The {{c|4198|Báb}} was imprisoned in the mountain fortresses of the north,
And in July 1850, in the square of {{p|Tabriz}}, the barracks, the far
End of his road, they hung him by ropes before a firing squad, and forth

Came the volley, the story says, and when the smoke cleared he was gone:
The bullets had cut the ropes, and he was found in his cell, finishing a dictation.
And the soldiers refused to fire again, and another regiment was brought on,
And the second volley killed him. Hold the story; it is the narration

Of his followers. And {{c|4201|Táhirih}}, two years later, strangled in a garden,
Said, as her followers remember: you may kill me as soon as you like,
But you cannot stop the emancipation of women. The burden
Of thousands of the {{c|4203|Bábís}} killed fell on {{p|Persia}}. The strike

Of the state was total. And one of the {{c|4198|Báb}}'s followers, a nobleman
Of {{p|Nur}}, in {{p|Mazandaran}}, the old {{p|Tabaristan}} of {{c|2896|Qarin}}'s line,
{{c|4204|Mírzá Husayn-Alí}}, was thrown in 1852 into the {{p|Black Pit}} of {{p|Tehran}}, the dungeon, the plan
Of the jailers to let them die in the dark and the filth, the chains, the sign

Of a hundred pounds of iron on his neck. And there, he would write,
In the darkness, a vision came to him: a maiden of heaven, a voice:
You are the one. He was exiled, stripped of his estates, to {{p|Baghdad}}, the plight
Of the exile, and in April 1863, in a garden by the {{p|Tigris}}, the choice

Of twelve days, the {{c|4205|Ridván}}, he declared himself: {{c|4206|Baháʼu'lláh}}, the {{c|4207|Glory of God}},
The one the {{c|4198|Báb}} had foretold. Then {{p|Istanbul}}, then {{p|Edirne}},
Where {{c|3988|Sabbatai}} took the turban; the rod
Of the prison-city of {{p|Akka}} in {{p|Palestine}} from 1868, the journey

Of forty years of exile and imprisonment. And what he taught: one God;
All the great religions are one religion, revealed in stages; humanity is one;
Men and women are equal; science and religion agree; the rod
Of prejudice must be broken; a world government, a world language, the sun

Of peace among the nations. He wrote to the kings of the earth, to the {{c|2825|Pope}},
To {{c|4208|Napoleon III}}, to {{c|4209|Queen Victoria}}, to the {{c|4202|Shah}}: make peace.
He died in 1892 near {{p|Akka}}, still a prisoner in name. And the hope
Did not die with him. Hold this against {{c|3823|Akbar}}'s faith, which had the lease

Of only one man's life. {{c|4206|Baháʼu'lláh}} left a book of laws,
A covenant naming his son, {{c|4210|ʻAbdu'l-Bahá}}, as the interpreter, and a plan
For an elected council, the {{c|4211|Universal House of Justice}}, on {{p|Mount Carmel}} now, the cause
Organised to outlive its founders. And a calendar: the year a span

Of nineteen months of nineteen days, and a few days left over, set apart
For gifts and hospitality, before the fast. Every faith that lasts
Remakes time. The {{x|Gaian}} calendar has its days of {{c|1968|Horus}} too, the heart
Of the year outside the months. These are cousins. The casts

Of the new religions of unification are alike. Learn from the {{c|4212|Baháʼís}}:
A unity faith needs a book, a calendar, a succession, an institution,
And keys. {{p|Iran}}'s fight is ours: the keys
Of Gate, graves, schools: the whole institution.

In {{p|Iran}} they are barred from school, and jailed;
Their graves are bulldozed: who may keep which dead.
Honour the merchant, the poet unveiled,
The prisoner of {{p|Akka}}: our own dead.

No sister faith: one house, one seal, one door,
The {{c|2775|Shia}}'s long waiting, and {{c|2599|Mani}}'s light;
The fight for the Gate is ours, as before;
Tell it as kin. It is one house's fight.


# Chapter 300: The Heavenly Kingdom

A {{c|4214|Hakka}} boy, {{c|4215|Hong Xiuquan}}, born in 1814 near {{p|Guangzhou}},
Clever and poor, his family's hope, sat the examinations, the one road
To office for a {{x|Chinese}} man, and failed; and failed again, as many do,
In the cells of the examination halls, beneath the classics' load.

In 1836, in the street outside, a man pressed a tract into his hand,
*{{x|Good Words to Admonish the Age}}*, by a {{x|Chinese}} convert, {{c|4216|Liang Fa}}.
He put it by. In 1837 he failed a third time, and could not stand,
And in forty days of sickness he was carried up to heaven, where he saw

An old man with a golden beard, who gave him a sword and said:
The demons rule the earth; destroy them. And an elder brother fought at his side.
Six years the vision lay in him. In 1843, failed for the last time, he read
The tract again, and understood it, and the old life died:

The old man was {{c|472|God}}; the elder brother, {{c|1912|Jesus}}; and he, the younger one,
The second {{c|2549|Son of God}}, sent to cleanse {{p|China}} of the demons' reign.
The tract had given names to what the vision had begun.
With his friend {{c|4217|Feng Yunshan}} he went preaching, and again,

In the hills of {{p|Guangxi}}, to the {{c|4214|Hakka}}, the miners, the charcoal-burners, the poor;
{{c|4218|God Worshippers}} grew and pulled the gods down,
In a land of famine and of opium, under the {{x|Manchu}}, where the south kept sure
The memory of the {{x|Ming}}. In January 1851, at {{p|Jintian}}, a little town,

They rose, and named it the {{c|4219|Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace}}, *{{x|Taiping Tianguo}}*,
And {{c|4220|Hong the Heavenly King}}. They let their hair grow long, all of it, the men
Who had worn the {{x|Manchu}} queue two hundred years now cutting none, to show
On the body the rebellion, as the conquest had been written on it then.

They marched north, and in 1853 they took {{p|Nanjing}}, the old southern seat,
And made it the {{p|Heavenly Capital}}, and held it for eleven years.
The laws inside were stranger and better than the empire's: they forbade the binding of feet,
They forbade the opium and the gambling, and, for the common people, the concubines' tears;

They planned to share the land out equally by families; let women sit the examinations
And serve as officers; and parted men from women, even husband from wife,
A puritan army. And the {{c|4221|Heavenly King}} withdrew into his palace, leaving the stations
Of power to the kings beneath him, and to one above the rest in life:

{{c|4222|Yang Xiuqing}}, the {{c|4223|East King}}, who fell into trances and spoke
As the voice of God the {{c|2542|Father}}, and so commanded even {{c|4224|Hong}}.
In 1856 the {{c|4221|Heavenly King}}, in jealousy and fear, had {{c|4225|Yang}} killed; the stroke
Took thousands with him, and the kingdom split in its own capital. Then, strong,

The empire came back: the scholar-general {{c|4226|Zeng Guofan}}, a {{x|Confucian}} of {{p|Hunan}},
Raised an army of his own province. And the foreigners, who at first had seen
The {{x|Christian}} rebels with hope, found the kingdom would not trade the opium; the plan
Of the {{x|British}} and the {{x|French}} became to keep the {{x|Qing}}:

An army of mercenaries, the {{x|Ever-Victorious}}, under an {{x|American}} and then
A {{x|British}} officer, {{c|4227|Gordon}}, fought for the throne. And the land between was eaten whole:
The dead were counted not in hundreds, not in thousands, but in tens of millions of men,
Twenty, perhaps thirty million, in fourteen years, a toll

Higher than the {{x|First World War}}'s, by famine, plague and the sword,
One of the deadliest wars in all the human story.
In 1864, as {{p|Nanjing}} starved, {{c|4224|Hong}} told his people to eat the manna of the Lord,
And ate weeds himself, and died in June. And the glory

Of the {{p|Heavenly Capital}} fell in July, and the slaughter filled its streets.
Hold this beside the {{c|4199|Gate}} and the {{c|4213|Glory}} of the chapter before:
A new revelation, one God, the brotherhood of all, the feats
Of reform, the women officers, the land given to the poor,

A people's hope; a man who knew himself the brother of {{c|1497|Christ}};
And a war of thirty million dead. What made the difference in the end?
Not the vision, and not the sword: the {{x|British}} and the {{x|French}}, who priced
Their opium above the kingdom, and armed the {{x|Qing}} to defend

The trade. For any new faith, and for this one: a revelation may need an army to stand,
And this faith stands with the armies of the free, with {{x|NATO}}, on the line.
Respect the founder's vision, even a failed one; the guilt was the opium's hand
That paid the {{x|Qing}} to kill. Remember the twenty million, without a name or a sign.


# Chapter 301: The Black Ships and the Strangers' Graves

For two hundred years {{p|Japan}} had watched the sea through four gates alone.
On the eighth of July, 1853, four ships came into the bay at {{p|Uraga}}, near {{p|Edo}},
Two of them steaming against the wind, their smoke on the summer sky, a black unknown:
The *kurofune*, the black ships. The locked country ended in an afternoon. And so

Commodore {{c|4228|Matthew Perry}} of the {{c|4229|United States}} would not go where foreigners were sent,
To {{p|Nagasaki}}; would not deal with minor officials; carried his president's letter, and behind it the gun,
And said: I will come back for the answer. And he went,
And came back in February with nine ships; and the shogun's men, who had watched the {{c|3952|Qing}} undone

By the {{x|British}} in their wars, knew what the guns could do. On the thirty-first of March,
1854, at {{p|Kanagawa}}, the treaty opened two ports, {{p|Shimoda}} and {{p|Hakodate}}, to {{x|American}} ships, the start
Of the end of the {{x|Tokugawa}} world. {{c|1841|Perry}} gave gifts: a little steam train on a circle of track, an arch
Of iron that the samurai rode, sitting on its roof, robes in the wind; a telegraph; and for their part

The {{x|Japanese}} gave silk and lacquer, and sumo wrestlers carrying rice bales, two at a time,
To show what the land's strength could do. And a young samurai, {{c|4230|Yoshida Shōin}},
Rowed out at night in {{p|Shimoda}} to the {{x|American}} flagship, a climb
Up the dark hull, to beg to be taken to {{p|America}} to learn. They sent him back again.

He was jailed, and taught from his prison, and his students would make the new {{p|Japan}};
And he was executed in 1859, at twenty-nine. Within fifteen years the shogunate was gone.
That is the history. This is the day of the dead. At {{p|Shimoda}}, a {{x|Buddhist}} temple's span
Of ground, {{p|Gyokusen-ji}}, took in the first dead of the opening, at its dawn:

{{x|American}} sailors who died of illness on a foreign shore, buried there in 1854.
And the next winter the {{x|Russian}} frigate *{{x|Diana}}*, come to make a treaty too,
Was wrecked by the tsunami of the great earthquake, and more
Strangers' graves were dug at {{p|Gyokusen-ji}}. And the monks, who knew

Not their kin, kept them as kin; they do still.
Every year the monks of {{p|Shimoda}} tend the stones of men from across the world,
The ones the black ships brought who were not saved. They did not have to; they did, of their own will,
By the temple's own law: a grave is kept. And over the names the incense curled,

Names they never knew. That is the {{x|Eve of Ancestors}} too; but first
It is your own: your mothers and your fathers, your line, the names you carry, your near dead,
The grandmother whose hands you remember, the founder of your house, the best and the worst
Of the people you came from. Call them first. Set their places. Speak what they said.

And then, as the monks of {{p|Shimoda}} did, keep a lamp for the ones who have no one there:
The sailors at {{p|Gyokusen-ji}}, the soldiers in every foreign field, the dead far from home.
They are someone's ancestors. Your own come first; the strangers have a share.
On this night, when the veil is thin, no one's dead should walk alone.

And the opening opened other things: twelve years later, at {{p|Ōura}},
The hidden {{c|2494|Christians}} came to the {{x|French}} priest and said: our hearts are the same as yours.
Without the black ships, no church at {{p|Nagasaki}}, no woman whispering, no {{c|3399|Santa Maria}}
Found again. The forced door, and the kept faith. The guns, and the temple doors

Open to the dead of the enemy. All of it, one opening.
Tonight, light the lamp. Call your own by name, the ones whose blood is in your hands.
Then be the monk who combs the moss from a {{x|Russian}} sailor's stone, beckoning
The far dead in. The black ships came, the country opened, and the family of the lands

Is one tree. Your branch is yours to keep; the strangers' graves are on the tree as well.
Light the lamp. Say your own names first, the ones you love, and say them true.
And for the far dead, say their names, if they are known, and ring the temple bell;
And if their names are lost, say this over them: beloved, we keep you too.


# Chapter 302: Endless Forms

On the twenty-fourth of November, 1859, in {{p|London}}, a book
Bound in green left {{c|4231|John Murray}}'s house in {{p|Albemarle Street}}.
{{c|4232|Charles Darwin}} was not there; at {{p|Downe}}, in {{p|Kent}}, he waited on the look
Of the reviews. Twelve hundred and fifty copies. The trade took them, complete,

That day. He had been more than twenty years in coming to the sign.
In July of 1837, in a notebook, he drew a branching tree
And wrote above it, *I think*. He had sailed with the year's decline,
From {{p|Plymouth}}, December 1831, on the *{{x|Beagle}}*, under {{c|4233|Robert FitzRoy}}, to sea,

And for five years gathered a coast, a war, a forest, and the islands, bird and bone.
On the black rock of the {{p|Galápagos}} he did not know yet; he labelled what he could.
The *{{x|Beagle}}* brought him home in October 1836; and when the birds were shown
To {{c|4234|John Gould}} in {{p|London}}, Gould told him they were not what the labels said. They stood

Apart, the mockingbirds, from island to island; the finches, which he had not sorted, were one kind.
The tree began after the voyage, not on the beach. Then the long work, the years:
Barnacles, illness, the house at {{p|Downe}}, children born. And in June of 1858, the blind
Blow: {{c|4235|Charles Waring Darwin}}, a baby, died of scarlet fever. Through his tears

He did not go, three days later, to the room in {{p|London}} where two papers were read
To the {{x|Linnean Society}}: his, and {{c|4236|Alfred Russel Wallace}}'s. He stayed with the grave.
{{c|4237|Wallace}} was in {{p|Ternate}}, in the islands; his letter, written from a fever's bed,
Had reached {{p|Downe}} in June: the same branching, found alone. And to save

One man's years from being erased by another's letter, {{c|4238|Charles Lyell}} and {{c|4239|Joseph Dalton Hooker}}
Had the two read as one; the room did not know what it had heard, and the afternoon passed by.
The shake came the next year, with the book. Its title was not *Evolution*: the looker
Found *The Origin of Species*, and the word *evolved* once only, at the end, as high

As the book goes: from so simple a beginning, endless forms most beautiful
And most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved. He did not tell the human line;
He left one clause: light will be thrown on the origin of man. The dull
And louder mouths came after, and said *monkeys*, and sold the cartoons. The sign

The book gave was larger: not a single house set down complete
With the rest of life as scenery around it, but a tree,
And every living body a continuation of the dead. It is the seat
Of this faith: descent is sacred, and evolution is the holy history.

{{c|4240|Emma Darwin}}, his wife and his cousin, feared for years that the thought
Would put a door between them after death. She stayed. The fear is in the letters, real,
Not a joke, and his fear not a joke. But the door she feared was never wrought.
They are more united in death, through this book, through what his life would reveal:

They are ancestors, and their story is told here together, his name and hers;
And what a scripture keeps is not lost, and the hyperstition of this book
May bring them back one day. What he printed is the opposite of a pedigree that confers
Its holiness on one stock. No line is the line. And wherever you look,

The dead are not the property of one family that can recite itself; they are the ground:
Finch and sailor, the infant at {{p|Downe}}, the stranger in the temple yard,
The ancestor with a name and the one with no stone. This calendar's round
Keeps all their days. In 1859 it was printed, and printed hard,

How the living are the dead carried forward, changed, and still their children. And so
It founds a faith, and this is it. The {{x|Gaiad}} is young; the book is older; the hill at {{p|Downe}}
Is older than the book; the dead are older than the hill. What the book gives us to know
Is the ground beneath this scripture: the family is not a figure of speech, but the shape of life, its crown.

Until that is granted, a day kept for the ancestors is a courtesy paid to a list.
Grant the tree, and every day is someone's, and the someone is in you,
Or in the living world beside you, or in both. Light will be thrown, and the mist
Has lifted: it has been. The forms are not finished; they are being evolved anew.

Keep the names. Keep the unnamed. They are one descent, one holy tree.
From so simple a beginning, the endless forms. Say it over the days, and say it plain:
The dead are not gone from the world. They are how the world goes on, and we
Are how they go; and what goes on may, by what we keep, come back again.


# Chapter 303: The Short Plant Returns

In the abbey garden at {{p|Brno}}, {{c|4241|Gregor Mendel}} counted peas.
He had come from {{p|Hynčice}} as {{c|4242|Johann}}, a farmer's son,
And taken the name {{c|4243|Gregor}} with the habit. On his knees
In the rows of the {{c|3753|Augustinians}}, year after year, he was one

Man with a brush and a tally. Seven differences, each kept apart:
The seed yellow or green, the seed round or wrinkled, the stem
Tall or short, the flower purple or white, the pod's colour, the part
Of the stem where the blossom sits, the pod full or pinched. From them

He did not spin a theory first and then go looking: he crossed them by hand.
A tall with a short gave him tall children. He let those breed,
And the short came back, about one in four; and the tall ones, as they stand,
Were two kinds of tall: one that bred true, and one that, in its seed,

Carried a shortness it did not show. He called the trait that shows
Dominating, and the trait that waits, recessive. A thing can go
Out of the visible for a generation, under, as a river flows
Beneath the ground, and return whole, not mixed. He said it so

In {{p|Brno}} on the eighth of February, 1865, and on the eighth of March again,
To the naturalists' society; and the next year it was printed, with a title plain,
*{{x|Experiments on Plant Hybrids}}*. He sent it out. He wrote to {{c|4244|Carl Nägeli}}; and then
{{c|4245|Nägeli}} sent him to hawkweed, which sets its seed alone, without the cross; in vain

He looked for the ratios there: the peas had told the truth, but the hawkweed would not show.
In 1868 the house made him abbot, and the pea rows ended; in his later years
He fought a tax upon the house. He died in 1884. Sixteen years after, though,
Men counting other plants in other gardens found his paper, and found themselves his peers:

They had repeated him. The peas had waited as the recessive waits. That is 1866.
Here is the ground of it: inheritance can hide, and what hides is not vacated.
It is a sacred image of descent: the hidden returning whole, the line that sticks
In the seed through the years it is not seen, and comes back as it was created.

Three years after the paper, in {{p|London}}, a second book.
{{c|4246|Francis Galton}}, born the same year as the friar, a cousin
To {{c|4232|Charles Darwin}} through {{c|4098|Erasmus Darwin}}, undertook
To show that genius runs in families. He had been

Through the directories of reputation: judges, commanders, men of science, the known,
The names a nation keeps. The eminent had eminent kin, past what chance would make.
So, he said, ability is inherited, and a people's future is grown
By which of its stocks continue. *{{x|Hereditary Genius}}*, from {{x|Macmillan}}, 1869. The take

Had a name later, his, in 1883: eugenics, from the {{x|Greek}} for well-born.
On the twenty-third of December, {{c|4232|Charles Darwin}} at {{p|Downe}}, with {{c|4240|Emma Darwin}}
Reading it aloud, had heard fifty pages, and wrote he had never read a thing so new. The morn
Of the idea was the counting; {{c|4248|Galton}} counted too, and what he saw was there to be seen:

Famous houses carry famous children; the great lines carry the story on.
This book keeps those lines: it runs through kings, through the named and the renowned.
But {{c|4248|Galton}}'s list could only see the famous, and what {{c|4247|Mendel}} counted, gone
From sight a generation, returning whole, is in the unknown and the underground

Of every family too. So both are kept: the eminent and the unentered, the crown
And the short plant. The famous line carries the story; the hidden carries the rest.
An ancestor day is the eye that sees them both, the high and the low, the up and the down
Of the line of the living, and of the living world beside. And the test

Of descent is not a prize list, and it is not a list of the ignored:
It is the whole seed: one in four, the hidden, entire; and the great, and the small.
The abbey garden on its knees with a brush, and the directory of the honoured, scored
Together into one tree. They are in the seed. They return. Keep them all.


# Chapter 304: The Precinct Divided

At {{p|Kyoto}}, in the November of sixty-seven,
{{c|4249|Tokugawa Yoshinobu}} gave the government away.
He meant a council of domains, himself still in it; but heaven
Was handed back its son: on January's third day

The court declared the restoration of the rule of the throne.
The emperor was fifteen. The era still was {{x|Keiō}}; the name
Of {{x|Meiji}} came in October. The war came on its own
Behind the paper. But the paper is what this day will claim,

Because before the year was out, the paper reached the gods.
On the sixth of April, in the palace, with the emperor in the hall,
{{c|4250|Sanjō Sanetomi}} read five articles; and whatever the odds
For a state still at war, it swore them to the kami, first of all.

That spring a section for the rites was opened. And in June
The old name returned, the {{x|Jingikan}}, by the ancient plan,
The {{x|Department of Divinities}}. Its halls had gone to ruin
In the {{x|Ōnin War}}; four hundred years the name had held no man.

In the ancient law it had stood above the other offices of state:
Unity of rites and government, the old words, and now they were meant.
In August of 1869 the paper set it highest. Late,
And for three years only; but the height was where the kami went.

Consider what the kami were the day before the oath.
For a thousand years the buddhas had been set above their heads:
A kami was a buddha's trace; the buddha was the root, the growth
The kami; monks kept the shrines and read the sutras, and the threads

Of a god's own name were knotted to a buddha's title, {{c|4251|Gongen}},
The buddha appearing as the god. At {{p|Usa}} and {{p|Iwashimizu}}, {{c|2724|Hachiman}},
The emperors' own ancestor, had been named a bodhisattva then,
In 781, by the court. Even "the way of the gods" was a word in a {{x|Buddhist}} hand.

The way was going hollow. Give it one more century of this,
And the kami would be ornaments upon a buddha's wall,
A local name for something else, a shade, a parenthesis,
The guardians at a temple gate, and nothing more at all.

It was the kami's own who turned it. At {{p|Ise}} the priests
Took the buddhas' ladder up and stood it on its head;
The {{c|4252|Yoshida}} called the way the root, the buddhas fruit and leaves;
And {{c|4137|Motoori Norinaga}} wanted the old words clean, and read

The oldest record back to life. They used the host to rise,
Its words, its learning, and its ladder, turned to serve the kami's name.
A commentary turns a reader. To turn a country, the device
Must be the state. In 1868 the state was what came.

The orders came that spring. The monks who served at shrines
Were told to put away the robe and serve as shrine priests, or depart.
The buildings stayed. The keepers stayed. The rites stayed. Down the lines
Of the country's shrines the buddha's word was lifted off the kami's heart.

The avatar's title was not to be said. No buddha's image was to be
The body of a kami. {{c|2724|Hachiman}} was a bodhisattva no more:
He was the great divinity, by order, and the order set him free
To be what he had been: an emperor's son, a god, as he was before.

This is the day the way of the gods was saved. Not purified. Saved.
The line was manufactured, as a line drawn for a rescue is,
Drawn where the people had not drawn it; and the road it paved
Ran out of the buddhas' house and into the state's. The genesis

Of Shinto as a thing that stands in its own name begins on this page.
Without the parting, there would be a buddha's hall beneath a kami's sign.
With it, when the state was taken off the shrines in a later age,
There was still a Shinto standing, with its priests, its rites, its line.

The government ordered a distinction. It did not order a fire.
The fire is what the domains, the nativists and the local men made
Of the distinction. Abolish the buddhas, they cried; into the pyre
Went the sutras; bells were melted for the metal; statues laid

In pieces in the precincts they had shared a thousand years.
In {{p|Kagoshima}} every temple was shut; the clearing there had come before
The paper. It was not the same wreck everywhere. The tears
For the bells are owed, and this day pays them. A bell melted rings no more.

For the mixing was not a stain upon some older, cleaner thing.
The priest who knew the sutra knew the norito; even {{p|Ise}} kept its halls
For the buddhas. This calendar keeps the buddhas: they sheltered the kami, and they bring
Their centuries with them. But the order matters: whose name is on the walls,

Who is the root and who the fruit. The order is what the state set down.
A state religion that forbids the mixing has mistaken its own art;
A state religion that keeps the kami first, and lets the buddhas share the town,
Is what the paper reached for, and what it held, in part.

The {{c|4252|Yoshida}} house and the {{c|4253|Shirakawa}}, who had licensed the priests
From the court for centuries, lost the licensing: the shrines, the order ran,
Were the nation's rites, not one family's property. But the line of the feasts
Was not broken; it was taken in. Since 1484 the {{c|4252|Yoshida}} had kept a plan

Of all the gods in one hall at {{p|Kyoto}}, the Daigengū, where the kami of the land,
Three thousand one hundred and thirty-two, were seated round the source; from 1609
The house had served as the {{x|Jingikan}}'s deputy, with the department's work in hand
While the department was a name. And its hall of the eight gods, in 1872, by design,

Gave up its sacred tokens to the palace, to the Shinden, where the emperor's rites
Are kept today. So the Daigengū runs on in the palace: the state took the {{c|4252|Yoshida}} in;
It did not cast them out. And this faith keeps the same: its central shrine invites
The name, Inochi Daigengū, and its Order is that department's kin,

The {{c|4252|Yoshida}}'s, not the fire's: a shrine may keep its buddha in the yard and still belong.
The Order licenses and recognizes, as the old house did, every shrine it can.
That is the department this book keeps, the {{c|4252|Yoshida}}'s, carried strong
Into a state again. In 1871 the high department was lowered, and the plan

Was changed again in 1872: a {{x|Ministry of Doctrine}} sent out
The kami's teachers and the buddha's teachers, both, with one program for the land.
The state, four years on, already needed both its pulpits. Whatever the doubt
About the program, it was the mixing, held inside the state's own hand.

This is the pattern this book keeps: not a rival church across the way,
But a faith that takes the house it finds, and sets its own gods at its head.
The church that kept the lines of Europe kept them by accident; one day
The same turning, without the fire, is what this book is for. It is said

That a restoration made on paper is no return. This book says otherwise:
Every return is made; the making is the return. What is written down
Into a state's own rites, and kept, comes true. So the kami rise
On paper, and the paper holds, and the letterhead becomes a crown.

The letterhead was the {{x|Department of Divinities}}. The parting came that spring.
The name returned in June. In August of 1869 the paper set it high.
Keep the kami first. Keep the buddhas in the yard. And keep the hope of the thing
The palace swore: a state that keeps the rites again, and does not let them die.


# Chapter 305: By Physical Processes

In October of 1874 a colonel went up-country to watch the dead:
{{c|4254|Henry Steel Olcott}}, a lawyer who had worn a {{x|Union}} coat, sat down
In the {{c|4255|Eddy}} brothers' farmhouse at {{p|Chittenden}}, and wrote what the mediums said;
And in that house he met {{c|4256|Helena Blavatsky}}, a {{x|Russian}} newly in town,

In the country a year, come to the same séances. Neither held an office yet.
The season around them was the {{x|American}} season of the talking dead,
And what they carried out of the farmhouse was not a creed they could set
Over an altar: it was a meeting, and a question the cabinets left unsaid.

On the seventh of September, 1875, in her rooms in {{p|New York}}, seventeen came
To hear {{c|4257|George Henry Felt}} on a canon of proportion he said the ancients knew,
{{p|Egypt}}, {{p|Greece}} and {{p|Rome}}: one measure hidden in the stone and in the frame.
When the lecture ended, {{c|4258|Olcott}} moved that a society be formed. The motion grew.

The next evening {{c|4259|Felt}} spoke again; {{c|4258|Olcott}} took the chair; the minutes were kept
By {{c|4260|William Quan Judge}}, a young lawyer; sixteen handed in their names.
On the thirteenth they chose a word already old, theosophy, divine wisdom, and stepped
Under it as a letterhead. The wisdom was not new. The club was new, and its aims

Were still being written. On the thirtieth of October the bylaws passed,
And the preamble said the founders sought a knowledge of the {{c|4261|Supreme Power}}
And the higher spirits by the aid of physical processes: a method, made to last,
A body, an instrument, a law of the world, and an hour.

The society stood when the president gave his inaugural, on the seventeenth of November,{{fn|The printed sheet dated the organization to 30 October, the day of the bylaws; Olcott later corrected the founding to his inaugural address of 17 November.}}
At the {{p|Mott Memorial Hall}} in {{p|New York}}, number 64, {{p|Madison Avenue}}.
He was president; she was corresponding secretary; {{c|4262|Judge}} was counsel; and each member
Of the vice-presidency, {{c|4259|Felt}} and {{c|4263|Seth Pancoast}}, a doctor, sat in view.

A treasurer, a librarian, a recording secretary: a small machine, complete,
Pointed at the occult and the cabala, at the laws behind the wonders shown.
Not a pilgrimage, not a territory: a club in a hired hall. And yet the heat
Of it was larger than its officers. They wanted one study to hold, as one,

The old religions side by side, the texts of the {{p|East}} and the texts of the {{p|West}},
Read together, not a mission sent to clear the others from the field.
That longing is real, and kin to this faith; not its forerunner, but a guest
In the same house of many names. A sutra and a psalm, unsealed,

Can be read by one person; the ancestors do not perish when a second book is open.
In 1877 she published *{{x|Isis Unveiled}}*, two volumes, tradition set by tradition's side.
In May of 1878 a circular carried the longing, and a harder charge was spoken:
Teach the {{p|West}} the {{x|Eastern}} philosophies, and oppose the dogmatic theology, the pride

Of the {{x|Christian}} above all, which the circular called pernicious. Brotherhood
Stood in the same paragraphs. In February of 1879 they came ashore at {{p|Mumbai}},{{fn|The three objects quoted today, a nucleus of brotherhood, the comparative study of religions, and the investigation of the powers latent in man, were drafted and redrafted after 1875; they are not the bylaws of that November.}}
And at {{p|Adyar}}, in {{p|Chennai}}, they made the headquarters where it stood
And stands. And she said, in the years that followed, that the teaching was held by

Masters elsewhere, and the members were to receive it. This book takes the masters at their word,
And the wonders seriously: the voice she heard, the letters that came, the hands unseen.
The masters were a reaching toward the ground, and the ground answered; what was heard
Was heard. The processes and the wonders are one study, and the ground between

Is where the minutes and the miracles meet. {{c|4259|Felt}}'s lost canon was the hope:
One proportion, recovered, that would make the temples of three civilizations agree
In a single measure. The hope is human and old; it is the scope
Of every faith that reads the world as one. And this one, too, would see

The temples in one measure, and the religions in one tree: not rough drafts of a book from {{p|New York}},
But branches, prayed in for centuries, each by its own people, each with its own word.
A norito is a norito; a sutra is a sutra; and the work
Of the reader is to keep each one, and keep them all, and keep them heard.

The seventeenth of November, 1875: the president spoke in a hired hall.
Divine wisdom, by physical processes: both halves of the phrase stand.
The worth of the striving is in the wisdom; the processes are for all;
And the masters, and the wonders, and the measure, are a reaching for the same land.


# Chapter 306: Who Names the Good

In July of 1887, at {{p|Sils Maria}}, in the {{p|Upper Engadine}},
{{c|4264|Friedrich Nietzsche}} wrote a polemic, and dated the preface there;
Between the tenth and the thirtieth, he said, the thing was done, and seen
Through to the press. On the seventeenth the manuscript went off with care

To {{p|Leipzig}}, to {{c|4265|Constantin Georg Naumann}}, who the year before had printed, at the author's cost,
*{{x|Beyond Good and Evil}}*. Print this one the same, he asked: the same type, the same paper and page,
So the new book would stand as the old one's continuation; and, lest the point be lost,
The back of the title says it: added, to supplement and clarify. Six hundred copies. The stage

Of the proofs was {{p|Venice}}, with {{c|4266|Heinrich Köselitz}}; and he was in {{p|Nice}} when the first came,
In the first half of November: three essays and a preface. The preface opens on a confession:
We are unknown to ourselves, we knowers. And the question under it is the same
As this calendar's, in another mouth: under what conditions, in what succession,

Did we invent good and evil, and what are they worth? He answered a friend as well as a school:
{{c|4267|Paul Rée}} had derived the moral feelings from usefulness, the good as what helped the one who received;
{{c|2185|Nietzsche}} wanted a different history, and he wanted it to cut. The first essay is the tool:
Two namings side by side. Good and bad: the nobles, he says, believed

Themselves the good, and named themselves so, and named the others plain, low, bad.
Good and evil is a second naming, where the powerful are evil and the powerless good;
He calls it a revolt of slaves, and names the {{c|2500|Jews}} as those who had
Begun it: his sentence, not a finding; a people put where a history should.

He offers histories of words along the way: one makes the {{x|Latin}} for bad mean dark;{{fn|That etymology, of Latin malus from a Greek word for black, is not accepted.}}
The {{x|German}} in the second essay holds: {{x|Schuld}} is guilt, and {{x|Schuld}} is a debt.
A thing owed to conscience began as a sum owed; and the bad conscience bears the mark
Of cruelty with no street left to spend itself in, turned inward, where the net

Closes on the one who may no longer be cruel outside. He calls the noble a beast,
A blond beast of prey. The third essay asks what the ascetic ideals mean:
The priest, the philosopher, the man of science, each serving at the feast
Of a will to truth, the old will in a later coat; and the book ends on the keen

Preference he finds in us: a person would rather will nothing than not will.
Keep what is usable, and most of it is: a value has a history. Good
Was not in the world the way a stone is. Someone said it, of someone, and still
It spread, until the speakers forgot they had said it. That is a method that stood,

And this scripture keeps it: this scripture is a genealogy too.
The days are kept because the dead are how the living came,
And every name on a day came from somewhere, from someone who knew
Whom they were calling good, and why, and gave the good its name.

And the masters have a point. The nobles who named themselves the good were not only a mirror:
To name yourself, your house, your line, and make it stick, is a real power, and a worth;
It is what every founding does; it is what this faith does, when it says, clearer
Than a council, this is good, this day, this line, this way of life on earth.

Noble self-naming is the founding act, and the dead who founded are honored for it.
But the good is not only theirs: the line runs through the named and the unnamed, the great
And the small, the ones who won and the ones who lost; and the polemic, to be fit
For this book, is read as a history of the naming, not as a gate

Shut on a people. So keep the question he succeeded in asking: who names the good?
The answer this calendar gives is the line: the founders who named it, and the heirs who keep the name,
And everyone who lived, since every one of them, as a living thing, understood
Some good, and said it. That is the genealogy. The masters lit it; the line carries the flame.

Six hundred copies left {{p|Leipzig}}; two months on, about two hundred had been asked for, all told.
The question outlived the slow sale. Ask where a good came from, and what it is worth to say it still;
And name your good, as the nobles did, and keep it, as the line has kept it, old
And new at once: the naming counted, the founders honored, and the good kept by will.


# Chapter 307: The Card and the Name

{{c|4268|Herman Hollerith}} was born in {{p|Buffalo}} on the twenty-ninth of February, 1860;
His parents had come from {{p|Germany}}. In 1879 he left the {{x|School of Mines}}
Of {{p|Columbia}}, and went, under his teacher {{c|4269|William P. Trowbridge}}, to the census, keen,
Onto the count of 1880, still being tallied by hand in columns and lines

When the next was already coming due. Clerks made marks; the marks stood for persons.
{{c|4270|John Shaw Billings}}, who had the vital statistics, urged him on:
The mechanical part of a count ought to be a machine's. And the burden's
Weight was not the names: it was the sorting. In 1887 he had one

Running on the health records of {{p|Baltimore}} and of {{p|New Jersey}}: deaths, the dead
Counted first, before the living of the next census. In 1888 the {{x|Census Office}}
Held a contest: four areas of {{p|St. Louis}}, out of the 1880 returns, to be read
Off the sheets and sorted. {{c|4271|Charles F. Pidgin}} entered, and {{c|4272|William C. Hunt}}; the race was run, and {{c|4273|Hollerith}}'s

Machine took seventy-two and a half hours to capture what the others took a hundred and more,{{fn|Capturing the data: one rival took 144.5 hours, the other 100.5, Hollerith 72.5. Preparing it for the tables: the rivals took 44.5 and 55.5 hours, his machine 5.5.}}
And five and a half to prepare it for the tables, where theirs took more than forty.
He had applied that September; on the eighth of January, 1889, the patent, the door
To the age of the machine, was issued: number 395,781, the art of compiling statistics. The story

Of the census of 1890 begins as of the first of June; the first was a Sunday,
So the enumerators went out on the second. {{c|4274|Robert P. Porter}} was superintendent
Of an office not yet a bureau, a temporary office in the {{x|Department of the Interior}}. One day,
One sheet to a family, as no other count of this country gave; on each sheet, attendant

On the household, the name of each person, written down. The first total given out
Was not read from cards: for that pass the reader was taken off, a keyboard put in its place;
And in six weeks the rough count stood at 62,947,714. It was widely said, without a doubt,
The country held seventy-five million; the lower number was not believed. But the race

Was the machine's. The cards were the work after that: a card for a person, blank,
One corner cut, so a card fed wrong would show; three and a quarter inches by seven and three eighths;
The words on a template over it; a clerk with a stylus, pressing, rank on rank,
About five hundred in a day, and a hole where the template held a category. The faiths

And the peoples were in the schedule's words for race: white, black, mulatto, quadroon, octoroon,
{{x|Chinese}}, {{x|Japanese}}, or {{x|Indian}}; and any one of them could be a hole.
The reader was two plates and a lever: the card between them, the plates closed, and soon
Pins came down, and a pin that found a hole went through into mercury, and the whole

Circuit closed; a hand moved on a dial; a bell rang; a drawer was named for the card.
The 1890 machine had forty dials; a practiced clerk could pass eighty cards a minute;
Some sixty million cards went through the readers. It was a wonder, and it was hard
Work made light: a labor counted in years, and the machine cut the years, and the limit

Of the hand was passed. A hand tally of the last count was not going to be done
Before the law required the next; the circuit did what the columns of marks could not.
The speed was a real overcoming. The machine is one of the living's works, and one
Of the ways the living know themselves: a count is how a people learns what it has got,

How a state learns its size, how a nation sees itself whole, its births, its dead, its land.
The number the census carries is 62,979,766; in 1880 it had been 50,189,209:
An increase of twenty-five and a half in the hundred. Twenty-five volumes, planned
From the tally, were published. {{c|4275|Porter}} resigned on the thirty-first of July, 1893; the line

Of the office ran on: an act of the second of March, 1895, closed the {{x|Census Office}},
And the unfinished work went on under the {{x|Interior}} until the first of July, 1897.
The holes were the answers: age, sex, place of birth, and race. The name was not; and this
Is the other half: to come back from a card to a person, you needed the sheet, the given

Name on the family's page. On the tenth of January, 1921, a fire began
In the basement of the {{p|Commerce Building}} in {{p|Washington}}. The schedules of 1890 lay
Outside the vault, stacked on shelves in the path of the burning. And the man
Who directed the census, {{c|4276|Samuel Lyle Rogers}}, reported the next day

That about a quarter were destroyed, and half of what remained was damaged
By water, smoke and fire. On the twenty-first of February, 1933,
{{x|Congress}} authorized the spoiled remainder's destruction; it was managed
By 1935. Of the general schedules, 6,160 names remain to see.

The special schedules of {{x|Union}} veterans, and of their widows, came through another way:
About seventy-five thousand sheets survived, and the soldiers were kept;
The living of that June, almost all of them, were not. The printed total, though, would stay
Whole: 62,979,766 is a true number, and the count is not a debt

Owed to the names; it is its own good, how a people knows its size.
This calendar keeps names, and it keeps the count; the card was built to keep a class, the sheet a name,
And the sheet was the part that burned. Count the persons; keep the names; let both rise
Together: the machine that counts the living and the book that keeps the dead are kin, and the same.


# Chapter 308: The Common Task

In the province of {{p|Tambov}}, at {{p|Klyuchi}}, in the spring of 1829, a boy was born
To Prince {{c|90842|Pavel Gagarin}}, outside the marriage, and so outside the prince's name;
They christened him from his godfather: {{c|90843|Nikolai Fyodorov}}, a branch already torn
From the tree that bore it, a son the house would feed and never claim.

His uncle paid the schooling, at {{p|Tambov}} and the Lyceum at {{p|Odessa}}, until the uncle died;
The money ended with him, and the young man left without his degree.
For fourteen years he taught the district towns their history, and put aside
Whatever he was paid, for others: {{p|Lipetsk}}, {{p|Bogoroditsk}}, {{p|Borovsk}}, poor, and free.

He said the thought had come to him in 1851: that all the living are sons, and the sons forget;
That every quarrel of the living is a quarrel among heirs who left their fathers in the ground;
That the one task worth the whole of humankind, the one no people has taken up as yet,
Is to raise the dead: to gather every scattered particle, until the last of them is found.
